 National foreword
 This document is part of the series of Eurocodes. Eurocodes have reference numbers from EN 1990 to EN 1999 and are regarded as a consistant set of design rules. Eurocodes assume the use of a number of parameters to be determined nationally, denoted Nationally Determined Parameters (NDP), given in a corresponding National Annex (NA). Eurocodes can only be used for the design of structures together with the NDPs applicable in the country where a structure or product is to be used.
 Therefore, this document can only be used as a basis for design of structures or products to be used in Norway together with the NDPs given in the Norwegian NA. This document specifies recommended values for the NDPs, but these cannot be used as replacement for the NDPs.
 NAs are in principle informative. According to § 10-2 of the Technical Regulations to The Planning and Building Act (pbl), it may be assumed that the requirements in The Planning and Building Act and the Technical Regulations are met, provided that methods and execution are in accordance with Norwegian Standard. Use of Eurocodes assumes that the corresponding NA, with the NDPs, is used as basis for the design. Consequently, the NAs shall be considered as normative.
 Information on the Eurocodes is found on www.eurokoder.no.

(1) EN 1993-1-3 gives design requirements for cold-formed thin gauge members and sheeting. It applies to cold-formed steel products made from coated or uncoated thin gauge hot or cold rolled sheet or strip, that have been cold-formed by such processes as cold-rolled forming or press-braking. It may also be used for the design of profiled steel sheeting for composite steel and concrete slabs at the construction stage, see EN 1994. The execution of steel structures made of cold-formed thin gauge members and sheeting is covered in EN 1090.
 NOTE: The rules in this part complement the rules in other parts of EN 1993-1.
 (2) Methods are also given for stressed-skin design using steel sheeting as a structural diaphragm.
 (3) This part does not apply to cold-formed circular and rectangular structural hollow sections supplied to EN 10219, for which reference should be made to EN 1993-1-1 and EN 1993-1-8.
 (4) EN 1993-1-3 gives methods for design by calculation and for design assisted by testing. The methods for design by calculation apply only within stated ranges of material properties and geometrical proportions for which sufficient experience and test evidence is available. These limitations do not apply to design assisted by testing.
 (5) EN 1993-1-3 does not cover load arrangement for testing for loads during execution and maintenance.
 (6) The calculation rules given in this standard are only valid if the tolerances of the cold formed members comply with EN 1090-2

Supplementary to EN 1993-1-1, for the purposes of this Part 1-3 of EN 1993, the following terms and definitions apply:
 1.3.1
 The flat sheet steel material out of which cold-formed sections and profiled sheets are made by cold-forming.
 basic yield strength
 The tensile yield strength of the basic material.
 1.3.3
 Structural behaviour involving in-plane shear in the sheeting.
 1.3.4
 liner tray
 Profiled sheet with large lipped edge stiffeners, suitable for interlocking with adjacent liner trays to form a plane of ribbed sheeting that is capable of supporting a parallel plane of profiled sheeting spanning perpendicular to the span of the liner trays.
 1.3.5
 Restriction of the lateral or rotational movement, or the torsional or warping deformation, of a member or element, that increases its buckling resistance in a similar way to a spring support, but to a lesser extent than a rigid support.
 1.3.6
 relative slenderness
 A normalized non-dimensional slenderness ratio.
 1.3.7
 Restriction of the lateral or rotational movement, or the torsional or warping deformation, of a member or element, that increases its buckling resistance to the same extent as a rigid support.
 1.3.8
 A design method that allows for the contribution made by diaphragm action in the sheeting to the stiffness and strength of a structure.
 A location at which a member is able to transfer forces or moments to a foundation, or to another member or other structural component.
 A target average thickness inclusive zinc and other metallic coating layers when present rolled and defined by the steel supplier (tnom not including organic coatings).
 1.3.11
 A nominal thickness minus zinc and other metallic coating layers (tcor).
 the steel core thickness used in design by calculation according to 1.5.3(6) and 3.2.4.

The provided image is a scanned page (apparently from the European steel-design standard EN 1993-1-3:2006(E)) detailing Section 1.5 “Terminology and conventions for dimensions,” specifically Subsection 1.5.1 “Form of sections.” Its layout and content break down as follows:

1. Header  
   • Top line: “EN 1993-1-3: 2006 (E)” in bold, indicating the standard number and year.  

2. Section Title  
   • “1.5 Terminology and conventions for dimensions” in bold, centered beneath the header.  
   • Sub-heading “1.5.1 Form of sections” immediately underneath, also in bold.  

3. Numbered Paragraphs (1) through (3)  
   1) Describes that cold-formed members and profiled sheets have, within permitted tolerances, a constant nominal thickness over their entire length; they may have a uniform cross section or a tapering cross section.  
   2) States that the cross-sections of these members/sheets essentially consist of plane (flat) elements joined by curved elements.  
   3) Introduces “Typical forms of sections for cold-formed members” and refers to Figure 1.1.  

4. Inline NOTE  
   • Immediately after point (3) is a note in italics: “NOTE: The calculation methods of this Part 1-3 of EN 1993 does not cover all the cases shown in figures 1.1 – 1.2.”  

5. Figure 1.1 – Typical Forms of Sections for Cold-Formed Members  
   The figure is divided into three groups (a), (b) and (c). Each group shows a row of simple outline drawings of cross-section profiles. They are rendered as thin black line-drawings on white background, with minimal shading to indicate built-up plates where relevant.  

   a) Single open sections  
     - A variety of single open profiles:  
       • Equilateral L (angle), unequal L  
       • Channel (C) shapes with straight flanges  
       • Zed sections (straight and with slight curvature at flange edges)  
       • Hat profiles (flat top with inward-turned lips)  
       • A tapered teardrop-like profile  
     All are standalone, single-piece cold-formed shapes.  

   b) Open built-up sections  
     - Illustrates built-up “I” or “H” shapes assembled from two or more cold-formed elements:  
       • Double-channel back-to-back with spacing (shaded to indicate separate plates)  
       • Two channels face-to-face bolted together through a spacer plate  
       • A simple built-up I-section formed by welding/bolting two angles back to back  

   c) Closed built-up sections  
     - Examples of fully closed-section assemblies:  
       • A rectangular hollow section formed by bending a single profiled sheet and joining edges  
       • A larger box-section built from two C-shaped lipped channels facing each other, welded or bolted to form a closed box  

   Under each group heading is a label in italics:  
   - “a) Single open sections”  
   - “b) Open built-up sections”  
   - “c) Closed built-up sections”  

6. Footer / Caption  
   • Below the drawings is the centered caption: “Figure 1.1: Typical forms of sections for cold-formed members.”  

7. Marginalia  
   • Along the left margin (rotated 90°) is small text: “NS-EN 1993-1-3: 2006 + NA : 2015” with a timestamp/date code line “191 / 2025-08-04 12:44” indicating a national annex or editorial insertion.  

Overall, the page combines normative text (defining the geometry and classification of cold-formed steel cross-sections) with illustrative line drawings. The drawings are schematic, lacking dimensions, and intended only to exemplify the general shapes of single-piece and built-up cold-formed steel profiles (open vs. closed). The emphasis is on the variety of plane and curved elements composited to form standard sections used in steel construction.

The image is a black‐and‐white line‐drawing composed of three distinct groups of cold‐formed steel cross‐section profiles, labeled (a), (b) and (c), together illustrating “Examples of cold‐formed members and profiled sheets” (as in figure 1.2 of EN 1993-1-3). All profiles share a uniform nominal thickness and are made up of straight (plane) plate elements connected by curved or folded edges. A dashed pair of orthogonal axes through each shape indicates the principal bending axes (y–y and z–z for symmetric sections, u–u and v–v for asymmetric).  

1. Group (a): Compression members and tension members  
 • Top row (single open and closed built-up):  
 – A simple channel (C-section) with inward‐turned lips at each flange tip.  
 – A rectangular hollow section (RHS) or box, with continuously folded corners, shown as a closed section.  
 – An I-section (two parallel flanges joined by a straight web).  
 – A channel section with one flange folded over to form a deeper lip.  
 – A channel with both flanges turned inward sharply to create a narrow, stiffened lip on each side.  
 – A box-section variant where the flanges are folded back inside the section, producing a thicker closed profile.  

 • Bottom row (built-up open and closed):  
 – A four-armed, symmetric open section resembling two intersecting C-channels oriented at 90°, lips facing outward.  
 – A star-shaped open section formed by six equally spaced “C” or “U” arms radiating from a central node, lips on the ends.  
 – An eight-armed star or multi-lobed closed section, each arm connected in a continuous loop around the circumference.  
 – A square closed built-up section composed of four channel elements folded to form a box with internal seams.  

2. Group (b): Beams and other members subject to bending  
 • Top row (simple open beams):  
 – A shallow channel with flat flanges and small lips.  
 – A deeper U-channel (no lips) with a wider web.  
 – A back-to-back channel assembly making an I-type section with an enlarged web.  
 – A pair of channels joined lip-to-lip to form an X-shape.  
 – A true I-beam profile roll-formed from a single strip with tapered flanges.  

 • Bottom row (built-up and special open beams):  
 – Two channels welded back-to-back (the “Y”-shaped section) with central web intersection.  
 – A double-channel X-section with flanges splayed in opposite directions.  
 – An X-shaped section comprising two U-channels interlocked at mid-web.  
 – A slender, tapered channel assembly forming a high-strength built-up I or H-section with angled flanges.  

3. Group (c): Profiled sheets and liner trays  
 • Left and center columns (corrugated/proﬁled decking):  
 – A series of trapezoidal profiles: regularly spaced ridges and troughs of constant depth, some with minor stiffening ribs along the crest and valley.  
 – Variants with asymmetric corrugations (one side taller than the other), and multi-repeat small troughs between larger ribs.  
 – Profiles showing hooked or interlocking edges for lap-joint assembly (liner trays).  

 • Right column (liner trays and composite decks):  
 – Long span shallow trapezoidal profiles with locking hems at each edge.  
 – Multi-corrugation liners with alternating wide and narrow ribs, small clip-in beads, and integrated stiffening folds designed to act compositely with a concrete or steel deck above.  

Overall, the figure demonstrates the broad variety of cold-formed cross-sections—open or closed, single or built-up, symmetric or asymmetric, with or without stiffening lips—used in compression/tension members, flexural beams, and profiled sheet applications. All sections maintain constant thickness, utilize plane and curved elements, and are referenced about their principal bending axes.

(1) Cold-formed members and profiled sheets have within the permitted tolerances a constant nominal thickness over their entire length and may have either a uniform cross section or a tapering cross section along their length.
 (2) The cross-sections of cold-formed members and profiled sheets essentially comprise a number of plane elements joined by curved elements.
 (3) Typical forms of sections for cold-formed members are shown in figure 1.1.
 NOTE: The calculation methods of this Part 1-3 of EN 1993 does not cover all the cases shown in figures 1.1-1.2.

In some cases the bending axis is imposed by connected structural elements whether the cross-section is symmetric or not.
 (5) Cross-sections of cold-formed members and sheets may either be unstiffened or incorporate longitudinal stiffeners in their webs or flanges, or in both.

The illustration, labeled “Figure 1.3: Typical forms of stiffeners for cold-formed members and sheeting,” is divided into three sub-figures (a, b and c), each showing a different category of local stiffening detail commonly used in thin cold-formed steel sections and sheet panels.  These stylized, black-line cross-section sketches convey the geometry of simple bends, pressed grooves and discrete bolted elements that enhance local stiffness without the need for heavy hot-rolled sections.

1) Sub-figure (a): “Folds and bends”  
   • Two typical bent-thin-strip profiles are shown. Both derive their stiffness from acute bends in the plane of the web or flange:  
     – The upper profile is a single offset bend: the web is bent downward at a small angle, offset horizontally, then returned to its original plane. This creates an “inverted Z” or offset lip that stiffens the main panel.  
     – The lower profile is a simple right-angle fold: a short vertical lip (≈90°) is formed at the edge of the panel. This L-shaped lip increases the local moment of inertia and resists local buckling along the free edge.  

2) Sub-figure (b): “Folded groove and curved groove”  
   • Two in-plane stiffening grooves pressed into the web or flange are shown in single-line form. They reinforce the flat panel by creating a shallow channel section:  
     – To the left, the “folded groove” is shown as a symmetrical, sharp-angled V-shaped indentation pressed into the sheet. Its crisp geometry offers high stiffness gain per unit depth but may concentrate stresses at the corner.  
     – To the right, the “curved groove” is drawn as a smooth, U-shaped pressed channel. The radiused profile is easier to form without inducing high strain, and it smooths out stress concentrations while still adding appreciable flexural rigidity.  

3) Sub-figure (c): “Bolted angle stiffener”  
   • A small hot-formed or cold-formed steel angle is shown attached beneath the sheet or web by a single bolt. The drawing shows the main sheet as a horizontal line, with a perpendicular leg of the angle projecting downward. A dashed vertical line marks the bolt axis, illustrating how the stiffener is located on the neutral axis or offset slightly to tailor section properties. The bolted angle serves as a discrete, secondary member that can be added only where needed, simplifying repair or replacement and avoiding more complex roll-forming dies.

Together, these sketches capture the essence of local and intermediate stiffeners in light-gauge steel construction. Folds and bends (a) are the simplest to roll-form, pressed grooves (b) offer intermediate stiffness gains with minimal section depth, and bolted angles (c) allow designers to add reinforcement exactly where bending or shear demands exceed what the parent section can carry.

The image entitled “Figure 1.4: Typical edge stiffeners” presents three simple line‐drawing cross‐section profiles, each representing a common way to stiffen the free edge of a cold-formed steel flange. All three shapes are rendered as single‐line black outlines on a white background; the long horizontal top edge of each profile corresponds to the flange of a sheet‐metal member, while the vertical and inclined legs indicate folds in the lip. Below is a detailed description of each profile from left to right:

1. Single Edge Fold Stiffener – Right‐Angle Variant  
   - A straight horizontal line representing the flange.  
   - At the far right end of that flange, the sheet is bent through 90°, producing a vertical leg of roughly the same length as the thickness of the flange.  
   - This simple “L-shaped” lip stiffener increases the local bending stiffness and helps prevent out-of-plane buckling at the flange edge.

2. Single Edge Fold Stiffener – Angled Variant  
   - Again, a horizontal flange line.  
   - At the rightmost end, instead of a 90° bend, the sheet is folded downwards at an acute angle of approximately 135° (i.e., about 45° measured from the vertical).  
   - This slanted lip can be easier to form in certain roll-forming processes, and its shallower return still provides a moderate stiffening effect while saving material and reducing tooling complexity.

3. Double Edge Fold Stiffener  
   - The horizontal flange is folded twice in quick succession at its edge.  
   - First, a short vertical down‐turn produces a small downward leg.  
   - Immediately following, a second fold turns the small leg back inward (horizontally) under the main flange, creating a narrow return lip that sits parallel and closely underneath the flange.  
   - This “Z-shaped” or “U-shaped” double‐fold stiffener forms a closed or semi‐closed lip, maximizing local section modulus and providing superior resistance to both local and overall flange buckling.

All three stiffener types are examples of “edge stiffeners” (as contrasted with intermediate stiffeners that would be located away from the sheet edge). In practice, these profiles are formed continuously along the length of a cold-formed member—either by press brakes, roll formers, or specialized folding tooling. The choice among a single-fold right angle, a single-fold slanted lip, or a double-fold return depends on factors such as load demands, manufacturing cost, material yield strength, and the desired stiffness‐to‐weight ratio. Typical sheet thicknesses for these stiffeners range from 0.8 mm to 3 mm in light‐gauge steel applications.

By converting a plain flange edge into one of these bent profiles, designers significantly increase the section’s moment of inertia about the weak axis and raise the critical buckling stress of the flange. Figure 1.4 thus encapsulates three of the most common edge-bond stiffening strategies used in cold-formed steel construction and sheet‐metal fabrication.

Figure 1.5 is a black-and-white line drawing, divided into two labelled groups (a) and (b), showing typical intermediate stiffening details for cold-formed steel members. No dimensions are given, but each sketch uses simple continuous lines to represent flanges, webs and attached or pressed-in stiffeners.  

a) Intermediate flange stiffeners  
Four cross-sectional profiles of a flat flange are shown in two rows, illustrating common embossments pressed directly into the flange plate to raise its local bending and buckling resistance:  
• Top left: A single, shallow “U”-shaped dimple formed roughly mid-span of the flange, with gently curved sides blending back into the flat surface.  
• Top right: A narrower, triangular (V-shaped) indentation of similar depth, positioned centrally in the flange.  
• Bottom left: Two identical semi-circular or lobe-shaped corrugations placed side by side, each with smooth curves, giving a small “double-dimple” appearance.  
• Bottom right: A single, more angular corrugation located closer to one end of the flange, its sidewalls meeting at a sharper internal corner before returning to the flat flange line.  

b) Intermediate longitudinal stiffeners  
To the right of the flange-embossment sketches are two views of discrete stiffening sections that would be welded or mechanically fastened along the length of a member:  
• Left sketch: A slender, three-segment profile comprising an inboard vertical leg, an obtuse-angled mid-leg inclined back toward the flange, and an outboard leg parallel to the web. This resembles a shallow “Z” or skewed channel section, rotated out of plane.  
• Right sketch: A mirrored or slightly varied version of the same shape, with similar leg lengths but a different inclination on the central segment.  

Beneath these groups is the caption “Figure 1.5: Typical intermediate longitudinal stiffeners.” Together, subfigure (a) demonstrates inward-pressed flange stiffeners—simple embossments integrated into the member’s cross section—while subfigure (b) shows small, attached open-section profiles that run longitudinally to reinforce either the web or flange against local buckling.

 (2) Longitudinal flange stiffeners may be either edge stiffeners or intermediate stiffeners.
 (3) Typical edge stiffeners are shown in figure 1.4.
 (4) Typical intermediate longitudinal stiffeners are illustrated in figure 1.5.

The illustration depicts a typical cold-formed steel cross-section—often encountered in purlins, girts or trapezoidal sheeting— and annotates its principal overall dimensions.  Viewed in elevation, the section resembles a shallow, offset “Z” with short end “lips.”  Its salient features and the conventions used in measuring them are as follows:

1. Overall Width, b  
   • Shown as a horizontal double-arrow on the top flange, b spans from the outer face of the left vertical leg to the outer face of the right horizontal leg.  
   • In accordance with clause (1), because b is a dimension without a sub- or superscript, it is measured “to the face of the material.”  

2. Overall Height, h  
   • Indicated by a vertical double-arrow along the left side of the section, h runs from the bottom face of the lower flange up to the top face of the upper flange.  
   • Also a face-to-face measurement, consistent with clause (1).  

3. End-Lip Depth, c  
   • The short turned-up lip on the rightmost flange is dimensioned c, again shown by a vertical double-arrow.  
   • Like b and h, this is an external feature measured to the face of the material (no subscript).  

4. Internal Bend Radius, r  
   • An arrow points into the inside corner where the top flange meets the vertical web.  
   • r denotes the internal bend radius, measured from the intersection of the flange and web centerlines to the inner surface, per usual cold-forming practice.  

5. Web and Flange Arrangement  
   • Starting at the top left: a horizontal flange of width b transitions through an inside corner (radius r) into a long, vertical web (height h).  
   • At the bottom of that web, a short horizontal flange “steps” outward, then immediately through a small inside bend forms a very short return lip (un-dimensioned here).  
   • The profile then “steps” up into another vertical segment and terminates in the right-hand flange (depth c), shown horizontally in the sketch.  

Measurement Conventions (from provided context)  
   – Dimensions denoted by symbols without subscripts (b, h, c, r) are face-to-face external measures.  
   – If additional cross-sectional metrics were shown (e.g. bd, hw, sw), they would be taken to the midline of the material or to corner midpoints as per clause (2).  
   – Web and flange developed lengths—were they to include stiffeners—would follow the midline (clauses (4) and (5)).  
   – The material thickness t (not shown) would be the design core thickness less any tolerance (clause (6)).  

Overall, figure 1.6 succinctly captures how to identify and measure the key external dimensions of a cold-formed section, ensuring consistency in specification, fabrication and quality control.

(1) Overall dimensions of cold-formed members and sheeting, including overall width b, overall height h, internal bend radius r and other external dimensions denoted by symbols without subscripts, such as a, c or d, are measured to the face of the material, unless stated otherwise, as illustrated in figure 1.6.
 (2) Unless stated otherwise, the other cross-sectional dimensions of cold-formed members and sheeting, denoted by symbols with subscripts, such as bd, hw or sw, are measured either to the midline of the material or the midpoint of the corner.
 (3) In the case of sloping elements, such as webs of trapezoidal profiled sheets, the slant height s is measured parallel to the slope. The slope is straight line between intersection points of flanges and web.
 (4) The developed height of a web is measured along its midline, including any web stiffeners.
 (5) The developed width of a flange is measured along its midline, including any intermediate stiffeners.
 (6) The thickness t is a steel design thickness (the steel core thickness extracted minus tolerance if needed as specified in clause 3.2.4), if not otherwise stated.

The image presents “Figure 1.7: Axis convention” in two side-by-side schematics of an L-shaped section (a profiled sheet or liner tray corner), each showing the same coordinate-axis layout but with subtly different corner radii. Both drawings are rendered as thick black lines for the profile and thin dashed/dash-dot lines for the axes.

Left schematic  
• Profile geometry: Two straight legs meet at a sharp 90° inside corner. One leg is vertical (extending upward), the other horizontal (extending to the right).  
• Corner: Appears with essentially zero or large, undrawn fillet radius, giving a crisp right-angle intersection.  
• Coordinate axes through the inside corner:  
  – y–y axis (horizontal, dashed line) passes through the corner, oriented parallel to the plane of sheeting.  
  – z–z axis (vertical, dash-dot line) passes through the same point, oriented perpendicular to the plane of sheeting.  
• Oblique axes: Four equally spaced at 45° increments around the corner:  
  – Upper-right diagonal (45° to the z-axis) labeled “u.”  
  – Upper-left diagonal (45° each side of the z-axis but on the opposite side) labeled “v.”  
  – Lower-left diagonal (225° from the positive z direction) labeled “u” (sometimes shown as u′ in related conventions).  
  – Lower-right diagonal (315° from the positive z direction) labeled “v.”  

Right schematic  
• Profile geometry: Identical L-shape orientation (vertical leg up, horizontal leg right), but with a small, rounded internal fillet at the 90° corner.  
• Corner radius: A neat curved arc replaces the sharp intersection, illustrating a more realistic bent profile.  
• Coordinate axes: Exactly the same y–y (dashed horizontal) and z–z (dash-dot vertical) through the geometric corner point (vertex of the arc).  
• Oblique axes: Again four rays at 45° intervals: the upper right is “u,” the upper left “v,” the lower right “v,” and the lower left “u.” They are drawn as thin dash-dot or dashed lines, radiating from the corner center.

Overall conventions illustrated (as referenced to EN 1993 Part 1-1, Figure 1.7):  
1. y–y axis lies in the plane of the profiled sheet or tray.  
2. z–z axis is perpendicular to that sheet plane.  
3. The u and v axes are the two principal oblique directions at ±45° to the z–z axis, used for stiffness, buckling and strength checks in design codes for cold-formed members.

• Each row constitutes a distinct vectorizable “entity” with attributes: product family, standard, grade, f_yb, f_u.

It is divided into five subfigures (a) through (e), each showing a different typical bend or stiffener arrangement and how bp is measured from midlines of adjacent corner elements.

2. Subfigure (b): notional flat width bp of plane parts of flanges

   – Depicts a Z-shaped or rolled Z-section. The central web is inclined through an angle φ between two flanges of full depth h. The slanted web height sw (along its mid-line) equals the notional flat width bp of that web element. Flange tip height hw and overall height h are dimensioned.

Below is a prose description of “Table 5.2: Modelling of elements of a cross-section” suitable for downstream ingestion into a RAG vector store.  It explains, row by row, how individual plate or profile‐elements are represented in a simplified beam/spring‐support model.  References in brackets (e.g. “note (2)”) point back to the contextual notes provided.

1. Title  
   Table 5.2: Modelling of elements of a cross-section (from EN 1993-1-5)  

2. General remarks  
   •    Unless more refined models are adopted (see EN 1993-1-5), each plate or lip in a cold-formed or hot-rolled profile may be idealized by a line‐element with classical beam degrees of freedom.  Boundary conditions (fixed, pinned, spring) account for continuity, partial restraint or free edges.  (note (1))  
   •    When more than one stiffener or lip shares the same bounding plates, mutual stiffness influence must be modeled—typically by introducing multiple springs or a stiffness‐matrix at the node.  (note (2))  
   •    Initial imperfections for flexural and torsional-flexural buckling are taken from EN 1993-1-1, Table 5.1.  (note (3))  
   •    For lateral–torsional buckling, a weak-axis bow e₀ may be assumed (e₀/L = 1/600 for elastic, 1/500 for plastic analyses is recommended in the National Annex) without simultaneous initial twist.  (note (4))  

3. Row-by-row breakdown  

Row 1: Single unstiffened plate (e.g. one flange of a channel or Z-section)  
   – “Type of element” graphic: a single bent plate (horizontal leg with a small inward lip, plus a vertical web).  
   – Simplified model (left column): one end fully fixed (built-in) to adjacent elements, the other end pinned (hinge) with no spring.  
     • This simulates a flange whose one end is continuous into the web (clamped) and whose free end is free to rotate at the lip (hinged).  

Row 2: Single plate with one end partially supported by adjacent elements  
   – “Type of element” graphic: similar plate but at its free end there is a stiffening lip or secondary plate.  
   – Simplified model (right column): one end built-in, the other end supported by both a hinge and a translational spring.  
     • The spring stiffness represents the restraint offered by the small lip or adjoining stiffener (see note (2)).  

Row 3: Plate with multiple stiffeners or lips along the free edge  
   – “Type of element” graphic: a vertical web and two disconnected horizontal lips oriented in different directions.  
   – Simplified model (right column): one end built-in, two discrete spring supports and a hinge at the free edge.  
     • Two springs capture the mutual influence of two lips or stiffeners at the free side (see note (2)).  

Row 4: Plate continuous between two stiffeners (e.g. a flange held between two adjacent plates)  
   – “Type of element” graphic: a single plate whose both ends are connected to adjacent elements (for example the top flange of a box section).  
   – Simplified model (center column): beam with simple supports (pinned at both ends).  
   – Simplified model (right column): similar pinned supports but with one or more springs along the span if intermediate stiffeners are present.  

Row 5: Inclined or skew-connected plate (e.g. a web at an angle)  
   – “Type of element” graphic: two curved connection symbols (representing continuity in the cross-section) joined by an oblique zig-zag line (the inclined plate).  
   – Simplified model (center column): an inclined beam element, pinned at both ends.  
   – Simplified model (right column): pinned supports plus one spring at one end to reflect partial restraint (e.g. out-of-plane restraint from adjoining plates).  

4. How to use this in an analysis workflow  
   – Identify each plate or lip in your cross-section and decide which row of Table 5.2 it most closely resembles.  
   – Assign beam elements with the matching boundary‐condition pattern (fixed/pinned/spring).  
   – If a plate shares edges with multiple stiffeners, include one spring per stiffener node (and consider spring‐stiffness interaction).  
   – Impose initial out-of-straightness imperfections as prescribed in EN 1993-1-1 when running stability checks.  

This structured mapping ensures each physical plate or stiffener in the cross-section is represented by a 1D element with boundary conditions and springs that capture the actual continuity and restraint provided by the adjacent geometry.

(1) Unless more appropriate models are used according to EN 1993-1-5 the elements of a cross-section may be modelled for analysis as indicated in table 5.2.
 (2) The mutual influence of multiple stiffeners should be taken into account.
 (3) Imperfections related to flexural buckling and torsional flexural buckling should be taken from table 5.1 of EN 1993-1-1
 NOTE: See also clause 5.3.4 of EN 1993-1-1.
 (4) For imperfections related to lateral torsional buckling an initial bow imperfections e0 of the weak axis of the profile may be assumed without taking account at the same time an initial twist
 NOTE: The magnitude of the imperfection may be taken from the National Annex. The values e0/L = 1/600 for elastic analysis and e0/L = 1/500 for plastic analysis are recommended for sections assigned to LTB buckling curve a taken from EN 1993-1-1, section 6.3.2.2.

Below is a detailed, stand-alone description of the schematic labeled “Figure 5.3: Flange curling.” It is intended to capture all the key visual and dimensional information needed for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) or vector-store indexing, along with its relationship to the accompanying technical context.

1. Overall View  
   • The drawing presents a transverse cross-section of a cold-formed steel beam or profile, viewed perpendicular to its longitudinal axis.  
   • Only the top half of the section is shown: a single, wide horizontal flange, two inclined webs (one on each side), and two short bottom lips (small horizontal returns).  
   • A straight horizontal line across the middle denotes the neutral axis of the section prior to loading.

2. Main Geometric Features  
   • Top flange: A nearly flat, wide plate section, shown slightly curved inward at its free edges.  
   • Webs: Two identical, symmetrically inclined elements, each running downward from the outboard ends of the top flange.  
   • Bottom lips: Short, outward-facing horizontal segments at the lower ends of each web.

3. Dimensional Call-outs and Annotations  
   • “2 b_s” (double arrow above the top flange): Span of the flange portion projecting from one web to the other, i.e., twice the half-width b_s.  
   • “t” (double arrow at the center of the flange): Thickness of the flange plate.  
   • “δ” (small arrow pointing from the original flat line to the bent curling): Represents the inward deflection or curling of the flange toward the neutral axis. Three equally spaced δ arrows are shown along the top flange, indicating localized inward curvature.  
   • “Z” (vertical dimension at the left side, between the neutral axis line and the underside of the top flange): Distance from the neutral axis to the extreme fiber at the flange (used in stress and curvature calculations).

4. Curling Geometry  
   • The inward curvature (curl) is depicted by a slight concave dip in the top flange; this is the deformation under compressive stresses (or tensile, in an inverted case).  
   • No stiffeners or close transverse elements are drawn; it is the basic form for both straight (Figure 5.3a) and arched (Figure 5.3b) beams prior to loading.

5. Relation to Accompanying Text  
   • δ corresponds to “bending of the flange towards the neutral axis (curling), see figure 5.3.”  
   • b_s matches “one half the distance between webs in box and hat sections, or the width of the portion of flange projecting from the web.”  
   • t is flange thickness.  
   • Z is used to compute the lever arm reduction when curling exceeds 5% of section depth.  
   • The figure supports formulae (5.3a) and (5.3b) for straight and arched beams, respectively, which calculate the magnitude of flange curling under flexural loading, based on mean flange stress σ_a, flange geometry, and curvature radius.

6. Purpose and Usage  
   • Provides a clear visualization of the parameters entering the curling-reduction calculations: width (2 b_s), thickness (t), neutral-axis distance (Z), and curling (δ).  
   • Used to determine whether flange curling remains below the 5 % threshold or requires a correction to predicted loadbearing resistance (lever arm shortening, web bending effects).

The provided artwork is a black-and-white schematic, reproduced under the caption “Figure 5.4: Examples of distortional buckling modes.” It is composed of three side-by-side subfigures—labeled a), b) and c)—each showing a cold-formed steel profile in its undeformed (dashed lines) and buckled (solid lines) configurations. All three are two-dimensional section-view drawings, with the original cross-section envelope sketched in fine dashed strokes and the distorted shape overlaid in a heavier continuous line.

Subfigure a)  
– Geometry: a channel-type section whose back-to-flange web is slightly curved, with two outward-projecting horizontal flanges (each terminating in narrow stiffening lips).  
– Undeformed shape: shown by a light dashed outline that encloses the full depth of web and flanges.  
– Buckled shape: the continuous heavy line shows the web arching outward (toward the free-flange side), while each flange/lip assembly has rotated out of its original plane: the flange tips move out of the dashed envelope, forming a distinct “breathing” mode localized at the web-flange junction.  

Subfigure b)  
– Geometry: very similar to (a)—the same curved-web channel with two horizontal flanges and lips—but the buckling relief is depicted at the opposite flange or oriented slightly differently to illustrate an alternate distortion pattern.  
– Undeformed shape: again via dashed lines outlining the straight-leg channels.  
– Buckled shape: continuous lines reveal the web bulging, but here the flange nearest the viewer tilts more prominently, and the stiffening lip re-curves, suggesting an asymmetric distortional mode. The opposing flange shows almost pure out-of-plane rotation without as much curvature in the lip.  

Subfigure c)  
– Geometry: a shallower U- or hat-profile with inward-inclined flanges. The bottom of the section may include a very slight fillet or rounding (depicted as a gentle arc).  
– Undeformed shape: two inward-sloping flanges and a nearly straight web are outlined in dashes.  
– Buckled shape: heavy lines depict the web bowing slightly, while the flanges kink near mid-span and rotate such that their free edges move toward and slightly past the original envelope. The bottom arc remains largely planar, anchoring the mode there but highlighting the flange distortions.  

Overall, these three sketches illustrate typical distortional buckling behaviors of cold-formed thin-walled members with edge or intermediate stiffeners (cf. EN 1993-1-5). The dashed envelopes serve to emphasize how portions of the cross-section—flange lips, webs or stiffener elements—deflect out of their nominal plane. Subfigures a) and b) show two variant modes for a lipped channel, while c) shows a distinct mode for a more tapered U-shaped profile. These pictorial examples directly support the clauses in section 5.5.3 on how distortional buckling should be identified, analyzed (linear or nonlinear), and accounted for via reduced thickness or effective width procedures in the determination of member resistance and stiffness.

The image is a composite chart and set of three accompanying 3-D line sketches, illustrating how the elastic critical buckling stress of a thin-walled, cold-formed member varies with the half-wave length of the buckling mode.  It is labeled “5.5a: Examples of elastic critical stress for various buckling modes as function of half-wave length and examples of buckling modes.”

1. Chart axes  
  • Horizontal axis: “Halve-wave length” (increasing from left to right).  
  • Vertical axis: “Buckling stress” (increasing from bottom to top).  

2. Three distinct curves on the chart  
  a) Local buckling curve (leftmost, lowest-stress minimum):  
    – At very short half-wave lengths, the critical stress is relatively high but quickly drops to a pronounced minimum.  
    – As the half-wave length lengthens beyond that minimum, the local-buckling stress rises again.  
    – This curve is marked with the label “a) Local buckling.”  
  b) Distortional buckling curve (middle-length region):  
    – Begins at higher stress for very short half-wave lengths, dips to its own minimum at an intermediate half-wave length, then rises again at longer waves.  
    – Its minimum lies at larger half-wave length than the local-buckling minimum, and at a somewhat higher stress.  
    – Identified by the label “b) Distortional buckling.”  
  c) Overall buckling curve (broad, gentle “U-shaped” curve extending to the right):  
    – At very short half-wave lengths, the overall-buckling stress is higher than the distortional mode.  
    – As the half-wave length increases into the member-length region, the curve descends to a comparatively low minimum (governed by flexural or lateral-torsional buckling of the entire section).  
    – Rises again only for extremely long waves, reflecting stiff-member behavior.  
    – This is labeled “c) Overall buckling.”

3. Three 3-D side-view sketches to the right of the curves  
  • Sketch (a): A thin-walled section (e.g. channel or lipped section) with highly localized “wavy” deformations confined to a single flange or web segment.  Arrows at the top indicate the applied axial load.  
  • Sketch (b): The same cross section showing distortional deformation: adjacent elements (flange, web, stiffener lips) move as a group, producing an intermediate-wave shape.  Dashed lines outline the original cross-section geometry, and solid lines show the buckled shape.  
  • Sketch (c): A global flexural or lateral-torsional buckled shape of the entire member, with a single half-wave spanning the nominal member length.  The sketch shows gentle curvature of the whole section.

Overall, the figure demonstrates how a cold-formed member can fail in (1) local buckling of individual elements at short wavelengths, (2) distortional buckling involving flange-lip assembly at intermediate wavelengths, or (3) overall (global) buckling at long wavelengths.  In practice, the governing elastic buckling stress is the lowest of these curves at the relevant half-wave length, and the corresponding mode determines whether local- or distortional-buckling reductions (effective widths or reduced thickness) must be applied per EN 1993-1-5 before calculating ultimate resistance.

The image is a two-axis line chart that schematically illustrates how various elastic buckling loads and corresponding buckling resistances of a cold-formed member change as its unbraced length increases.  Axes:  
• Horizontal axis (abscissa): “Member length,” increasing from left to right.  
• Vertical axis (ordinate): Buckling load (or buckling resistance), increasing upward. No numerical scales are shown—this is purely qualitative.  

Curves and annotations:  
1. Elastic local buckling curves (dashed thin lines)  
   – On the far left (short lengths), a steep dashed curve labeled “Elastic local buckling, one wave” rises rapidly as length decreases.  
   – As member length grows, that curve dips, flattens and then splits into dashed segments labeled “two waves” and “three waves,” indicating that longer plates accommodate more half-waves in their local buckling mode. These curves represent the theoretical elastic buckling stresses for successive local‐buckling half-wave shapes as length increases.  

2. Local buckling resistance (solid thick curve)  
   – A nearly horizontal solid line plotted slightly below the elastic local buckling curves. It undulates very gently to reflect small variations in effective width computations but remains roughly constant over a wide mid-length span.  
   – This line indicates the design buckling resistance after accounting for local buckling using effective widths per EN 1993-1-5, based on yield strength fyb.  

3. Elastic distortional buckling (dashed medium-weight curve)  
   – Starting at shorter lengths to the left, another dashed curve labeled “Elastic distortional buckling” lies above the local buckling resistance. It shows a shallow trough in the mid-length region, illustrating the length at which distortional modes become critical.  

4. Distortional buckling resistance (solid medium-weight curve)  
   – A horizontal solid line drawn just below the elastic distortional buckling curve. This indicates the reduced design resistance once distortional buckling effects have been accounted for—via reduced thickness or effective widths of stiffened elements (edge or intermediate stiffeners) per section 5.5.3 of EN 1993-1-5.  

5. Elastic overall buckling (dashed bold curve)  
   – At longer lengths, a steep dashed curve labeled “Elastic overall buckling” slopes downwards, illustrating the classical Euler-type global buckling load decreasing with increasing unsupported length.  

6. Overall buckling resistance (solid bold curve)  
   – A thick solid curve running below the elastic overall buckling line in the long-length region. It shows the design resistance against overall buckling (flexural, torsional or lateral-torsional per EN 1993-1-1, clause 6.2), based on the effective cross-section determined after accounting for local and distortional buckling.  

7. Interaction and transition zones  
   – A transition point where the solid local buckling resistance curve meets the solid overall buckling resistance curve is annotated “Possible interaction local–global buckling,” indicating that at certain intermediate lengths both modes may interact.  
   – The shift from local to distortional and then to overall buckling dominance is highlighted by the relative positions of the elastic and resistance curves:  
     • For very short spans, local buckling controls both elastic load and resistance.  
     • At moderate lengths, distortional buckling is critical, and its resistance curve sets the design capacity.  
     • Beyond a critical length, overall (global) buckling becomes the governing limit state.  

Contextual linkage to EN 1993-1-5:  
• The local buckling resistance curve is derived using effective widths based on the element’s compressed stress, taking fyb for resistance checks (clause 5.5.2).  
• Serviceability checks (clause 5.5.2(4)) require effective widths based on service‐level compressive stress.  
• Distortional buckling effects for stiffened elements can be simplified via clause 5.5.3 or evaluated by linear/non-linear numerical buckling analysis (clause 5.5.1(7)).  
• The overall buckling resistance is found per clause 6.2, using effective cross-section properties after reductions for local and distortional buckling.  

Overall, the graphic provides a clear qualitative overview of how design buckling resistance is progressively reduced from the elastic buckling loads of local, distortional, and global modes, and how each mode governs over different ranges of member length.

 (3) In determining resistance to local buckling, the yield strength fy should be taken as fyb when calculating effective widths of compressed elements in EN 1993-1-5.

In these cases the effects of distortional buckling should be determined performing linear (see 5.5.1(7)) or non-linear buckling analysis (see EN 1993-1-5) using numerical methods or column stub tests.

Figure 5.6 is a composite, three-part schematic illustrating how to idealize an edge or intermediate stiffener under compression as an equivalent spring whose stiffness per unit length K must be evaluated by applying a unit load u at the stiffener’s effective centroid and measuring its lateral deflection δ.

1. Subfigure (a) “Actual system”  
   – On the left is a slender plate or flange element with a continuous stiffener welded or pressed into its edge. The plate is supported at one end (left) by a built-in or simply supported boundary, while the stiffener projects downward or outward.  
   – A concentrated unit load u per unit length acts vertically at the centroid of the effective stiffener cross-section, located at a distance b₁ from the support.  
   – As a result of u, the stiffener deflects by δ at that centroid and the attached plate segment rotates through an angle θ. The total effective flange width bp is also indicated.  
   – To the right is a mirror image showing an intermediate stiffener attached to both sides of a plane element; here two flange-effective widths b₁ and b₂ (and corresponding parts b₁,e₂, b₂,e₁) are highlighted, and the stiffener ends at each side are locally restrained by rotational springs of stiffness Cθ,₁ and Cθ,₂.

2. Subfigure (b) “Equivalent system”  
   – Each actual stiffener plus plate boundary is reduced to a beam element of length be₂ representing the effective lever arm of the flange, pinned at the plate junction.  
   – A translational spring of stiffness K per unit length, carrying the same unit load u at its top end, resists the deflection δ.  
   – On the right, the intermediate-stiffener case is shown similarly but with two “lever arms” b₁,e₂ and b₂,e₁ feeding into a single spring K.

3. Subfigure (c) “Calculation of δ for C and Z sections”  
   – Three small cross-sectional views show how the unit load u is applied in different practical configurations:  
     a. Compression loading of a lipped C-section: u acts at the stiffened flange tip, causing overall lateral deflection δ.  
     b. Pure bending of a lipped C-section about its weak axis: u is applied on the same flange, producing δ at its tip.  
     c. Compression loading of a Z-section stiffener: here the stiffener projects on one side, and u is applied at its free lip in the opposite sense.  
   – In each case the dashed lines indicate the deflected shape under the same reference load u, and the deflection δ is measured normal to the original flange or stiffener plane.

Overall, Figure 5.6 demonstrates the process of replacing a stiffened plate element by an equivalent spring model: apply a unit strip load at the stiffener centroid, measure the resulting lateral deflection δ, then compute spring stiffness K = u/δ. The right-hand sketches further indicate how to include rotational restraint effects through springs Cθ (e.g. for edge stiffeners on lipped C or Z sections), and how to handle multiple stiffeners by adjusting lever arms b₁, b₂ and effective flange widths be₂. These graphical models underpin the formulae (5.9) through (5.11) and the subsequent distorti­onal buckling reduction factor χd described in the accompanying text.

The illustration (Figure 5.7) shows two generic steel‐plate stiffener cross-sections—(a) a single edge-fold stiffener and (b) a double edge-fold stiffener—together with the key geometric labels used in the calculation of effective widths, areas and buckling resistance.  Both are drawn in longitudinal section, as if “unwrapped” from the web of a beam or plate, with the stiffener projecting from a horizontal plane element and folding back on itself to form one or two vertical legs.

General layout and supports  
• The horizontal plane element (plate) has an overall width “b” and supports the stiffener at one edge. In each case the stiffener is assumed to be simply supported (hinge symbols) at its root on the plane plate.  
• In the magnified detail circle around the fold, the vertical leg of the stiffener is shown restrained by a continuous linear spring of stiffness K per unit length—this models the flexural restraint provided by the connected plane element to distortional buckling of the stiffener.  
• An axis a–a is drawn through the centroidal fold line; this is the axis about which the second moment of area Is of the effective stiffener section is taken when evaluating the elastic buckling stress σcr,s.

Key dimensions and effective portions  
1. Overall widths  
   – b: full width of the stiffened plate section (span under consideration).  
   – bp: width of the horizontal plane element immediately adjacent to the stiffener root; this portion may contribute to the effective stiffener cross-section under high compression (see element bp,c defined below).  

2. Effective horizontal parts (shaded)  
   – be1: initial effective width of the flange away from the stiffener root, determined by assuming infinite restraint (K→∞) and a uniform compression σcom,Ed = fyb/γM0.  This width lies between the stiffener root and the first “loss” of compression capacity in the adjacent plate.  
   – be2: analogous effective width measured toward the interior of the structure, again under full restraint.  

3. Effective vertical parts (shaded)  
   – For a single-fold stiffener (a), only one folded leg: the effective portion of the vertical leg is ceff, measured from the fold line a–a downwards.  It is obtained by applying the effective-width reduction factor ρ (clause 5.5.2) to the actual depth bp,c of the plane element connected at the fold.  
   – For a double-fold stiffener (b), there are two folded legs.  Their combined effective heights are ce1 and ce2 (from the two folds) plus deff for the outstand leg.  Each is determined using the appropriate buckling factor kσ (tables 4.1 and 4.2 of EN 1993-1-5) and effective‐width relations (5.13d,e).

4. Aggregated effective cross-section  
   – As = t·(be2 + ceff) for the single edge-fold case  
   – As = t·(be2 + ce1 + ce2 + deff) for the double edge-fold  
   where t is the plate thickness.

Dimensional limits  
• The overall plate slenderness b/t is limited to ≤ 60 for single folds and ≤ 90 for double folds (to remain within the classical plate‐buckling range).  
• The ratio bp,c/bp controls the choice of buckling factor kσ when evaluating ρ for ceff (see clauses 5.13b,c).

Procedure context (referenced in adjacent text)  
– Step 1: assume full rotational restraint (K=∞) and calculate be1, be2, ceff, deff via clause 5.5.2.  
– Step 2: form As and Is about a–a, compute σcr,s from (5.15) or by numerical buckling analysis (5.5.1(7)), then find reduction factor χd for distortional buckling (5.5.3.1(7)).  
– Step 3 (optional): iterate ρ and be’s using σcom,Ed,i = χd·fyb/γM0 until convergence, then adopt reduced thickness tred and reduced area As,red = χd·As (5.17).

Visually, the effective portions are cross-hatched; unsupported parts of the stiffener are left blank. The magnified bubble around the fold focuses on how ceff and bp,c relate to the vertical leg, and the attached spring symbol “K” emphasizes the role of elastic restraint in distortional buckling.

content:
The illustration (labelled “EN 1993-1-3: 2006 (E)” and titled in its caption as “Figure 5.8: Compression resistance of a flange with an edge stiffener”) presents a step-by-step visualization of how to determine the effective cross-section and compressive resistance of a horizontal flange (plane element) reinforced by a vertical edge stiffener under combined elastic restraint and local buckling effects. Six paired sketches (a through f) show side‐views of the gross and evolving effective sections, supports and springs, and how successive iterations refine the stiffener’s effective width and thickness.

1. a) Gross cross-section and boundary conditions  
   - Left figure: a horizontal plate (thickness t) of total width b_p is simply supported at its left end (pin symbol) and carries a concentrated rotational spring (stiffness per unit length C_Θ) at the right end where the stiffener attaches.  
   - Right figure: the vertical stiffener of height c is welded at the plate’s right edge at 90°. This shows the initial “gross” geometry before any reduction for local buckling or effective–width considerations.

2. b) Step 1: Initial effective cross-section assuming full restraint  
   - Left: the flange is split into two effective flange widths: b_e1 adjacent to the pin support (fully effective) and b_e2 adjacent to the stiffener and spring. Both are shaded to indicate they carry the full design compressive stress σ_com,Ed = f_yb/γ_M0.  
   - Right: the stiffener’s corrugated‐shaded portion c_eff (tapered pattern) is its effective width under the assumption of infinite restraint (K → ∞). A coil spring symbol at the weld line denotes the continuous elastic restraint with stiffness K.

3. c) Step 2: Elastic critical buckling stress σ_cr,s for the stiffener  
   - Left: identical to the left of (b), highlighting the portion of flange under full stress.  
   - Right: shows σ_cr,s labelled at the top of the stiffener, indicating the onset of distortional (flexural) buckling. The same c_eff shading is retained; the spring and flange configuration remain as in Step 1.

4. d) Reduced strength χ_d f_yb/γ_M0 for effective area A_s  
   - Left: flange left portion under f_yb/γ_M0.  
   - Right: the stiffener’s shaded portion is now hatched to a reduced height, reflecting that the effective thickness t has been reduced by the buckling reduction factor χ_d (computed from σ_cr,s via clause 5.5.3.1). The label χ_d f_yb/γ_M0 appears at the top.

5. e) Step 3: Iteration of effective widths  
   - Two sketches labelled “Iteration 1” and “Iteration n”:  
     • Flange left side still under full f_yb/γ_M0.  
     • Stiffener right side shows progressively smaller effective width c_eff (iteration 1) and c_eff,n (iteration n), as χ_d is fed back to recalculate the compressive stress σ_com,Ed,i = χ_d f_yb/γ_M0.  
     • Each iteration shows the spring symbol at the weld, the same support condition, and updated shading to reflect the new effective stiffener width.

6. f) Final adopted effective cross-section  
   - Two final sketches side by side:  
     • Left: flange split into b_e1 (unchanged) and the converged flange width b_e2,n (smaller than original b_e2). A reduced thickness t_red is shown at the interface to the stiffener, indicating that the flange element adjacent to the stiffener must also be thinned in proportion to the stiffener’s reduced effective area.  
     • Right: the final stiffener effective width c_eff,n and height c (unchanged) appear with a dashed outline; the nominal thickness has been replaced by t_red = t A_s,red/A_s to represent the reduced effective area A_s,red.

Throughout the figure the following conventions are used:  
• Solid black outlines for gross geometry, thinner lines for elastic supports.  
• Shading (vertical lines) for portions assumed fully effective.  
• Tapered or hatched shading for portions reduced by local buckling (c_eff or c_eff,n).  
• Spring symbols at the flange–stiffener junction to emphasize the continuous elastic restraint.  
• Annotations f_yb/γ_M0, σ_cr,s, χ_d f_yb/γ_M0 mark the stress levels used at each step.  

Together, these sequential diagrams graphically summarize the method set out in clauses 5.5.2–5.5.3 of EN 1993-1-3 for determining the distortional‐buckling‐resistant cross‐section of a flange stiffened edge under compressive loads.

   • Within each plane element, the effective portions that contribute to the stiffener’s area are indicated:  
       – On the left side of the stiffener: b1,e2 (inner portion adjoining the stiffener) and, further out, b1,e1.  
       – On the right side: b2,e1 (inner portion) and b2,e2 (outer portion).  
   • The intermediate stiffener itself is drawn as a U-shaped groove or emboss centered on the middle axis. An arrow spanning the inner faces of its legs is labeled “bs,” denoting the stiffener’s effective width.

   • The overall spans are again b1 (to the left support) and b2 (to the right support), with the effective plane widths bp,1 and bp,2 identified.  
   • Near the stiffener, the inner effective widths b1,e2 (left) and b2,e1 (right) are again marked by double-headed arrows.

   • The axis a–a is drawn at mid-depth through the horizontal flanges. A dashed circle of identical size to the one above encloses the stiffener bend plus adjacent flange strips, again defining As and Is.

sections: 5.5.3 Plane elements with edge or intermediate stiffeners

content:
The image is a multi-part schematic (labelled a–f) illustrating the step-by-step procedure, as described in EN 1993-1-5 clause 5.5.3, for assessing the compression resistance of a plate (flange) incorporating a single intermediate stiffener. Each sub-figure combines simple cross-section sketches, support representations, springs for continuous restraint, and stress‐block symbols (hatched rectangles) to show how loads and effective widths evolve through the calculation.

a) Gross cross-section and boundary conditions  
- On the far left is a small plate element of thickness t, simply supported at its bottom edge, representing one adjacent panel.  
- Next, the central sketch shows the full flange segment: a horizontal plate of thickness t, with an intermediate stiffener (groove or bent lip) projecting downward. Beneath the stiffener is a spring of stiffness K per unit length, modelling the continuous elastic restraint provided by the neighbouring plane elements. The two effective widths b1,e2 (left panel) and b2,e1 (right panel) are indicated by horizontal arrows between the outer supports and the base of the stiffener.  
- On the far right is the other adjacent panel, similarly supported. Above all three, a hatched block marked f_yb / γ_M0 denotes that an assumed uniform compressive stress equal to the design yield stress is applied.

b) Step 1 – initial effective cross section for K = ∞  
- Three cross-section views show the plate–stiffener–plate assembly again, but now the springs are regarded infinitely stiff (full restraint). The upper stress block remains at f_yb / γ_M0. This step uses Clause 5.5.2 to compute initial effective widths b1,e2 and b2,e1 by treating each plane element as doubly supported under that compressive stress.

c) Step 2 – elastic critical stress σ_cr,s  
- The central figure now carries a larger stress block labelled σ_cr,s, the elastic critical buckling stress of the intermediate stiffener plus its adjacent effective portions (area A_s from step 1). The supports (triangles) remain at the plate ends and the spring of stiffness K is reintroduced. This shows how to derive σ_cr,s either from the analytical expression (5.19) or from a numerical first‐order buckling analysis.

d) Reduced strength χ_d f_yb / γ_M0  
- Once σ_cr,s is known, the distortional buckling reduction factor χ_d is obtained (per 5.5.3.1(7)). The three-part sketch is repeated, but the top stress block over the stiffener is now scaled down to χ_d f_yb / γ_M0 while the outer panels still carry f_yb / γ_M0. This represents the reduced compressive stress that the stiffener can sustain.

e) Step 3 (optional iteration)  
- Iteration 1: the assembly is shown as before, with the central spring and supports. The left and right panels remain at f_yb / γ_M0, and the stiffener’s top block is still f_yb / γ_M0 (initial guess).  
- Iteration n: after computing χ_d, 1 from step 2, one recalculates effective widths using a reduced centreline compressive stress σ_com,Ed,i = χ_d f_yb / γ_M0. The central block is updated to χ_d,n f_yb / γ_M0. Iterations continue until χ_d,n converges (χ_d,n ≈ χ_d,(n–1) and χ_d,n ≤ χ_d,(n–1)).

f) Final adoption of effective cross-section  
- The last sketch reinstates the three-element assembly under full f_yb / γ_M0 in the outer panels, but with the intermediate stiffener’s effective widths now labelled b1,e2,n and b2,e1,n. The image shows three schematic side-elevation views (left to right) of the effective cross-sections of trapezoidal profiled metal sheet webs under bending or axial compression. Each diagram is annotated with dimensional labels that identify the various “effective” strip widths (seff,i), stiffener locations and folds (ssa, ssb), overall web depths (ha, hb, etc.), and distances from the effective centroidal axis to the compression and tension edges (ec and et). Below the three figures appears the caption “Figure 5.12: Effective cross-sections of webs of trapezoidal profiled sheets.”

1. Unstiffened Web (left diagram)  
   • A single sloping web element is shown between two horizontal lines that represent the compression flange (top) and the tension flange (bottom).  
   • The total distance from the compression flange to the effective centroidal axis is marked ec; from the centroid to the tension flange is et.  
   • At the top, a small horizontal dimension line with arrowheads and the label “seff,1” marks the width of the effective compression strip adjacent to the compression flange.  
   • At the bottom, a similarly drawn dimension “seff,n” marks the effective tension strip adjacent to the centroidal axis.  
   • The overall sine-like deflected shape of the web foot is indicated by an angle φ measured at the base, illustrating possible rotation at the support.

2. Web with One Intermediate Stiffener (centre diagram)  
   • In addition to the top and bottom effective strips (seff,1 and seff,n), a single intermediate stiffener is affixed to the web.  
   • The stiffener fold width is denoted ssa; its vertical location above the stiffener is ha, and below the fold is hsa. A horizontal projection from the fold to the web (distance a) is also shown.  
   • Two additional effective strip widths—seff,2 immediately adjacent to the compression flange side of the stiffener and seff,3 adjacent to the tension-side web element—are marked.  
   • The total depth to the centroid remains ec, with et unchanged. The base rotation φ is again indicated.

3. Web with Two Intermediate Stiffeners (right diagram)  
   • This view shows two stiffeners spaced along the web: the upper stiffener with fold width ssa at height ha (above its fold) and hsa (below), and the lower stiffener with fold width ssb at height hb and below fold hsb.  
   • Five effective strip widths, seff,1 through seff,5, partition the compression zone around the two stiffeners:  
     – seff,1 at the very top, adjacent to the compression flange  
     – seff,2 between the flange and the first stiffener fold  
     – seff,3 between the first and second stiffener folds  
     – seff,4 just below the second stiffener fold  
     – seff,5 between the second stiffener and the centroidal axis  
   • The final effective tension strip at the centroid is again labeled seff,n.  
   • The overall web depth to the centroid ec and to the tension flange et are shown, and the base rotation φ is annotated.

All three diagrams share a common style—thin solid lines for the sheet profile, arrow-tipped dimension lines for all effective widths and heights, and dashed horizontal line at the effective centroidal axis. The notation corresponds directly to the series of equations and definitions in clauses (1) through (16), where seff,i, ssa, ssb, ec, et, ha, hb, hsa, hsb, a and φ are used to compute reduced effective areas, buckling stresses, rotational restraint coefficients, and ultimately the effective section properties of the web and its stiffeners.

content:
The illustration (Figure 5.13) is divided into two parts.  On the left is a transverse section through trapezoidal profiled sheeting showing the locations and nomenclature of two web stiffeners.  A single trapezoidal corrugation is drawn in bold outline: a horizontal bottom flange, two inclined web-legs rising to a small top flange, then two further inclined legs and a horizontal crest.  Partway down each inclined leg is a small folded lip (the stiffener).  Key dimensional arrows are superimposed:

 • “sₙ or s_w” is drawn from the bottom flange up to the top flange, measured perpendicular to the adjacent web-plane, denoting the overall web depth.  
 • “sₐ” is an arrow on the upper inclined leg from the top flange down to the first stiffener fold, measured normal to that plane.  
 • “s₂” marks the corresponding distance on the lower inclined leg from the bottom flange up to the second stiffener.  
 • A dot is placed on the lower stiffener fold to indicate the reference for “s₁,” an arrow spanning between the two adjacent web-planes across that point.  This distance s₁ enters into the buckling slenderness formula for the stiffener.  

On the right are two greatly enlarged detail sketches of the stiffener cross-section itself:

 1. The upper detail shows the zig-zag bent metal forming the fold.  A dimension line labelled “s_sa” marks the inside width of the folded lip—this is the stiffener fold width used in area and inertia calculations (ssa in the text).  
 2. The lower detail presents the same fold but with an arrow denoted “s_e” (or “s_eff”) drawn perpendicular to the web-plane, illustrating how the effective strip width adjacent to the stiffener is measured.  These effective widths (seff,1, seff,2, etc.) are combined with the fold width to determine the second moment of area Is for each stiffener (see clause 5.5.3.1(7) in the standard).  

Together these graphics define all the geometric parameters—profile height, positions of up to two stiffeners, fold width and effective widths—required to compute the reduced effective areas Asa,red and Asb,red, the elastic critical buckling stresses σcr,sa and σcr,sb, and ultimately the effective cross-sectional properties of trapezoidal profiled sheeting with web stiffeners.

content:
The illustration is a black-and-white line drawing of a trapezoidal profiled metal sheeting section equipped with intermediate stiffeners in both its flanges and its webs. The section is shown in cross-section, symmetric about a vertical centerline. Starting from the top, the profile has a narrow flat crest that is slightly crowned by a small, half-round trough. This top crest carries a single flange stiffener, shown as a short inward bend in the sheet, and is annotated As — the effective cross-sectional area of an intermediate flange stiffener. Just below this top region, two sloping webs descend outward at a moderate incline. On each sloping web there are small inward bends or „lips,“ each representing an intermediate web stiffener. One of these is specifically labelled As­a, denoting the effective cross-sectional area of a web stiffener (or of the stiffener closer to the compression flange if two are present).

A horizontal dashed line across the drawing marks y­eff, the effective neutral axis of the cross-section. From that line, two arrows indicate distances to stiffeners on one slope: s­eff,1 is the vertical distance from y­eff to the first (upper) stiffener in the web or flange, and s­eff,n is the distance from y­eff to the nth (lower) stiffener. On the right side of the drawing, two solid vertical dimension lines span from the same neutral axis up to the top of the section and all the way from bottom to top, respectively. The shorter of these is labelled ec — the effective depth from y­eff to the extreme compression edge — and the longer is labelled hw, the overall height of the profiled sheeting.

At the very bottom of the profile, each sloping web terminates in an outward-facing flange with a small curl or return. These bottom flanges are not explicitly labelled with area or stiffener notation but visually mirror the top flange in shape, albeit without the additional stiffener lips.

Overall, figure 5.14 clearly identifies:

 • The trapezoidal, symmetric profile geometry  
 • Intermediate flange stiffeners (As) at the crest  
 • Intermediate web stiffeners (As­a) along the slopes  
 • The effective neutral axis y­eff  
 • Vertical spacings seff,1 and seff,n from y­eff to stiffeners  
 • Effective depth ec and full section height hw

The image, titled “Figure 6.1: Effective cross-section under compression,” is a two-part line drawing that contrasts (a) the gross cross-section of a cold-formed channel member with (b) its effective cross-section after local and/or distortional buckling reductions have been applied. A pair of orthogonal centerlines (one horizontal, one vertical) marks the principal axes of each section, and small circles at their intersection denote the centroids. Between the two sections a double-headed vertical arrow, labeled eₙ, indicates the shift of the neutral-axis (centroid) when the effective area is substituted for the gross area.

1. Left-hand “Gross cross-section”  
   • Shape: A channel section with a horizontal top flange, two vertical webs, and downward-turned lips at the free edges. The overall profile resembles a squared “C” with short return flanges.  
   • Axes: Dashed lines show the vertical and horizontal centroidal axes; their intersection is marked with a small open circle.  
   • Label: Immediately to the right of the centroid circle is the notation Nₛd, denoting the internal design axial force assumed to act at the gross‐section centroid.  
   • Appearance: All material is rendered as a continuous outline, indicating that no part of this cross-section has been reduced for buckling.

2. Right-hand “Effective cross-section”  
   • Shape: The original channel is “broken up” into the segments that remain effective under compression—typically the more interior portions of the flanges and webs whose width-to-thickness ratios lie below the slenderness limits. The outer stiffened lips and extreme flange edges (most prone to local buckling) have been omitted. The resulting geometry is a collection of four shorter, parallel strips (two at the top, two at the bottom), symmetrically arranged about the horizontal centroidal axis.  
   • Axes: The same dashed centerlines and centroid circle are shown; here the circle corresponds to the centroid of the effective area and is labeled N_Rd, marking the point of action of the design resistance.  
   • Appearance: Only those portions of the original cross-section deemed stable under the applicable λ (relative slenderness) criteria from Section 5.5 are outlined, illustrating how effective area A_eff is derived from the gross area A_g.

3. Centroidal shift (eₙ)  
   • The double arrow between the two sections quantifies the lateral offset between the gross‐section centroid (where Nₛd acts) and the effective‐section centroid (where N_Rd must be assumed).  
   • This shift eₙ arises because the removal of plate elements (due to local or distortional buckling) alters the distribution of area about the axes.

Contextual linkage to design rules:  
  - In accordance with Eurocode provisions, if A_eff < A_g (i.e., the section requires reduction for buckling), the design compression resistance N_Rd,c is calculated via formula (6.2) using A_eff.  
  - If no reduction is needed (A_eff = A_g), N_Rd,c follows formula (6.3) based on the gross area and adjusted yield strengths.  
  - Clause 6.1.9 requires that when A_eff’s centroid does not coincide with the gross centroid, the offset eₙ be accounted for in combined‐stress checks. However, if the shift proves favorable and was evaluated at the basic yield stress (y_bf), it may be neglected under the Eurocode guidelines.  
  - Finally, the internal axial force is conservatively taken at the gross‐section centroid (see bullet (2) in the additional text), though further analysis can reposition it more realistically if a uniform buildup of normal force is shown.

The image is a schematic “resistance‐versus‐slenderness” plot (labelled Figure 6.2) showing how the design bending moment capacity Mₙ,Rd of a prismatic steel cross‐section falls off as its plate elements become more slender (local buckling begins to reduce the effective section modulus).  Along the horizontal axis is a nondimensional slenderness parameter λ̅ₑ₀, running from zero at the left to ever larger values at the right.  The vertical axis is the bending moment resistance (Mₙ,Rk or Mₙ,Rd) expressed in terms of the section modulus times the yield stress, normalized to show three characteristic levels:

  • At the very top is a horizontal plateau at Wₚₗ f_yb (the full plastic modulus times yield stress).  
  • A second, lower plateau at Wₑₗ f_yb (the full elastic section modulus times yield stress).  
  • Beyond that, a gently downward‐sloping curve labeled W_eff f_yb, representing the reduced “effective” section modulus once local buckling starts to cut back the width of plate elements.

A vertical dashed line marks the critical slenderness λ̅ₑ₀ that separates two regimes:

1. Left of λ̅ₑ₀ (low‐slenderness region):  
   – The capacity is first controlled by the plastic section modulus, so Mₙ,Rd = Wₚₗ f_yb (constant).  
   – Just before the vertical line, the curve steps down from Wₚₗ f_yb to Wₑₗ f_yb if there is an intermediate range over which only elastic resistance is mobilized (formula 6.5).

2. At λ̅ₑ₀ and beyond (moderate‐to‐high slenderness):  
   – Local (and possibly distortional) buckling reduces the effective width of flanges/webs.  The bending‐resistance curve follows W_eff f_yb, decaying monotonically as λ̅ₑ₀ increases.

Below the resistance plot are a series of cross‐section “cut‐through” sketches, arranged from left to right in correspondence with increasing slenderness:

• Far left: a fully compact cross‐section (shown as a U- or C-shaped profile) with no hatch—indicating all its plate elements remain fully effective up to the plastic moment.  
• Next: the same section overlaid with solid horizontal hatching across its flanges/web, signifying that under elastic bending it attains the full elastic modulus Wₑₗ before any buckling.  
• At the λ̅ₑ₀ boundary: a triangular (linear) stress‐distribution sketch is superimposed on the section, representing that yielding just begins at the compression edge (elastic distribution) and triggers the transition in the governing formula (from plastic to elastic limit state).  
• To the right of λ̅ₑ₀: an outline of the same profile appears shown in dotted lines (gross section), with only small hatched strips on the flanges/web—these hatched regions depict the remaining “effective” parts of each plate element after local buckling has eliminated the outboard material.  The width of these hatched strips dwindles as slenderness increases, and the overall curve W_eff f_yb slopes downward accordingly.

In summary, Figure 6.2 visualizes:
– A three‐stage bending‐moment capacity law (plastic, elastic, and buckled‐reduced).  
– The governing section modulus in each stage: Wₚₗ, Wₑₗ, and W_eff.  
– The corresponding cross‐section graphics that show full, elastic, and progressively reduced effective widths as slenderness grows.  
This diagram underpins Equations (6.4)–(6.5) in Eurocode 3 (and related commentary) by linking the algebraic formulas directly to the geometric loss of capacity through buckling of individual plate elements.
