content:
Figure 6.4 is divided into two distinct sketches side by side.  On the left is a simplified outline of a trapezoidal or corrugated profiled steel sheet, shown in elevation so that its repeating peaks and troughs run horizontally.  Three full corrugation cycles are drawn in solid lines (peak–valley–peak–valley–peak–valley–peak), and to the right of the third peak a short dashed line indicates that the pattern continues.  Each corrugation has a flat top flange, then slopes down at a constant angle into the trough, rises again at the same slope into the next flat crown, and so on.  The flat crowns are wider than the troughs, so the overall section looks like a succession of “shallow U-shapes” joined by wider flat plates at the tops.

On the right is a vertical schematic of the section’s stress distribution under bending, used to define the effective width bc.  The outer boundary of the cross section is shown as a thin rectangle.  Inside this, the compressed portion (upper zone) is indicated by closely spaced horizontal hatching; the tension portion (lower zone) is indicated by diagonal (45°) hatching.  A single straight diagonal line separates the two hatch patterns, sloping downward from left of center at the top down to the lower right corner: this line marks the transition from a linear stress variation in compression above to a bilinear distribution in tension below.

Two double-headed arrows, one at the top edge of the rectangle and one at the bottom edge, both labelled “bc,” show that the effective width in each zone is measured horizontally between the vertical sides of the section.  In practice, bc is determined by projecting the stress diagram back onto the physical plate width according to a bilinear tension stress law (constant beyond yield in the outer layer, linear from zero at the neutral axis up to yield in an inner layer) and a purely linear compression stress law up to a maximum compressive stress of fyb/γM0.  By assuming ψ = –1 for the stress gradient, clause 5.5.2 of the code gives the same bc for both compression and tension zones in this idealized bilinear/linear case.

content: (1) The effects of shear lag should be taken into account according to EN 1993-1-5.

The table titled “Table 6.1: Shear buckling strength f_bv” summarizes the shear‐buckling strength coefficients to be used in the calculation of Vb,Rd (the design shear resistance of a web) under two different support‐stiffening conditions. It is intended to work together with equation (6.8)  
    Vb,Rd = hb · tw · sin φ · f_bv / γM0  
where all terms are as defined in the standard (hb = clear web height, tw = web thickness, φ = web slope angle, γM0 = partial safety factor).  

1. Column Headings  
- “Web without stiffening at the support”  
- “Web with stiffening at the support”¹  

  ¹ A footnote specifies that “stiffening at the support, such as cleats, is arranged to prevent distortion of the web and designed to resist the support reaction.”  

2. Buckling‐strength regimes  
For each column, three numerical expressions are given. They correspond to three ranges of the relative web slenderness \bar λ_w (see formulas 6.10a and 6.10b):  

a) Compact or stocky webs (lowest slenderness)  
  – Both columns:  
    f_bv = 0.58 · f_yb  
  In this regime the web is stout enough that buckling does not reduce its shear capacity; a constant fraction (0.58) of the web’s yield stress f_yb may be taken.  

b) Intermediate‐slenderness webs  
  – Both columns:  
    f_bv = 0.48 · f_yb / \bar λ_w  
  Here the shear‐buckling strength decreases inversely with relative slenderness. The coefficient (0.48) is the same whether or not the support is stiffened.  

c) High‐slenderness webs (most slender)  
  – Web without support stiffeners:  
    f_bv = 0.67 · f_yb / \bar λ_w²  
  In the absence of stiffening, very slender webs suffer a quadratic drop in shear‐buckling strength.  
  – Web with support stiffeners:  
    f_bv = 0.48 · f_yb / \bar λ_w  
  With stiffeners, even highly slender webs only follow the milder, linear‐inverse reduction.  

3. Relation to slenderness formulas  
The boundary values of \bar λ_w that define the transitions between these regimes are given in clause (6.10a) for unstiffened webs and (6.10b) for webs with longitudinal stiffeners. In essence:  
- Compute \bar λ_w from web height, thickness, material properties E and f_yb, and any stiffener spacing or end conditions.  
- Determine which slenderness range applies.  
- Pick the appropriate f_bv expression from Table 6.1.  
- Insert that f_bv into equation (6.8) to obtain Vb,Rd.  

By packaging the three behavioral regimes—rigid, intermediate, and highly flexible—this table provides a concise lookup for the shear‐buckling strength factor needed in limit‐state design of plate girders or other members whose webs may buckle under shear.

The image is a black-and-white line drawing, labelled “Figure 6.6: Examples of cross-sections with a single web.”  Across the top of the figure are six schematic profiles of thin-walled steel sections, each drawn in elevation (i.e. as if you have cut straight through the member and are looking at its outline).  Beneath each profile is a small, filled triangular arrow pointing upward, with the notation “Rw,Rd” immediately to the right of the arrow.  This arrow marks the point of application (at or near the mid-depth of the web) and the resistance parameter Rw,Rd, i.e. the local transverse resistance of the web.

From left to right, the six profiles are:

 1. A straight C-channel (single open section).  The web is vertical on the left, and the two flanges extend to the right.  Both flanges are unstiffened (no lips), and the corners between web and flange are square or very gently rounded.

 2. A slightly deeper C-channel, again with the web on the left and two flanges projecting to the right, but with a small internal lip or stiffening return at the flange tips (i.e. the flanges are lip-stiffened).  The corner between web and flange appears as a small radius.

 3. A Z-section (sometimes called an S-shape), in which the web is inclined at roughly 45° from the vertical.  The two flanges lie parallel to one another but slanted, forming the characteristic “Z.”  Both flange tips have small return lips.

 4. A back-to-back pair of C-channels, each channel facing inwards so that their webs are separated by a narrow gap at mid-depth.  The two outer flanges extend outward in opposite directions.  Each web carries its own upward arrow (i.e. two arrows in very close proximity), but both are labelled collectively Rw,Rd.

 5. A tighter back-to-back C-channel assembly, where the two channels have been pressed or welded so that their flanges nearly touch, creating a very narrow gap between the webs.  Again, two upward arrows side by side indicate the Rw,Rd resistance on each web.

 6. An I-section (classic I-beam): two flanges directly opposite each other, joined by a single continuous central web.  The web is vertical; the flanges lie horizontal above and below it.  One arrow at mid-depth of the web denotes Rw,Rd.

All six profiles are drawn with uniform line weight, and the flange and web thicknesses are indicated purely by the equal-width lines.  No dimensions or numerical values are given in the sketch itself; its sole purpose is to illustrate the variety of cross-section shapes—unstiffened and stiffened C-sections, Z-sections, back-to-back channels, and I-beams—that qualify as having “a single web” for the purpose of the transverse resistance criteria given in the surrounding text.  The caption underscores that these diverse shapes can all be treated by the same set of formulae (see figures 6.6 and 6.7 in the text).

sections: 6.1.7.2  Cross-sections with a single unstiffened web

content:
The figure (labelled “Figure 6.7b: Local loads and supports — cross-sections with a single web”) comprises two schematic cross-sectional views of an unstiffened single-web beam, together with the design expression for the local transverse resistance Rw,Rd in the case  
ii) where the clear distance c from a free end is greater than 1.5 times the web height hw.

1. Geometry of the cross-section  
  • The beam consists of two parallel flanges connected by a flat web of thickness t.  
  • The distance between flange mid-lines (the web height) is denoted hw.  
  • No additional stiffeners are shown; this is the “single unstiffened web” situation.

2. Top schematic (two opposing local transverse forces)  
  • Two sets of downward‐acting reaction forces (arrows) are applied on the top flange over a bearing length ss.  
  • Corresponding upward support reactions (arrows) act on the bottom flange, directly below the applied load regions.  
  • The clear distance from the free (left) end of the beam to the nearer edge of the loaded bearing is labelled c.  
  • The eccentricity between the centroids of the load and the support reaction is labelled e.  
  • The bearing length of each load or support reaction is ss (measured along the flange width).

3. Bottom schematic (single local load or support reaction)  
  • A single patch of downward load arrows of width ss is applied near the free end (top flange).  
  • An opposing set of upward support arrows of width ss is applied on the bottom flange, at the same longitudinal position.  
  • The distance from the free end to the patch of downward load is again c, and the eccentricity between load and support centroids is e.  
  • In both views, the overall web height hw is indicated by a vertical dimension line between flange mid-lines.

4. Design equation for case ii) (c > 1.5 hw)  
   Rw,Rd  =  k3 · k4 · k5  ·  [ (21.0 − (hw/t) / 16.3) ]  ·  [ 1 + 0.0013 (ss/t) ]  ·  t² · fyb  
            ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
                                    γM1  

   where  
   – t      = web thickness  
   – hw     = distance between flange mid-lines  
   – ss     = bearing length of the local load or support reaction  
   – fyb    = characteristic yield strength of the web material (N/mm²)  
   – γM1    = partial safety factor for material and design  
   – k3, k4, k5 = dimensionless coefficients, defined in the standard as functions of  
       • the web inclination φ (if any)  
       • the ratio r/t (corner radius to thickness)  
       • the ratio k = fyb/228  
     with the following formulae (from the additional text):  
       k3 = 0.70 + 0.30·(φ/90)²  
       k4 = 1.22 − 0.22·k  
       k5 = 1.06 − 0.06·(r/t),  subject to k5 ≤ 1.0  

5. Interpretation  
   • This formula applies when the local transverse load (or support reaction) is applied sufficiently far (c > 1.5 hw) from a free end, so that the web rotation is effectively unrestrained by the free edge.  
   • The bracketed factors capture:  
     – a reduction in resistance as the slenderness hw/t increases (first bracket), and  
     – a small increase due to spreading of the bearing load over a longer length ss (second bracket).  
   • The product t²·fyb gives the basic strength per unit length of web, modified by k-factors and safety factor γM1.  

Together, the diagrams and the equation allow the designer to calculate the local transverse resistance of an unstiffened web to concentrated loads or reactions spaced well inside the span of the beam.

metadata.sections: 6.1.7.2  Cross-sections with a single unstiffened web

content:
The table under review (clause 6.17) defines three geometric criteria that an unstiffened web must satisfy if its local transverse resistance is to be calculated via the simplified expressions in clause 6.18.  These criteria ensure that the web is neither too slender nor too sharply inclined relative to its flanges.  Each row of the table corresponds to one criterion, giving (a) the parameter or ratio being limited, (b) its maximum or allowable range, and (c) the clause reference for the corresponding formula.  In practice, these criteria form a quick “acceptance check” before proceeding to the more detailed bearing‐length calculation in clauses 6.19–6.20.

1. Columns  
   – Parameter (left column): identifies the geometric ratio or angle under consideration.  
   – Limit (middle column): states the numerical bound or range that must not be exceeded (for ratios) or that must be met (for an angle).  
   – Equation reference (right column): directs the reader to the exact sub-clause for that limit (6.17a, 6.17b or 6.17c).

2. Rows (detailed)  
   a. r∕t ≤ 10  (clause 6.17a)  
      • “r” is the internal corner radius of the web–flange junction, and “t” is the web thickness.  
      • This ratio limit (r/t ≤ 10) prevents excessively large radii which might mask local plate‐bearing behaviour.  
   b. hw∕t ≤ 200 sin φ  (clause 6.17b)  
      • “hw” is the clear web height measured between the mid-lines of the flanges.  
      • The product 200 sin φ scales the slenderness limit according to the web’s inclination angle φ, allowing slightly more slender webs as φ approaches 90°.  
   c. 45° ≤ φ ≤ 90°  (clause 6.17c)  
      • φ is the angle between the web and its adjacent flange.  
      • A minimum of 45° ensures the web is not too shallow (near full decking or light lip angles), while the upper bound of 90° represents a vertical web.

3. Context and Usage  
   – These three checks, taken together, verify that the cross‐section lies within the scope for which the “unstiffened‐web” formula in clause 6.18 (the Rw,Rd equation) was derived.  
   – If any criterion is not met (for example, a very thin or highly inclined web), a more rigorous finite‐element or strip‐method analysis is required, or the section must be treated as a stiffened web according to the provisions in clauses 6.6–6.15.  
   – When multiple webs are present (as in composite sheeting, multi-span purlins, or cold-formed profiles), all webs must individually satisfy these criteria in order to apply the simplified approach.

By laying out the parameter, its allowable limit, and the clause reference in tabular form, the standard gives designers a rapid go/no-go check before investing effort in the full local‐bearing resistance calculation.

sections: 6.1.7.3  Cross-sections with two or more unstiffened webs

content:
The image is a black-and-white line drawing entitled “Figure 6.8: Examples of cross-sections with two or more webs.” It is laid out in two rows, each row containing three separate cross-section profiles. Under every individual cross-section sketch a small upward-pointing triangle (support symbol) is drawn at each web bearing location; each triangle is annotated “Rw,Rd,” indicating the local transverse resistance to be calculated per web.

Row 1 (sheeting profiles with multiple corrugations):

 1. Leftmost profile: a single trapezoidal corrugation. At the top is a long horizontal flange; on each side this flange steps down at a small inclined segment to a narrow horizontal segment (the valley), then slopes back up symmetrically to the opposite flange. Two bearing triangles (Rw,Rd) are located directly under the floor of each valley (i.e. at the bottom of each web).

 2. Centre profile: a double corrugation. The shape begins with a flat top flange, followed by a pair of identical trapezoidal waves in series—each wave consisting of an inclined web down to a valley, then back up to an intermediate flange, then repeated. Each of the two valleys carries its own pair of support triangles (Rw,Rd), so there are two Rw,Rd annotations spaced along the length.

 3. Rightmost profile: a triple corrugation. This consists of three back-to-back trapezoidal waves, producing three valleys. Three upward triangles labeled Rw,Rd appear beneath each valley, indicating three separate web-bearings in this continuous sheet profile.

Row 2 (cold-formed sections and liner trays):

 4. Leftmost: a symmetric “hat” or channel section with two parallel vertical webs and horizontal flanges at both top and bottom. The two vertical webs project down from the top flange, then transition into the bottom flange. Two support triangles (Rw,Rd) are positioned under the bottom corners of these vertical webs.

 5. Centre: a U-shaped channel with inward-turned flanges. A single deep vertical web extends down from the top horizontal flange, terminating in a bottom flange that turns up at each end; two arrows labeled Rw,Rd sit under the feet of these upturned elements, marking the web-to-support bearings.

 6. Rightmost: a compound profile combining a U-shaped liner tray on the left and a short trapezoidal corrugation on the right. The left portion resembles a deep channel with vertical side walls and a horizontal base; on the right, a small inclined web drops to a tiny valley before rising again to complete the sheet. Two support triangles (Rw,Rd) indicate the bearing beneath the U-section’s base and beneath the corrugation valley.

All six sketches share the same simple line-drawing style, with clear, unshaded outlines. The profiles illustrate typical cross-sections having two or more load-bearing webs—corrugated roofing sheets, hat sections, C-channels and combined liner/sheet trays—each web location directly above a support point where the local transverse resistance Rw,Rd must be evaluated. At the bottom center of the overall figure is the caption “Figure 6.8: Examples of cross-sections with two or more webs.”

sections: 6.1.7.3  Cross-sections with two or more unstiffened webs

content:
The illustration is a technical schematic (Figure 6.9 from EN 1993-1-3:2006) showing seven standardized loading-and-support arrangements for open steel sections with two or more parallel webs (for example purlins with sheeting). It is organized into two columns and seven rows. The left column contains side‐view line drawings of the cross-section; the right column labels each sketch as “Category 1” or “Category 2” and states the clearance condition that defines that category.

Common graphical elements in every sketch:  
• Two vertical lines represent the web plates, spaced apart.  
• Narrow horizontal lines at top and bottom represent the flanges.  
• A bundle of small black arrows on the top flange indicates a local downward load (sheeting bearing).  
• A bundle of small black arrows beneath the bottom flange indicates a support reaction.  
• A double-headed arrow above the loaded region (or below the reaction) is labeled sₛ, the bearing length (spacing of load or support).  
• A double-headed arrow between the loaded/reaction zone and the nearest support line or free end is labeled e (when measuring to a support) or c (when measuring to a free end).  
• A vertical double-headed arrow at the right side of each sketch, between midlines of top and bottom flanges, is labeled h_w (the web height).

The seven cases are:

1. Category 1 – Local load applied on the top flange.  
   The clear distance e from the edge of the loaded zone to the nearest support (depicted by upward arrows under the bottom flange) is ≤ 1.5 h_w.

2. Category 1 – Local load applied on the top flange adjacent to a free end of the member.  
   The clear distance c from the loaded zone to the free end is ≤ 1.5 h_w.

3. Category 1 – Support reaction at an end support on the bottom flange.  
   The clear distance c from the reaction zone to the free end is ≤ 1.5 h_w.

4. Category 2 – Local load applied on the top flange at mid-span.  
   The distance e from the loaded zone to the nearest support exceeds 1.5 h_w.

5. Category 2 – Local load applied on the top flange away from the free end.  
   The distance c from the loaded zone to the free end exceeds 1.5 h_w.

6. Category 2 – Support reaction at an end support on the bottom flange.  
   The distance c from the reaction to the free end exceeds 1.5 h_w.

7. Category 2 – Support reaction at an internal (intermediate) support on the bottom flange.  
   No free end is within 1.5 h_w of the reaction.

At top of the page is the reference “EN 1993-1-3: 2006,” and along the left margin is a document code and date stamp. This figure sets out the geometric classification criteria used when determining local transverse resistance of unstiffened webs in multi-web sections.

 (2) The effects of local and distortional buckling should be taken into account as specified in Section 5.5.

(1) The design buckling resistance Nb,Rd for flexural buckling should be obtained from EN 1993-1-1 using the appropriate buckling curve from table 6.3 according to the type of cross-section, axis of buckling and yield strength used, see (3).
 (2) The buckling curve for a cross-section not included in table 6.3 may be obtained by analogy.
 (3) The buckling resistance of a closed built-up cross-section should be determined using either:
 - buckling curve b in association with the basic yield strength fyb of the flat sheet material out of which the member is made by cold forming;
 - buckling curve c in association with the average yield strength fya of the member after cold forming, determined as specified in 3.2.3, provided that Αeff = Ag.

Table 6.3 in EN 1993-1-1 gives, by means of simple cross‐section sketches, the mapping from the geometric symmetry of a member’s open or closed cross-section to the designation of the buckling curve that must be used when determining its resistance to torsional or torsional-flexural buckling about the z–z axis.  In practice one reads the table as follows:

1. Closed, doubly symmetric sections  
   – Examples: cold-formed or welded box (rectangular or square hollow) and circular hollow sections.  
   – Symmetry: both about y–y and z–z axes; shear centre and centroid coincide.  
   – Buckling curve: curve “a” for both axes.  

2. Open, doubly symmetric sections  
   – Examples: rolled or welded I- and H-beams (flanges and web symmetric about both axes).  
   – Symmetry: about y–y (strong) and z–z (weak) axes; shear centre = centroid.  
   – Buckling curves:  
     • For flexural buckling about y–y: curve “b”  
     • For flexural buckling about z–z: curve “c”  

3. Mono-symmetric open sections  
   – Examples: C-sections (single-sided channel) with the web centreline on one side only; singly symmetric cold-formed shapes.  
   – Symmetry: only about one principal axis (usually the y–y axis); the shear centre is offset from the centroid.  
   – Buckling curves:  
     • Bending about the axis of symmetry (y–y): curve “c”  
     • Bending about the mono-symmetric axis (z–z): curve “d”  

4. Non-symmetric open sections  
   – Examples: unequal leg angles, angle-based channels bent or welded so that neither principal axis is a symmetry axis, custom or built-up shapes with eccentricity.  
   – Symmetry: none (centroid and shear centre do not coincide on either principal axis).  
   – Buckling curves:  
     • For both y–y and z–z directions: curve “d”  

Notes on use and context:  
• Even for open cross-sections that are point-symmetric (e.g. Z-purlins with equal flanges) or mono-symmetric, one must check whether resistance to torsional or torsional-flexural buckling governs rather than pure flexural buckling (see EN 1993-1-1 6.3.1.1).  
• The design buckling resistance N b,Rd is obtained by applying the appropriate curve (a, b, c or d) to the non-dimensional slenderness parameter λ in the usual EN 1993-1-1 expression.  
• In all cases, use of the yield strength in the minor direction f y,a for the column formula is not permitted unless the effective cross-sectional area A eff equals the gross area A g (i.e. no reductions for local buckling).  

By referring to these four sketch‐based categories, the engineer can immediately pick the correct buckling curve classification for use in torsional or torsional-flexural buckling checks, ensuring consistency with the clauses of EN 1993-1-1.

The figure presents eight typical monosymmetric, open‐section cold‐formed steel profiles that are particularly prone to torsional–flexural buckling (EN 1993-1-1 clause 6.3.1.1, see context note 2).  All profiles are drawn in plan-view as thin‐wall cross‐section outlines, each superimposed on its principal centroidal axes (vertical and horizontal dashed lines).  In every case only one axis (the vertical one) is a line of symmetry; there is no mirror symmetry about the horizontal axis, which makes these shapes monosymmetric.

Row 1 (left to right):

 1. Back-to-back equal‐angle assembly (a V-shaped built-up section). Two L-profiles are cold-or self-pierce-riveted together at their legs, forming a V opening.  
 2. As above but with edge lips added on each leg (often called a lip-stiffened V or Z purlin without equal flanges).  
 3. Standard channel (C-section) with straight flanges—flange width roughly equal to web depth—and no lips.  
 4. Lip-stiffened channel: a C-section with narrow lips turned out of each flange to improve local and distortional buckling resistance.

Row 2 (left to right):

 5. A shallow channel (short, wide flanges with a deep web), flipped 180° relative to the one above, again without horizontal symmetry.  
 6. Built‐up angle-and-plate T-section: one angle leg welded to the center of a flat plate to form a single-sided T, monosymmetric about the vertical axis.  
 7. Twin back-to-back channels: two identical C-sections bridged at the flanges or web to make a composite profile, still only symmetric about the vertical centerline.  
 8. Back-to-back angles or channel-angle composite: a more complex built-up member in which two open-sections are assembled off-centre, maintaining only one line of symmetry.

Key features common to all eight shapes:

 • Open cross‐section (no closed cell)  
 • Thin walls (cold‐formed geometry)  
 • One centroidal symmetry axis (vertical dashed line) but no horizontal symmetry line  
 • Exposed flanges and/or lips, generating warping and shear‐centre eccentricity (yo≠0 or zo≠0)  
 • Subject to combined torsional and flexural buckling modes rather than pure flexural buckling  

Because these sections lack full (doubly) symmetry, their elastic critical buckling load Ncr,TF (torsional–flexural mode) must be checked against the lower of the torsional critical force Ncr,T and flexural critical forces about y–y and z–z. The associated warping constant, torsion constant, and shear‐centre offsets (yo, zo) appear in equation (6.33a,b); the appropriate buckling curves for N b,Rd follow from Table 6.3 (EN 1993-1-1 clause 6.3.1.1).

It is labelled “Figure 8.1: End distance, edge distance and spacings for fasteners and spot welds.”

Overall layout  
– A flat rectangular plate is drawn with its length running left–right and its depth running top–bottom.  Mid‐span of the plate is omitted (broken line style) to focus on one end region.  
– Two horizontal dashed centre‐lines run left–right, indicating the two rows of fasteners.  
– Three fasteners are shown in each row, for a total of six equally spaced holes, depicted as solid circles at the intersections of the dashed lines.  

Key dimension annotations  
1. Direction of load transfer  
   • A large double‐headed arrow to the left of the plate, labelled “Direction of load transfer,” shows that the external force is applied along the plate’s longitudinal axis (left–right).  

2. Longitudinal spacing (p₁) and end distance (e₁)  
   • Above the top row of holes, a pair of dimension arrows mark the centre‐to‐centre pitch between adjacent fasteners in the load‐transfer direction, labelled p₁.  
   • A shorter arrow‐pair between the rightmost hole centre and the plate’s end face is labelled e₁, indicating the end distance (centre of fastener to end of connected part, in the direction of load transfer).  

3. Transverse spacing (p₂) and edge distance (e₂)  
   • To the right of the plate, two vertical dimension arrows span the distance from the lower row of hole‐centres to the upper row, labelled p₂.  
   • A shorter vertical arrow from the upper dashed centre‐line up to the top edge of the plate is labelled e₂, denoting the edge distance (centre of fastener to adjacent edge of the connected part, perpendicular to load transfer).  

4. Hole‐diameter offset (dₒ)  
   • A small arrow pair, drawn at an angle emanating from one of the fastener holes, is labelled dₒ to indicate the nominal diameter of the drilled or punched hole in the plate.  

Graphical conventions  
– Dashed lines: represent the theoretical centre‐lines along which fasteners are aligned.  
– Broken (jagged) sides of the plate: indicate that the drawing is a partial detail rather than the full member.  
– Solid circles: denote existing or proposed fastener positions.  

Purpose and context  
This diagram illustrates the fundamental layout parameters required by EN 1993-1-8 (clause on mechanical fasteners) for calculating connection resistance.  The symbols e₁, e₂, p₁, p₂ and dₒ appear throughout the code’s tables and formulae governing bearing, shear, pull‐through and prescriptive spacing checks.  Ensuring the correct end distances and spacings is critical to avoid premature tear‐out, excessive bearing stresses or loss of clamp‐up force in bolted—or analogous—connections under static loads.

The image is a black-and-white schematic entitled “Figure 8.2: Reduction of pull through resistance due to the position of fasteners.” It consists of three adjacent, horizontally aligned cross-section sketches of a profiled steel sheet and underlying support plate, each illustrating a different fastener location and the corresponding design pull-through resistance value. Below is a detailed description of each of the three subfigures and their common elements:

1. Common profile geometry  
   - Each sketch shows a sheet metal section with a single trough or “valley” in the center. The top flange segments slope down at an angle into the trough, forming essentially a trapezoidal profile in cross section. Beneath the trough is a straight horizontal support plate or substrate.  
   - A vertical dashed centerline marks the geometric mid-axis of the trough in all three drawings.  
   - A downward-pointing solid arrow represents the tensile pull-through load applied at the fastener location. The arrow tip touches the bottom surface of the trough and the arrow shaft is drawn thick to emphasize the load path through the sheet into the substrate.  

2. Left subfigure: central location  
   - The fastener is positioned exactly on the vertical centerline of the trough. The dashed line passes through the arrow, indicating zero eccentricity.  
   - The arrow is labeled “Fp,Rd” at its lower end, denoting the design pull-through resistance for a centrally located fastener. There is no reduction factor applied in this case.  

3. Middle subfigure: single offset (quarter-point)  
   - Here the arrow is shifted laterally away from the centerline toward one side of the trough’s base by a small distance. A short horizontal tick mark on the trough floor and the dashed centerline indicate the offset e1 (end distance) from the center.  
   - The arrow is labeled “0,9 Fp,Rd,” signifying that when a fastener is placed at a quarter-point (one-quarter of the sheet width from the center), its pull-through resistance must be reduced to 90 % of the central value.  

4. Right subfigure: dual offsets (both quarter-points)  
   - Two fasteners are shown, symmetrically located at the left and right quarter-points of the trough bottom. Two vertical arrows descend from those points.  
   - Each arrow is individually labeled “0,7 Fp,Rd.” This indicates that if fasteners are located at both quarter-point positions, the allowable pull-through resistance per fastener is limited to 70 % of the nominal central resistance.  

Contextual notes from EN 1993-1-3:  
- These reductions account for non-central load eccentricity in the sheet profile and the resulting uneven deformation of the sheeting.  
- The quarter-point reductions apply specifically to self-tapping screws and cartridge-fired pins and correspond to clause 8(7) of the standard.  
- The illustration is intended to guide designers in applying the correct partial factors when calculating pull-through resistance Fo,Rd under tension.

content:
The input shows “Table 8.1: Design resistances for blind rivets” extracted from EN 1993-1-8. Below is a structured, detailed description of its contents and how it fits into the wider connection-design provisions:

1. Table Title and Scope  
   • Title: “Design resistances for blind rivets”  
   • Purpose: To give characteristic and design values of shear and pull-through (tension) resistance for blind rivets used in thin‐sheet connections, subject to static loads.  
   • Applicability limits: Nominal rivet diameters d between 2.6 mm and 6.4 mm; hole diameter at most 0.1 mm larger than d; sheet thickness ordering requirement (thinnest sheet next to preformed head).

2. Column-and-Row Layout  
   • Column 1 (d): Nominal rivet diameter categories: 2.6–3.2 mm, 3.4–4.0 mm, 4.5–6.4 mm.  
   • Column 2 (Fv,Rd): Design shear resistance per rivet, defined as Fv,Rk/γM2.  
   • Column 3 (Fb,Rd or Fp,Rd): Design pull-through (or block-shear) resistance of the sheet under the rivet head, generally obtained by testing.  
   • In some presentations a fourth column lists the characteristic tensile resistance Ft,Rk for pull-out of the rivet shank, again to be determined by test.

3. Key Formulas and Parameters  
   • Partial factor γM2: Used for mechanical fasteners; recommended value γM2 = 1.25 (unless national annex specifies otherwise).  
   • Shear resistance:  
     Fv,Rd = Fv,Rk / γM2  
   • Pull-through resistance limit formula (if test data are not available or to check bounding value):  
     Fb,Rd ≤ fu · e1 · t  ÷ (1.2·γM2)  
     where fu is ultimate tensile strength of the sheet material, e1 is the end-distance from fastener centre to sheet end in load direction, and t is sheet thickness.  
   • α-factor for shear resistance interpolation:  
     α = 3.6 · √(t/d)  but limited to α ≤ 2.1  
     For intermediate t/d ratios, α is obtained by linear interpolation between tabulated extremes.

4. Footnotes and Special Conditions  
   • “*) by testing”: Many values (especially pull-through and pull-out resistances) must be established by laboratory tests if not covered by tabulated data.  
   • Gross-section distortion may be neglected in shear capacity checks provided that the flange width does not exceed 150 mm.  
   • If the sheet’s pull-out resistance is less than its pull-through resistance, then the deformation capacity of the connection must be determined experimentally.  
   • National Annex may give further supplemental values or reduction factors (e.g. for long joints, for shear of blind rivets in shear plus tension, etc.).  

5. Cross-References to EN 1993-1-8 Provisions  
   • Reduction factor for long joints βLf: See clause 3.8.  
   • Second-order bending moment ΔMEd: Not directly in this table but required for compression members with mechanical splices.  
   • Additional design rules (e.g. combined shear and tension check, hole-diameter criteria, torque limits) are found under clauses 8.2.1–8.2.4 and in the National Annex.

In sum, Table 8.1 organizes rivet diameters into size bands and provides baseline design resistances in shear and pull-through, supplemented by formula-based upper bounds, α-interpolation rules, partial factors (γM2), and footnotes requiring testing and national adjustments. This structured data is essential for any RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store targeting connection-design calculations in structural steelwork.

content:
The excerpted Table 8.2 from EN 1993–1-8 provides the design resistances of self-tapping screws loaded in tension, bearing (pull-through) and pull-out. It is organized into four main parts—tension resistance, shear resistance, bearing/pull-through and pull-out resistance—and closes with minimum spacing and sheet-thickness requirements plus a series of notes.  

1. Tension Resistance (F b,Rd)  
   • Formula:  
     F b,Rd = α · f u · d · t  / γ M2  
     – γ M2 is the partial factor (recommended 1.25).  
     – f u is ultimate tensile strength of the screw.  
     – d is the nominal screw diameter.  
     – t is the thickness of the thinner sheet (sheet in tension).  
   • Determination of α:  
     – For 3.0 mm ≤ d ≤ 6.0 mm: α = 3.2·√(t/d), but capped at α ≤ 2.1.  
     – For d > 6.0 mm: α = 2.1.  
     – For intermediate values (e.g. 6.0 < d < ?), interpolate linearly.  
   • Net-tension check:  
     F n,Rd = A net · f u  / γ M2  
     where A net is the net cross-section of the screw (i.e. tensile stress area).  
   • Interaction criterion (if shear and tension act together):  
     Either 1.2·F b,Rd (tension capacity) or ∑F v,Rd (sum of shear capacities) ≥ 1.2·F n,Rd.  

2. Shear Resistance (F v,Rd)  
   • Not tabulated: must be determined by testing in accordance with clause 9(4).  
   • Interaction with tension is covered by formula (8.2) in EN 1993–1-8.  

3. Bearing ⁄ Pull-Through Resistance (F p,Rd)  
   • Formula for static loads or wind combinations:  
     F p,Rd = 0.5·d w·t·f u / γ M2  
     – d w is diameter of washer (or head).  
   • For purely static loads: F p,Rd = d w·t·f u / γ M2.  

4. Pull-Out Resistance (F o,Rd)  
   • Dependent on supporting sheet thickness t sup, its f u,sup, and thread pitch s:  
     – If s < 1: F o,Rd = 0.45·d·t sup·f u,sup / γ M2  
     – If s ≥ 1: F o,Rd = 0.65·d·t sup·f u,sup / γ M2  
   • Tensile-pull-out F t,Rd must be verified by testing if F o,Rd < F p,Rd.  
   • Acceptance criterion: ∑F p,Rd or F t,Rd ≥ F o,Rd.  

5. Minimum Spacing & Sheet-Thickness Conditions  
   • Longitudinal spacing: p₁ ≥ 3·d, valid for 3.0 mm ≤ d ≤ 8.0 mm.  
   • Transverse spacing: p₂ ≥ 3·d.  
   • Sheet thicknesses: thinner sheet t ≤ 1.5 mm; thicker sheet t₁ ≥ 0.9 mm.  
   • The thinner sheet must be adjacent to the screw head.  

6. Key Notes and Conditions  
   • Washer must be rigid enough to avoid local deformation or “pull-over.”  
   • The table is valid only if hole diameter does not exceed manufacturer’s recommendation—typically ≤0.1 mm above d for blind rivets, and specific allowances for bolts (see EN 1993–1-8).  
   • If pull-out resistance is lower than pull-through, deformation capacity shall be confirmed by testing or guaranteed by other structural elements.  
   • For long joints, a reduction factor βLf (EN 1993–1-8 §3.8) must be applied.  
   • National Annexes may specify γ M2, additional footnotes on shear/pull-through for self-tapping screws, and extensions of validity beyond the listed ranges.  

This detailed breakdown of Table 8.2 makes explicit the governing equations, the meaning of each symbol, the limiting values and caps (α ≤ 2.1), the criteria for combined loading, and the geometric and material constraints that ensure a safe design for self-tapping screw connections under tension, shear, bearing and pull-out actions.

content:
Below is a structured, detailed description of Table 8.3 (“Design resistances for cartridge-fired pins”), suitable for indexing in a RAG vector store. It highlights each design resistance, the governing formula, key parameters and variables, applicability conditions, and minimum thickness requirements.  

1. Scope and Symbols  
  • Table 8.3 addresses pin connections loaded in tension, shear and pull-through.  
  • γM2 is the partial safety factor for mechanical fasteners (recommended γM2 = 1.25).  
  • d = nominal pin diameter; dw = washer or head diameter; Anet = net cross-sectional area of the connected sheet; fu = ultimate tensile strength of pin material; tf = thickness of the thinner sheet; tsup = thickness of the supporting member.  

2. Design Resistance in Tension (Fn,Rd)  
  • Equation:  
     Fn,Rd = (Anet · fu) / γM2  
  • Use the net area of the sheet through which the pin passes and the pin’s material strength.  

3. Design Resistance in Shear (Fv,Rd)  
  • Shear resistance is not given by formula in this table; it must be determined by test (*3).  
  • In the absence of test data, an alternative expression (Fv,Rk/γM2) may be used if tabulated characteristic shear strengths are available.  

4. Design Resistance in Pull-through (Fp,Rd)  
  • Full-load condition:  
     Fp,Rd = (dw · tf · fu) / γM2  
     – Applies when static loads dominate.  
  • Combined wind and static loads:  
     Fp,Rd = 0.5 · (dw · tf · fu) / γM2  
     – Reduces pull-through resistance by half under fluctuating wind action.  
  • If Fp,Rd < Fv,Rd (pull-out weaker than shear capacity), the connection’s deformation capacity must be verified by testing.  

5. Interaction and Verification Criteria  
  • Shear vs. tension interaction:  
     ΣFv,Rd ≥ 1.5 · Fn,Rd  
     or  
     ΣFv,Rd ≥ ΣFb,Rd (sum of bearing resistances)  
     – Ensures shear capacity significantly exceeds tension capacity by a factor of 1.5.  
  • Tension vs. pull-out interaction:  
     ΣFp,Rd ≥ Ft,Rd ≥ Fo,Rd  
     – The sum of pull-through capacities must exceed applied tensile force, which in turn must exceed any pull-out capacity if applicable.  

6. Minimum Supporting-Member Thickness (tsup)  
  Pin diameters covered: 3.7 mm ≤ d ≤ 6.0 mm. The following tsup minimums are required to prevent local failure in the supporting steel:  
  • d = 3.7 mm → tsup ≥ 4.0 mm  
  • d = 4.5 mm → tsup ≥ 6.0 mm  
  • d = 5.2 mm → tsup ≥ 8.0 mm  

7. Material and Geometry Limits  
  • Ultimate tensile strength of pin material: fu ≥ 300 N/mm² (typical).  
  • Thickness of the thinner sheet: tf ≤ 1.5 mm (in this table’s scope).  
  • Washer or head diameter dw typically ≈ 1.5 × d, subject to manufacturer’s guidance.  

8. Notes and Testing  
  • Shear resistance Fv,Rd and pull-through resistance under combined loads must be tested if values are uncertain (*3).  
  • Deformation capacity requirements: if the connection must provide ductility, ensure test data or alternative structural paths guarantee necessary deformation.  

This description captures the essential formulas, interaction checks, parameter definitions and geometric constraints in Table 8.3, making it readily searchable and reusable in a RAG-driven knowledge base.

Below is a structured, detailed description of “Table 8.4: Design resistances for bolts,” suitable for ingestion into a RAG vector store. Wherever relevant, cross-references to the EN 1993-1-8 provisions and notation from the accompanying text have been included.

1. Table title  
   “Table 8.4: Design resistances for bolts”

2. Purpose  
   Gives the characteristic formulae and limiting conditions for the design resistance of bolts loaded in tension, shear, pull-through, and combined shear-tension, for connections made through sheets or plates of thickness t between 0.75 mm and 3 mm.

3. Column headings and content  
   The table is organized into four primary rows (resistance modes), each with:  
   – Symbol for design resistance (F_x,Rd)  
   – Expression for F_x,Rd as a function of bolt and sheet parameters  
   – Key limiting conditions or definitions of factors

   a) Tension resistance, F_n,Rd  
      – Formula: F_n,Rd = min{A_net f_u / γ_M2, A_net f_u / γ_M2}  
        • A_net = net cross-sectional area of the connected part (sum of sheets)  
        • f_u = ultimate tensile strength of the fastener material  
        • γ_M2 = partial safety factor for mechanical fasteners (recommended 1.25)  
      – Note: A_net is computed per bolt, i.e. total net area / number of bolts in connection.  

   b) Shear resistance, ΣF_v,Rd  
      – Formula: ΣF_v,Rd = n_f A_s f_u / γ_M2  
        • A_s = tensile (stress) area of the bolt shank  
        • n_f = number of fasteners in the shear plane  
      – No further geometric limits specified in this row.

   c) Pull-through resistance, ΣF_p,Rd  
      – Formula: ΣF_p,Rd = β_b k_t n_f d t f_u / γ_M2  
        • β_b = min{1.0, e1 / (3 d)}, edge-distance factor with e1 measured along the load direction (see Fig 8.1)  
        • k_t = thickness factor: 0.8 for t ≤1.25 mm; 1.0 for t >1.25 mm  
        • d = nominal bolt diameter; t = thickness of thinner connected sheet  
        • n_f = number of fasteners in the pull-through plane  
      – Conditions:  
        • If pull-out resistance is smaller than pull-through, deformation capacity must be verified by testing.  
        • If fasteners lie off central trough of profiled sheeting, reduce F_p,Rd to 0.9 Fp,Rd at quarter-point, or 0.7 per fastener if two at both quarter-points (see Fig 8.2).

   d) Combined shear and tension  
      – Verification:  
        Either ΣF_v,Rd ≥ 1.2 F_n,Rd  
        Or use the interaction equation (8.2) from EN 1993-1-8, based on calculated Ft,Rd and Fv,Rd.

4. Additional table footnotes and constraints  
   – Gross section distortion may be neglected if the fastening is through a flange not more than 150 mm wide.  
   – Hole diameters for screws and bolts must follow manufacturer’s guidelines: applied torque just above threading torque, below thread-stripping or head-shear torque; threading torque < 2/3 of head-shearing torque.  
   – For long joints, apply reduction factor β_Lf per EN 1993-1-8 § 3.8.  
   – For bolts M12 & M14 with hole diameters 2 mm oversize, see EN 1993-1-8.  
   – For design by testing of mechanical fasteners, refer to § 9(4).

5. Special row: applicability limits  
   – Sheet or plate thickness range: 0.75 mm ≤ t ≤ 3 mm  
   – Minimum bolt size: M6  
   – Permitted strength grades: 4.6 to 10.9  
   – For t > 3 mm, use the rules for bolts in EN 1993-1-8.

6. Parameter definitions (in brief)  
   – A = gross cross-section area of fastener shank  
   – A_s = tensile stress area of fastener  
   – A_net = net area of connected part  
   – d, d_o, d_w = nominal bolt diameter, hole diameter, washer/head diameter  
   – e1, e2 = end and edge distances (see Fig 8.1)  
   – f_u, f_u,sup = ultimate strengths of fastener material and supporting member  
   – n, n_f = number of sheets per screw/pin; number of fasteners in connection  
   – p1, p2 = center-to-center spacings of fasteners in and across load direction  
   – t, t1, t_sup = sheet thicknesses; thickness of supporting member.

This description faithfully captures all formulae, parameters, limits and notes contained in Table 8.4, cross-linked to the broader design provisions for mechanical fasteners in EN 1993-1-8.

Below is a structured, self-contained description of Table 8.5 (“Design resistances for spot welds”) together with the relevant notes and definitions. This text can be ingested into a RAG vector store to support queries about spot-weld design in shear.

1. Scope and Applicability  
   • Table 8.5 gives the characteristic design resistance Fv,Rd of a single spot weld subjected to shear.  
   • It applies only when the parent materials are either as-rolled or galvanized sheet up to 4.0 mm thick, provided the thinner of the two sheets being joined does not exceed 3.0 mm (see Context Note 1).  
   • Spot welds may be produced by resistance welding or by fusion welding (Context Note 2).  
   • The partial safety factor for the weld metal, γM2, is taken according to EN 1993-1-8, Annex National. A recommended value is γM2 = 1.25 (Context Note 5).

2. Symbols and Definitions (Context Note 4)  
   t  
     – Thickness of the thinner connected sheet [mm].  
   t1  
     – Thickness of the thicker connected sheet [mm].  
   Anet  
     – Net cross-sectional area of the connected part (i.e. sheet area minus any holes) [mm²].  
   ds  
     – Effective diameter of the weld nugget [mm] as produced by the welding procedure. Must be verified by shear tests on single-lap specimens (Context Note 7).  
   nw  
     – Number of spot welds in the joint.  
   e1, e2  
     – End and edge distances from the center of a spot weld to the sheet edge [mm] (see 8.3(5)).  
   p1, p2  
     – Weld spacings along and across the sheet [mm] (see 8.3(5)).  
   fu  
     – Ultimate tensile strength of the sheet material [N/mm²].  
   Fe,Rd  
     – Design resistance of an edge-shear failure mode [N].  
   Fn,Rd  
     – Design resistance of a net-section failure mode [N].

3. Design Resistance Expressions  
   The design shear resistance of one spot weld, Fv,Rd, is the minimum of the following modes (all divided by γM2):  
   a) Shear-tear of sheet metal adjacent to weld:  
      – Ftb,Rd ≤ 0.7·ds²·fu  
      – Ftb,Rd ≤ 3.1·t·ds·fu  
   b) Edge tear-out of the thinner sheet:  
      – Fv,Rd = 1.4·t·e1·fu  
   c) Net-section tear-out of the thinner sheet (if holes or slots are present):  
      – Fv,Rd = Anet·fu  
   d) Shear failure across the weld nugget:  
      – Fv,Rd = (π/4)·ds²·fu  

4. Joint-level Checks  
   At least one of the following must be satisfied by the entire weld group:  
     – nw·25·Ftb,Rd ≥ 1.25·Fe,Rd  
     – nw·Fv,Rd ≥ 1.25·Fe,Rd  
     – Σ Fv,Rd ≥ 1.25·Fn,Rd  

5. Minimum Spacings and Edge Distances  
   For a weld layout to develop full capacity:  
     – 3·ds ≤ p1 ≤ 8·ds (along the joint)  
     – 3·ds ≤ p2 ≤ 6·ds (across the joint)  

6. Weld Nugget Diameter ds  
   The nominal nugget diameter to be achieved by the welding procedure is:  
     – Fusion welding: ds = 0.5·t + 5 mm  (Equation 8.3a)  
     – Resistance welding: ds = 5·√t    (Equation 8.3b)  
   The actual nugget size must be verified by destructive shear testing on single-lap specimens whose sheet thickness equals t (Context Note 7).

Key takeaways: Table 8.5 provides four potential failure modes for a single spot weld in shear, each with a formula proportional to either sheet thickness, net area or nugget area. The design value Fv,Rd is the minimum of these modes (all factored by γM2). The table also enforces joint-level capacity checks, minimum edge/spacings, and prescribes how to determine the required nugget diameter ds for both resistance and fusion-welded spots.

The image is labeled “Figure 8.3: Test specimen for shear tests of spot welds” and shows a single-lap plate specimen with a single spot weld, loaded in direct shear. It consists of three schematic views—two side elevations (one of the resistance-welded connection, one of the loaded specimen in service) and one plan (top) view of the full test piece. All key dimensions are expressed in terms of the weld-nugget diameter ds.  

1. Side-Elevation, Resistance-Weld Detail (top-left)  
   • Two flat metal sheets overlap and are joined by one spot weld (shown as a solid oval).  
   • The distance from the center of the weld nugget to the free edge of the overlap is marked “ds.”  
   • An arrow points from right to left along the overlap, labeled “Resistance weld,” indicating direction of nugget formation.  

2. Side-Elevation, Loaded Specimen (top-right)  
   • The same two plates, joined by the spot weld, are shown being pulled apart in opposite directions by axial shear forces Fsd on each plate end.  
   • Arrows at each end point away from the weld, each labeled Fsd, illustrating the shear load applied to test weld strength.  

3. Plan View of Full Test Specimen (bottom)  
   • Overall length of the specimen, measured along the plates’ centerline, is specified as 400 mm.  
   • Width of the overlapped region (plate cross-section) is given as 6 × ds.  
   • The spot-weld location is indicated by a small filled circle in the overlap, offset from the plate ends.  
   • From the center of the nugget to each end of the overlap region the edge distances are both labeled “e.”  
   • A note beneath the drawing reads “3,5 ds ≤ e ≤ 5 ds,” specifying the permissible range of e (edge distance) relative to ds.  

Key points in context:  
- The specimen thickness t should match that of the production weld.  
- The nut diameter ds produced by the welding procedure must be verified by testing.  
- During the test, the plates are tension-loaded so that the spot weld is subjected to pure shear.  
- The geometry (lap length, width, and edge distances) ensures a uniform shear stress distribution around the nugget.  

Together, these views fully define the geometry and loading arrangement for single-lap shear tests of spot-welded connections, allowing determination of the actual weld diameter ds and validation of design resistance Fv,Rd according to the provisions in Eurocode 3, Section 8.3 and Table 8.5.

The figure is a schematic, cross-section view of a fillet-welded lap connection, labelled “Figure 8.4: Fillet welded lap connection.” It shows two steel plates in lap: a smaller rectangular plate (the “connected part”) laid on top of a larger backing plate or member. The top plate projects into a cutout in the backing plate so that welds can be applied on both the side faces of the top plate and on its end face where it abuts the backing plate.

Key graphic elements and annotations:

1. Plates  
 - The lower (backing) member is drawn as a thick horizontal rectangle, with its right and left extreme edges broken by zig-zag “cut lines” indicating the view continues beyond the sketch.  
 - The upper (connected) plate is a narrower rectangle centered over the backing plate. Its left end is positioned flush with a vertical dashed reference line; its right end abuts the inside face of the backing plate.

2. Fillet-weld representation  
 - Two side-fillet welds are depicted by a diagonal hatch pattern (filled rectangles) along the long, top edge of the lap, one on each side of the upper plate (only one side shown in this view – the other is understood to be identical on the opposite side). This represents the “side fillet” weld(s).  
 - An end-fillet weld is shown by the same hatch pattern on the right-hand vertical face of the upper plate where it meets the backing plate. This is the “end fillet” weld.

3. Dimension annotations  
 - “b” is marked by a vertical dimension arrow on the left side of the upper plate, pointing between its top and bottom faces. This denotes the width (thickness in the projection plane) of the connected part or sheet.  
 - “Lw,s” is shown by a horizontal double-headed arrow above the top fillet weld, measured from the dashed reference line on the left to the start of the end-weld region on the right. This is the effective length of a side fillet weld.  
 - “Lw,e” is indicated by a vertical double-headed arrow adjacent to the end-weld’s hatch on the right, spanning the full height of the weld. This is the effective length of the end fillet weld.

4. Break lines  
 - Both the top edge of the backing plate and the bottom edge of the backing plate are shown with zig-zag breaks, implying that the member extends further to left and right beyond what is drawn. These breaks keep the focus on the region of interest where the welds occur.

Overall, the drawing clearly identifies the geometry relevant to the design formulas. It distinguishes side fillet welds (length Lw,s on both sides) from an end fillet weld (length Lw,e), and labels the connected plate width b. This visual supports the calculation of design resistance Fw,Rd according to the rules for side and end fillets (equations 8.4a–c) and the summation of their resistances in combined connections.

The position of the centroid and realistic assumption of the distribution of forces should be taken into account.

Figure title and context  
• The drawing is labeled “Figure 8.5: Arc spot weld with weld washer.” It shows a perspective view of a small connected part or sheet joined by an arc spot weld, using a weld washer, onto a larger supporting sheet or plate.

Overall geometry  
• Top member (“Connected part or sheet”): A relatively narrow, rectangular bar-shaped plate laid across the supporting sheet. Its edges extend beyond the weld washer, indicating the part to be attached.  
• Weld washer: A square washer with chamfered or rounded edges, centered under the arc spot weld. Its top surface carries a circular pattern of stippling (dots) that represents the visible weld nugget. The washer serves to reinforce very thin top sheets and to increase the effective interface area of the weld.  
• Supporting member (“Supportment” or supporting sheet): A larger, flat base plate beneath both the washer and the small top part. Its edges are shown using “broken” or jagged cuts at the front and right side to imply that the sheet extends indefinitely in those directions.

Weld detail  
• Interface weld nugget: Represented as a filled circle of fine dots on the top face of the washer. This denotes the projection of the weld metal where it has pooled and fused through the washer and into the support sheet.  
• Centerline indication: A dashed line running longitudinally through the connected part aligns with the center of the weld, marking the force‐transfer path.  
• Sheet thickness: Although not dimensioned numerically, the cross‐section view implied by the jagged edges suggests the relative thicknesses tsup (support sheet) and tt (connected sheet). The washer raises the weld slightly above the surface of the lower sheet, ensuring penetration into the support without burning through the thin top sheet.

Annotations and call-outs  
• “Connected part or sheet” arrow: Points to the upper plate, emphasizing which component is being joined.  
• “Weld washer” arrow: Points directly at the square washer element, clarifying its role and position.  
• “Supportment” arrow: Identifies the lower sheet as the structural backing that carries the weld. Broken lines on the right front edges denote that this member continues out of view.

Design implications  
• This illustrative arrangement supports the rule that arc spot welds through parts thinner than 0.7 mm require a weld washer. The washer increases effective interface diameter (ds) and prevents burn-through.  
• The circular weld interface (ds) must be at least 10 mm per design clause, and the washer helps meet that minimum while controlling distortion.  
• Adequate end and edge distances are achieved by centering the washer and weld nugget, in line with the dashed force-transfer centerline, so that minimal spacing from the weld center to part edges is maintained.

The illustration is labelled “c) Single connected sheet with weld washer” and appears as Figure 8.6 in the source text, which deals with the geometry of an arc-spot weld through a thin part (t < 0.7 mm) augmented by a weld washer. In this cross-sectional schematic:  

• The bottom member is a single steel sheet of nominal thickness t, shown as a solid horizontal strip at the very base of the drawing. Above it sits a prefabricated weld washer (a ring‐shaped plate with a central opening), depicted as the thinner horizontal bar immediately beneath the weld nugget.  

• The weld nugget itself is rendered as an approximately lenticular (lens-shaped) volume of fused material, shaded with stippling to indicate the fusion zone. The nugget spans from the underside of the washer, penetrates through its central aperture, and flares slightly in the sheet.  

• Two key diameters are dimensioned by horizontal double‐headed arrows:  
  – dw (visible diameter) is measured across the widest part of the nugget at the top of the washer, annotated by an arrowed line aligned with the washer’s top face. This corresponds to the “visible diameter of the arc spot weld” used in formulas (8.6) through (8.8).  
  – ds (interface diameter) is measured at the interface between the weld nugget and the connected bottom sheet. A dashed horizontal line denotes the level of this interface, and an arrowed line beneath it labels ds. In accordance with clause (3) of the code text, ds must not be less than 10 mm, and is computed from dw and the total sheet thickness Σt via equation (8.6).  

• The washer effectively increases the local thickness seen by the welding current, ensuring adequate heat input and nugget formation when the connected sheet itself is too thin (< 0.7 mm). This arrangement prevents burn-through and helps achieve the required minimum weld diameter and shear capacity.  

• At the very bottom of the figure, the caption “Figure 8.6: Arc spot welds” reaffirms that this drawing is part of a family of figures illustrating geometrical parameters (dw, ds, dp, Lw) and layout rules (end and edge distances) used to calculate the design shear resistance Fw,Rd in clauses (6)–(9).  

Together, the geometry shown here underpins the algebraic definitions in the adjoining text:  
  – Equation (8.6) specifies ds = 0.7 dw – 1.5 Σt (but not less than 0.55 dw), ensuring a minimum effective weld interface.  
  – The use of a Washer is mandated by rule (4) when sheet thickness < 0.7 mm, exactly the condition illustrated.  
  – Dw and ds serve as inputs to the shear‐resistance formula (8.5a–d), governing the allowable load transfer across the weld.

The sketch is a three-dimensional, cutaway view of an “elongated arc spot weld” joining a thin upper plate (“connected part or sheet”) to a lower support plate. In the figure, the upper sheet lies horizontally and overlaps a slightly recessed rectangular region of the support below. The plates are shown in perspective, with the back edges of both parts cut away to expose the weld and clarify thicknesses.

At the heart of the connection is an oval-shaped weld deposit, hatched with fine diagonal lines to indicate the fused metal. This elongated weld has a visible length along the direction of load transfer, labeled “Lw,” and a visible width across that direction, labeled “dw.” A dashed centerline passes longitudinally through the weld, marking the axis along which end- and edge-distance rules are measured.

Key callouts in the drawing:
• “Connected part or sheet” points to the top plate being welded. Its thickness may be tsup or ts, as described in the context text.  
• “Support” points to the lower plate or backing sheet that the upper plate is welded onto.  
• “dw” is shown by a double-headed arrow across the short axis of the weld, defining the visible weld-face diameter (or width) at the plate surface.  
• “Lw” is shown by a double-headed arrow along the long axis of the weld, defining the elongated weld length measured parallel to the direction of force transfer.

The support plate is depicted with hatched cross-section lines on its side face, indicating a solid metal backing. The upper plate sits flush on the support, and the weld metal bridges both surfaces. The cutaway edges of both plates are rendered with jagged lines to suggest that only a portion of the parts is shown.

This figure (labeled as “Figure 8.7: Elongated arc spot weld”) corresponds to clause (9) of the accompanying guidance, which provides:
- Equation (8.8a) for the design shear resistance Fw,Rd of the elongated arc spot weld, based on the weld length Lw and effective peripheral diameter dp.  
- An upper limit on Fw,Rd defined in (8.8b): Fw,Rd ≤ (0.5·Lw + 1.67·dp)·τSt·fuw⁄γM2, where τSt·fuw represents the shear yield of the electrode material and γM2 the partial factor.  
- The effective peripheral diameter dp is calculated from the visible weld dimension dw and the sheet thicknesses (Σt) per clauses (8.7a) and (8.7b) in the context text.

Overall, the drawing clearly illustrates how to measure the critical weld dimensions—Lw along the force axis and dw transverse to it—and how the adjacent plate geometry supports applying the shear-resistance formulae provided in the additional text.

The image is Figure 10.1 from a steel‐design context, showing how a laterally‐braced purlin with its free flange tied to sheeting can be idealized for buckling and deformation analysis. It is arranged in three tiers:

1. Top row – Cross‐sectional views under different load cases  
   • Four simplified sketches of a C–section purlin with its upper flange connected to roof sheeting. Vertical arrows indicate the applied load (gravity or uplift), the thin horizontal line the sheet, and the heavy bent line the steel section.  
   • Left two sketches (gravity loading):  
     – First: downward uniform load, slight downward bending of the sheeting, purlin web remains vertical, free flange unbuckled.  
     – Second: gravity load plus the onset of lateral movement in the free flange, showing the flange deflecting sideways and inducing additional twist in the section.  
   • Right two sketches (uplift loading):  
     – Third: upward uniform load, the sheeting and flange bend upward; the web bows out under compressive flange action.  
     – Fourth: same uplift load but with lateral displacement of the free flange, illustrating combined torsion and lateral bending under compression.

2. Middle row – Decomposition into two deformation modes  
   • On the left: The uplift‐loaded, laterally deflecting purlin sketched again. An arrow points to two separate idealized models on the right.  
   • On the right:  
     a) “In‐plane bending” model – the C–section web and flange remain in their original plane, bent by the uplift load but not twisted.  
     b) “Torsion and lateral bending” model – the free flange displaced out of plane, capturing twist and sideways deflection under the same load.

3. Bottom row – Rotational‐spring and elastic‐foundation idealizations  
   a) Two side‐by‐side line‐diagrams of the purlin cross‐section treated as laterally braced by the sheeting through a rotational spring of stiffness C_D:  
      – Left: flange connected via a spring at one end, pinned at the web–flange junction, and the other end fixed in the sheeting.  
      – Right: spring at the opposite end, pinned elsewhere, to show alternative restraint arrangements.  
   b) Simplified lateral‐spring model (left): a 3D sketch showing the free flange as a compression member in the y–z plane, supported continuously by a lateral spring of stiffness K along its length. Axes y (horizontal lateral direction), z (out of plane) and the spring symbol at the flange tip are shown.  
   c) Beam‐on‐elastic‐foundation model (right): a single‐span beam (representing the free flange) carrying upward arrows (uplift load q_h,Ed) and supported by a series of vertical springs (stiffness K) along its underside. Horizontal arrows along the beam illustrate how lateral load q_h,Ed times a factor k_h induces bending about the weak axis. The fixed supports at the ends represent the shear connections back into the main purlin web.

Altogether, the figure demonstrates:  
– how gravity versus uplift loading changes the compression/flange behavior;  
– how the total deformation splits into in‐plane bending and combined torsion/lateral bending;  
– how the rotational stiffness of the sheeting (C_D) may be idealized as either a rotational spring at the flange or an equivalent continuous lateral spring (K);  
– and finally how the free flange can be analyzed as a beam on an elastic foundation under a distributed lateral load, accounting for cross‐sectional distortion, St Venant torsion, and warping effects.

(1) Unless a second order analysis is carried out, the method given in 10.1.3 and 10.1.4 should be used to allow for the tendency of the free flange to move laterally (thus inducing additional stresses) by treating it as a beam subject to a lateral load qh,Ed, see figure 10.1.
 (2) For use in this method, the rotational spring should be replaced by an equivalent lateral linear spring of stiffness K. In determining K the effects of cross-sectional distortion should also be allowed for. For this purpose, the free flange may be treated as a compression member subject to a non-uniform axial force, with a continuous lateral spring support of stiffness K.
 (3) If the free flange of a purlin is in compression due to in-plane bending (for example, due to uplift loading in a single span purlin), the resistance of the free flange to lateral buckling should also be verified.
 (4) For a more precise calculation, a numerical analysis should be carried out, using values of the rotational spring stiffness CD obtained from 10.1.5.2. Allowance should be made for the effects of an initial bow imperfection of (eo) in the free flange, defined as in 5.3. The initial imperfection should be compatible with the shape of the relevant buckling mode, determined by the eigen-vectors obtained from the elastic first order buckling analysis.
 (5) A numerical analysis using the rotational spring stiffness CD obtained from 10.1.5.2 may also be used if lateral restraint is not supplied or if its effectiveness cannot be proved. When the numerical analysis is carried out, it should take into account the bending in two directions, torsional St Venant stiffness and warping stiffness about the imposed rotation axis.
 (6) If a 2nd order analysis is carried out, effective sections and stiffness, due to local buckling, should be taken into account.

When the numerical analysis is carried out, it should take into account the bending in two directions, torsional St Venant stiffness and warping stiffness about the imposed rotation axis.. (6) If a 2nd order analysis is carried out, effective sections and stiffness, due to local buckling, should be taken into account..
 NOTE: For a simplified design of purlins made of C-, Z- and Σ- cross sections see Annex E.

(1) For gravity loading, a single span purlin should satisfy the criteria for cross-section resistance given in 10.1.4.1. If it is subject to axial compression, it should also satisfy the criteria for stability of the free flange given in 10.1.4.2.
 (2) For uplift loading, a single span purlin should satisfy the criteria for cross-section resistance given in 10.1.4.1 and the criteria for stability of the free flange given in 10.1.4.2.

(1) The moments due to gravity loading in a purlin that is physically continuous over two spans without overlaps or sleeves, may either be obtained by calculation or based on the results of tests.
 (2) If the moments are calculated they should be determined using elastic global analysis. The purlin should satisfy the criteria for cross-section resistance given in 10.1.4.1. For the moment at the internal support, the criteria for stability of the free flange given in 10.1.4.2 should also be satisfied. For mid-support should be checked also for bending moment + support reaction (web crippling if cleats are not used) and for bending moment + shear forces depending on the case under consideration.
 (3) Alternatively the moments may be determined using the results of tests in accordance with Section 9 and Annex A.5 on the moment-rotation behaviour of the purlin over the internal support.
 NOTE: Appropriate testing procedures are given in Annex A.
 (4) The design value of the resistance moment at the supports Msup,Rd for a given value of the load per unit length qEd , should be obtained from the intersection of two curves representing the design values of:
 - the moment-rotation characteristic at the support, obtained by testing in accordance with Section 9 and Annex A.5;
 - the theoretical relationship between the support moment Msup,Ed and the corresponding plastic hinge rotation φEd in the purlin over the support.
 To determine the final design value of the support moment Msup,Ed allowance should be made for the effect of the lateral load in the free flange and/or the buckling stability of that free flange around the mid-support, which are not fully taken into account by the internal support test as given in clause A.5.2. If the free flange is physically continued at the support and if the distance between the support and the nearest anti-sag bar is larger than 0,5 s, the lateral load qh,Ed according to 10.1.4.2 should be taken into account in verification of the resistance at mid-support. Alternatively, full-scale tests for two or multi-span purlins may be used to determine the effect of the lateral load in the free flange and/or the buckling stability of that free flange around the mid- support.

The left support is a pinned bearing, the right support also a pinned bearing; both are shown as small triangular symbols beneath the beam ends. At each end of the beam a horizontal arrow labeled “NEd” points toward the interior, signifying an axial compressive force of magnitude NEd acting toward mid-span. Across the beam span a row of uniformly spaced, downward-pointing arrows represents the transverse design load qEd. On the right side an additional arrow pointing downward, located at a distance “h” below the beam’s centroidal axis, is labeled “kh qEd”; this indicates the equivalent lateral load on the free flange due to combined torsion and lateral bending.  

Beneath that, on the left of the middle tier, is a cross‐sectional outline of a C‐ or Z‐shaped cold‐formed steel purlin, oriented with its web vertical (z–z axis) and flange plane horizontal (y–y axis). To the right of the section, three simplified stress diagrams are arrayed in a row, each preceded by a downward arrow—indicating superposition of their effects in the cross-section:  

1. The first diagram, with a triangular‐shaded shape sloping from maximum compression at one flange to zero at the opposite flange, represents bending stresses due to the in‐plane moment My,Ed. Beneath it is the notation “My,Ed / Weff,y,” referring to the effective section modulus about the y–y axis.  
2. The second diagram, a uniformly shaded rectangle, denotes direct stress from axial compression NEd acting over the effective cross‐sectional area Aeff; it is labeled “NEd / Aeff.”  
3. The third diagram is another uniform rectangular block—this time representing the additional bending stress induced in the free flange by lateral bending moment M fz,Ed. It carries the label “Mfz,Ed / Wfz,” with Wfz the section modulus of the free flange plus its contributing web strip for bending about z–z.  

Below these three stress diagrams is the caption “Figure 10.2: Superposition of stresses.” Taken together, the graphic shows how the total stress at any point in the section is the algebraic sum of (a) bending about the y–y axis, (b) uniform axial compression, and (c) lateral bending about the z–z axis. In context of the adjacent formulas (10.3a), (10.3b), and (10.4), the diagram underpins the checks against yield strength for the restrained flange and free flange, the determination of equivalent lateral load kh qEd, and the computation of Mfz,Ed from torsional and lateral bending effects.

content:
The illustration presented is identified as Figure 10.3 and shows how the combined effects of torsion and lateral bending on a cold-formed purlin section can be represented by an equivalent lateral line load, denoted k_h · q_Ed, acting on the free flange. The figure is arranged in two main parts: the upper part defines the base factor k_h0 for different section geometries, and the lower part demonstrates how gravity or uplift loading and eccentricity modify k_h0 to yield the final factor k_h.

1. Upper-row diagrams: Base lateral-load factor k_h0  
   • Left—“Simple symmetrical Z section”:  
     – A symmetric Z-shaped profile is drawn in elevation, with overall depth h, flange width b, and lip length c marked.  
     – The formula below reads  
       k_h0 = h t ( b² + 2c b – 2 c² b/h ) / (4 I_y),  
       where t is sheet thickness and I_y the gross moment of inertia about the y–y axis.  
   • Right—“Z, C or Σ sections”:  
     – A typical single-sided (unsymmetrical) profile is shown, with the overall depth h and the vertical distance g_s from the shear-centre line to the free flange centreline indicated. The shear centre itself is marked, offset horizontally by e_s from the midpoint of the section web.  
     – The corresponding expression is  
       k_h0 = (I_yz / I_y) · ( g_s / h ),  
       in which I_yz is the product moment of inertia coupling axis y–y and z–z.

2. Lower-row diagrams: Equivalent factor k_h for service loads  
   Four stylized purlin cross sections are sketched, each loaded vertically by q_Ed at the top flange and resisting via the equivalent horizontal line load k_h q_Ed applied at the free bottom flange. Beneath each sketch is the rule for k_h:
   • Gravity loading, symmetric case:  
     – The vertical load aligns with the shear centre. No eccentricity exists, so k_h = k_h0.  
   • Gravity loading with eccentricity e (not passing through shear centre):  
     – The load is to the side of the shear centre by distance e (measured horizontally).  
     – The factor becomes k_h = k_h0 + e / h.  
     – Footnote: if e / h exceeds k_h0 in magnitude, the equivalent load reverses direction.  
   • Uplift (negative vertical), symmetric case with offset a:  
     – The vertical uplift is applied through the shear centre but the free flange location introduces an effective lever arm a.  
     – Here k_h = k_h0 – a / h.  
   • Uplift with arbitrary flange load position f:  
     – The vertical uplift q_Ed is applied at a horizontal offset f measured from the free flange edge.  
     – The factor is k_h = k_h0 – f / h, limited so f remains within the flange width.

3. Footnotes and notes:  
   – If the shear centre lies to the right of where q_Ed is applied, the sign of the generated k_h q_Ed load reverses.  
   – The magnitude of f is constrained by the flange width—q_Ed must not be placed outside the flange extremes.  
   – This diagram supports the designer by converting complex lateral-torsional behaviour into a simple equivalent lateral line load, which can then be used in the superposition checks of combined bending M_y,Ed, axial force N_Ed, and lateral-torsional effects on the free flange as defined elsewhere (see formulas 10.3a,b and clause 10.1.4 of the standard).
