content:
The input is an extract of “Table 10.1: Values of initial moment M₀,fz,Ed and correction factor κR” for the lateral bending (“curling”) of a purlin’s free flange under a uniformly distributed equivalent lateral load qh,Ed. The table provides ready‐to‐use expressions for the unfactored initial flange moment M₀,fz,Ed and the factor κR that corrects this moment for the actual elastic restraint provided by anti-sag bars or other lateral springs. The results are given for three common restraint configurations. Below is a detailed, column-by-column description:

1. System (restraint configuration)  
   The first column shows a simple beam with no intermediate support (i.e. anti-sag bars) along its span L (so La = L).  
   The second block shows a beam with one lateral support located at 5/8·La from the left end.  
   The third block shows a beam with two identical lateral supports, each located at La/2 from its neighbouring support (i.e. supports symmetrically at mid-span).  

2. Location  
   For each configuration two characteristic positions are considered:  
   – “m” for mid-span (maximum moment section)  
   – “e” for the section immediately adjacent to a support or anti-sag bar  

3. Initial lateral bending moment M₀,fz,Ed  
   This is the bending moment in the free flange due solely to the equivalent uniformly distributed lateral load qh,Ed, assuming no elastic restraint (i.e. infinite flange deflection). The expressions are:  
   System 1 (no bars):  
     m:   M₀,fz,Ed = (1/8)·qh,Ed·La²  
   System 2 (one bar at 5/8 La):  
     m:   M₀,fz,Ed = (9/128)·qh,Ed·La²  
     e:   M₀,fz,Ed = –(1/8)·qh,Ed·La²  
   System 3 (two bars at ±La/2):  
     m:   M₀,fz,Ed = (1/24)·qh,Ed·La²  
     e:   M₀,fz,Ed = –(1/12)·qh,Ed·La²  

4. Correction factor κR  
   The factor κR accounts for the beam-on-elastic-foundation effect, i.e. the partial restraint from the lateral spring stiffness K (per unit length). It is expressed as a rational function of the non-dimensional stiffness parameter R (see formula (10.6) for definition). Typical limits of applicability are R ≤ 40. The κR expressions in the table are:  
   System 1 (no bars):  
     κR = (1 – 0.0225·R) / (1 + 1.013·R)  
   System 2 (one bar):  
     at m: κR = (1 – 0.0141·R) / (1 + 0.416·R)  
     at e: κR = (1 + 0.0314·R) / (1 + 0.396·R)  
   System 3 (two bars):  
     at m: κR = (1 – 0.0125·R) / (1 + 0.198·R)  
     at e: κR = (1 + 0.0178·R) / (1 + 0.191·R)  

Key notes:  
• La is the span between lateral supports (or the full span L if no intermediate supports are present).  
• R is defined in equation (10.6) as R = K·La⁴/Ifz, where Ifz is the second moment of area of the free flange plus its contributing web.  
• The table entries give closed‐form values of the initial flange moment and its reduction factor; the factored lateral bending moment is then Mfz,Ed = κR·M₀,fz,Ed (unless the free flange is in tension, in which case Mfz,Ed may be taken as zero).  
• Valid for purlins where flange curling dominates and where anti-sag bars (or equivalent lateral springs) provide the only out-of-plane restraint.

content:
The excerpt you have provided (Table 10.2b) is a lookup table of the coefficients η₁–η₄ used to calculate the buckling length of a freely‐flanged purlin under uplift loading.  These coefficients enter into the empirical formulae (10.10a) and (10.10b) of EN 1993-1-3 (clause 10.1.4.2), which in turn give the effective buckling length L₀ for variations of compressive stress along the free flange when no axial tension is present (0 ≤ R₀ ≤ 200).  Here is a structured breakdown of the table’s content and usage:

1. Table Purpose  
   - Provides sets of coefficients η₁, η₂, η₃, η₄ that model how the compressive stress distribution over span L₀ influences the buckling length under uplift (negative bending)  
   - Applies only when anti‐sag bars laterally support the free flange at regular intervals (or none at all), and when the system behaves as a continuously supported beam (no local sleeve rotations)

2. Table Layout  
   - Column 1 “Span”: distinguishes between end spans and intermediate spans of a continuous beam system  
   - Column 2 “Anti-sag bar Number”: lists the count of equally‐spaced lateral supports along each span—0, 1, 2, or “3 and 4”  
   - Columns 3–6 “η₁” through “η₄”: numeric coefficients used in the buckling‐length formula (10.10a)

3. Row Groups and Coefficients  
   A. No anti-sag bars (Number = 0)  
    • End span:  
       – η₁ = 0.694  
       – η₂ = 5.45  
       – η₃ = 1.27  
       – η₄ = –0.168  
    • Intermediate span:  
       – η₁ = 0.515  
       – η₂ = 1.26  
       – η₃ = 0.868  
       – η₄ = –0.242  
    • “Middle” span (often for continuous three-span systems or symmetric cases):  
       – η₁ = 0.306  
       – η₂ = 0.232  
       – η₃ = 0.742  
       – η₄ = –0.279  

   B. One anti-sag bar (Number = 1)  
    • End spans:  
       – η₁ = 0.800  
       – η₂ = 6.75  
       – η₃ = 1.49  
       – η₄ = –0.155  
    • Intermediate span: (same as “middle” above for one bar)  
       – η₁ = 0.515  
       – η₂ = 1.26  
       – η₃ = 0.868  
       – η₄ = –0.242  

   C. Two anti-sag bars (Number = 2)  
    • End span:  
       – η₁ = 0.902  
       – η₂ = 8.55  
       – η₃ = 2.18  
       – η₄ = –0.111  
    • Intermediate spans: (identical to one‐bar end spans)  
       – η₁ = 0.800  
       – η₂ = 6.75  
       – η₃ = 1.49  
       – η₄ = –0.155  

   D. Three or four anti-sag bars (Number = 3 and 4)  
    • End spans: (same as two‐bar end spans)  
       – η₁ = 0.902  
       – η₂ = 8.55  
       – η₃ = 2.18  
       – η₄ = –0.111  
    • Intermediate spans: (same as two‐bar intermediate spans)  
       – η₁ = 0.800  
       – η₂ = 6.75  
       – η₃ = 1.49  
       – η₄ = –0.155  

4. How to Use in Calculation  
   - Identify the span type (end or intermediate) and the number of anti-sag bars providing lateral support.  
   - Read off η₁–η₄ from the relevant row.  
   - Compute the non-dimensional parameter R₀ = Nₑd·L₀² / (EI_fz⋅π²), where I_fz is the free-flange moment of inertia and K is another geometric factor (see 10.1.4.1(7)).  
   - Substitute R₀ and η-coefficients into equation (10.10a):  
        L₀ = η₁·L·[1 + η₂·R₀ + η₃·R₀² + η₄·R₀³]  
   - If preferred, an alternative approach uses Table 10.2b together with clause 10.1.4.2(3).

5. Limitations and Notes  
   - Valid for uplift loading only (no axial compression).  
   - Assumes uniform span length L and uniform spacing of anti-sag bars.  
   - Not applicable if significant rotation occurs at overlaps or sleeves—then a more rigorous buckling‐length analysis is required.  

In summary, Table 10.2b gives all the numerical η-coefficients needed to calculate the buckling length of a free flange under uplift for various patterns of lateral support. By classifying your span (end vs. intermediate) and counting your anti-sag bars (0–4), you can quickly extract the appropriate η₁–η₄ and feed them into the standard EN 1993-1-3 uplift buckling‐length formulae.

The image is composed of two schematic line‐drawings, stacked one above the other, each illustrating how the compressive stress in the “free” flange of a steel purlin varies along its length under uplift loading. A brief caption beneath both sketches reads “Figure 10.5: Varying compressive stress in free flange for uplift cases,” and a note in square brackets clarifies that “dotted areas show regions in compression.”  

Top Sketch (Single‐span case)  
– A straight, horizontal line represents the steel purlin. At each end it sits on a simple support (drawn as small, inverted triangular blocks).  
– Above the beam is a single, symmetrical “arch” or half‐sine curve, indicating the distribution of bending moment (and hence compressive stress in the top flange) under a uniform uplift load.  
– The entire arched region is hatched with a fine dot pattern to mark it as the compression zone of the free flange.  
– Directly beneath the beam is a double‐headed, horizontal dimension arrow labeled “L₀ = L,” indicating that the buckling length for compression (L₀) in this case equals the full span length (L).  

Bottom Sketch (Continuous or multi‐span case with anti‐sag intermediate supports)  
– Again a straight horizontal line depicts the purlin, but now it spans over three supports: one at each end and one located at mid‐span. The end supports are simple, inverted triangular blocks; the interior support is shown as a small, right‐side‐up triangular anti‐sag bar pressing upward against the underside of the beam flange.  
– Two half‐sine “arches” (dotted) appear above the beam: one between the left end support and the interior anti‐sag bar, the other between that bar and the right end support. Each of these dotted arches marks a region where the free flange experiences compression under uplift.  
– Beneath each of these arches a pair of horizontal dimension arrows is drawn: the inner pair is labeled “L₀,” marking the buckling‐length segment between zero‐moment points, while a longer outer pair is labeled “L,” denoting the full span between major supports. The two L₀ segments together equal the overall span L.  
– A vertical dashed centerline aligns the interior anti‐sag support with the symmetry of the two adjacent compressed regions.  

Visual Style and Annotation  
– All structural elements (beams, supports, dimension lines) are rendered in solid black lines.  
– Compression zones are filled with a uniform dot‐shading pattern distinct from any cross‐hatching.  
– Dimension arrows are simple, straight lines with arrowheads; text labels (L₀, L, “=”) are set plainly in a sans‐serif font.  
– The note “[Dotted areas show regions in compression]” appears just above the figure caption, tying the graphical shading back to the technical discussion of free‐flange buckling.  

Overall, the two‐part figure visually contrasts a single‐span purlin—where the compression zone extends uninterrupted along the entire unsupported length—with a continuous or multi‐span condition where anti‐sag restraints break the compression region into shorter, repeated segments. The annotated lengths L₀ and L directly correspond to the buckling‐length formulas and tabulated η-coefficients discussed in the accompanying clauses of EN 1993-1-3.

The illustration, labeled “Figure 10.6: Purlin and attached sheeting,” presents two side-elevation cross-sections of a cold-formed steel purlin supporting a roof or wall sheeting panel via mechanical fasteners. The two sub-figures contrast the geometry and load application for:

3. Purlin Cross-Section: a hat- or C-shaped cold-formed section with an upper flange, web, and lower flange. Rendered in bold outline; upper and lower flanges are horizontal, connected by a vertical web with slight lip flanges at the base.

This figure supports the calculation of lateral spring stiffness K per unit length for combined sheeting-purlin systems (see clauses 10.1.5.4 and formulas 10.11–10.13). Specifically, it defines the key horizontal distances used to determine the lever arm bmod in the distortion-stiffness term (KC) of the composite lateral spring model. By clearly indicating the fastener location relative to the web and flange and by annotating the corresponding distances, the figure enables precise input data for both testing-based and analytical evaluations of KA, KB, and the combined lateral stiffness K.

The image is labeled “Figure 10.7: Model for calculating CD,C” and consists of two schematic beam‐and‐spring models that represent how a continuous roof sheet spans between purlins (structural supports) and how the sheet’s flexural stiffness contributes to rotational restraint. In both models the sheet is idealized as a bending beam of unit width, and each purlin connection is represented by a rotational spring acting at the sheet’s top flange. An applied moment per unit width “m” and the resulting rotation “θ” are illustrated at one support; the ratio m/θ defines the rotational stiffness CD,C for the sheeting.

Top diagram:
• Three inverted‐C purlin profiles are drawn in cross section along the bottom, evenly spaced.  
• A sinusoidal (corrugated) line atop them represents the continuous roof sheeting.  
• At each purlin location the sheeting is connected and modeled by a rotational spring. The two outer springs are labeled with stiffness coefficients “k = 2” at the left support and “k = 4” at the right support.  
• The central support—also a purlin—is the point of interest: an arrowed curved arrow labeled “m, θ” indicates that a moment per unit width m is applied there, causing the sheet to rotate through an angle θ (in radians).  
• The distance between the first and last supports is marked by a horizontal double‐arrow “s,” denoting the constant span between purlins.

Bottom diagram:
• A second variant of the model is shown immediately below with a slightly different corrugated beam shape, indicating a different continuity or boundary condition case.  
• Four purlin profiles are implied, but only the two exterior rotational springs are explicitly labeled: “k = 3” on the left and “k = 6” on the right.  
• The applied moment “m” and rotation “θ” are again shown at the central support (second purlin from the left), just as in the top model.  
• No span length dimension is drawn here, but it is understood to be the same constant spacing “s” between adjacent purlins.

Together, these two simplified models illustrate how one can calculate CD,C by selecting an appropriate series of rotational‐spring stiffness ratios (the k values) that reflect the degree of sheet continuity and the relative stiffness of adjacent purlin connections. Under a unit moment m the rotation θ is determined (either analytically or by finite‐element simulation), and CD,C is then taken as m/θ. By comparing the two configurations (k = 2/4 versus k = 3/6), the effect of support continuity and spring‐constant distribution on the overall rotational restraint provided by the sheeting can be assessed.

The table reproduced below (Table 10.4) is a concise “look-up” for the design shear force per unit length qs and the design tensile force per unit length qt in each row of fasteners along a cold-formed purlin under gravity or uplift loading.  In practice, once qs and qt have been determined per unit length (N/mm or kN/m), they are multiplied by the fastener pitch e to give the force in an individual fastener (qs · e and qt · e).  

 1. Table structure  
    • Columns:  
      – “Shear force per unit length qs”  
      – “Tensile force per unit length qt”  
    • Rows, by purlin section and loading:  
      – Z-beam, gravity loading  
      – Z-beam, uplift loading  
      – C-beam, gravity loading  
      – C-beam, uplift loading  

 2. Definition of symbols  
    • qEd: the design vertical (gravity or uplift) or wind load per unit length on the sheeting, transferred to the purlin.  
    • kh: a stiffness or distribution factor for the connecting element (from Table 10.1 or the relevant national annex).  
    • ξ (xi): an eccentricity or moment‐distribution factor (see note below).  
    • h: the net depth (web height) of the purlin.  
    • a: the distance from the web centerline to the sheet-to-purlin fastener line.  (For Z-beams under symmetrical loading, a ≅ b/2; for C-beams, a is measured to the loaded flange.)  
    • b: the total flange width (used for C-beam uplift cases, so that b – a is the lever arm to the unloaded flange).  
    • e: fastener spacing (pitch) along the beam – not in the table but applied subsequently as qs · e, qt · e.  

 3. Row-by-row formulas  

    3.1 Z-beam, gravity loading  
      • qs  = (1 + ξ) · kh · qEd  
        – NOTE: in many design codes the stabilizing‐force portion (ξ·kh·qEd) may be neglected, permitting qs ≈ 0 if desired.  
      • qt  = 0  
        – No net tension in the fastener under downward (gravity) loading.  

    3.2 Z-beam, uplift loading  
      • qs  = (1 + ξ) · (kh  –  a/h) · qEd  
        – The term a/h accounts for the eccentricity of load application through the web.  
      • qt  = |ξ·kh·qEd·(h/a)|  +  qEd  
        – The first term is tension from moment‐distribution, the second is the direct uplift component.  
        – In a symmetric Z-section loaded on its upper flange, one often takes a ≅ b/2.  

    3.3 C-beam, gravity loading  
      • qs  = (1 – ξ) · kh · qEd  
        – Under gravity, part of the moment is resisted as shear but in the opposite sense to uplift.  
      • qt  = ξ · kh · qEd · (h/a)  
        – Tension arises from the stabilizing‐moment arm h/a, transferred into the loaded flange.  

    3.4 C-beam, uplift loading  
      • qs  = (1 – ξ) · (kh  –  a/h) · qEd  
      • qt  = ξ·kh·qEd·[h/(b – a)]  +  qEd  
        – Here b – a is the lever‐arm from web to the “uplifted” flange.  The +qEd term again represents direct uplift.  

 4. Contextual notes (from EN 1993-1-1 and related clauses)  
    • A supplementary shear from diaphragm action (parallel to the flange) is vectorially added to qs once qs·e is computed.  
    • Fasteners at supports (purlin‐to‐rafter connections) use a different set of tables (e.g., Table 10.5) for reaction forces Rw, R1, R2.  
    • For continuous purlins, the reaction at an intermediate support may be taken as 2.2 × (reactive forces from Table 10.5).  
    • The correction factor κ in EN 1993-1-3 for cold-formed members (used in kh, or to adjust qEd) appears in Table 10.1.  
    • For sloping roofs, vertical loads decompose into components perpendicular and parallel to the roof plane; only the perpendicular component enters the “sheathing-to-purlin” load for qs and qt in Table 10.4.  

In summary, Table 10.4 provides a parametric, geometry-based method to derive shear and tension demand per unit length in each fastener row on Z- or C-purlins, under both downward (gravity) and upward (wind) loading.  These expressions feed directly into the design check where:  
  qs(e) = qs · e  
  qt(e) = qt · e  
and are then combined vectorially with supplemental shear or stabilizing forces as required by EN 1993-1-1.

10.1.6  Forces in sheet/purlin fasteners and reaction forces

content:
The illustration, labeled “Figure 10.8: Reaction forces at support,” is a black-and-white line drawing showing a cold-formed steel purlin section resting on an inclined support. The purlin is a C-shaped channel with two parallel flanges and a vertical web. It is drawn in solid lines, slightly rotated so that its bearing flange contacts a sloping plane (the roof rafter or main beam) at the lower end. A dashed outline of roof sheeting is attached atop the upper flange, indicating the sheet profile and the line of fastener connections that transfer loads into the purlin.  

Four key forces are shown with thick arrows and annotated with standard symbols:  
• qEd: A vertical arrow pointing downward onto the top flange of the purlin, labeled qₑd. This represents the design load from the roof sheeting, acting perpendicular to the plane of the sheeting.  
• R₂: A horizontal arrow along the axis of the top flange, pointing toward the left. This denotes the transverse reaction force in the plane of the flange, transferred from the sheeting through the fasteners. In the context of a sloped roof, R₂ includes both perpendicular and parallel components of the vertical loads, as explained in the accompanying text.  
• Rw: An arrow running downward parallel to the web, indicating the in-plane reaction force on the web (reaction Rw). This force arises from the fasteners fixing the purlin to its support, resisting shear in the purlin’s web.  
• R₁: A horizontal arrow at the lower flange, pointing toward the right, labeled R₁. This force is the reaction in the flange plane at the support. The notation in the text clarifies that if R₁ is positive, the fastener is not in tension.  

The sloped support beneath the purlin is shown as a straight line inclined up and to the right. The C-section profile is oriented so that its lower flange sits flush on this sloping surface. The web leans under the top flange and meets the lower flange at right angles, illustrating the typical geometry used in roof structures. The dashed sheet profile overlays the purlin’s crown and returns, suggesting the sheeting’s curvature or trapezoidal shape and indicating how the load qEd is applied through the fasteners.  

Overall, the diagram conveys how gravity (qEd) and wind uplift (in a different loading case) generate reaction forces R₁, R₂ and Rw at the support interface. It supports the surrounding commentary on checking fastener capacities: shear forces perpendicular to the flange (qs e), tension forces (qt e) from table 10.4, and web reactions per table 10.5. The figure underscores the need to vectorially add diaphragm and stabilizing shear components, to consider the 2.2 factor for continuous purlins at inner supports, and to route R₂ through cleats or shear connectors into the rafter system.

10.1.6  Forces in sheet/purlin fasteners and reaction forces

content:
The following is a structured breakdown of “Table 10.5 Reaction force at support for simply supported beam,” together with its key variables and how it fits into the broader fastener–purlin–rafter design context.

1. Table title and purpose  
   - Title: “Reaction force at support for simply supported beam”  
   - Purpose: To provide closed-form expressions for the support reactions resolved into two components—one acting on the bottom flange (R₁) and one on the top flange (R₂)—for two common cold-formed purlin shapes (Z-beam and C-beam) under both gravity and uplift loading. These flange reactions are essential when checking the shear and tension capacities of the fasteners that attach purlins to their supports (see context notes under point 2).

2. Variables and parameters  
   - R₁: Reaction force on the bottom flange of the beam, positive in the direction that would tend to pull the bottom flange away from its support.  
   - R₂: Reaction force on the top flange, positive in the direction that would tend to pull the top flange away.  
   - qₑd: Design uniformly distributed load (force per unit length) acting on the beam.  
   - L: Span length of the simply supported beam (distance between supports).  
   - kₕ: Correction factor accounting for non-uniform load distribution (from Table 10.1).  
   - ζ (zeta): Load-distribution factor reflecting continuity or fixity at the support. For an interior support of a continuous purlin, reaction values may be multiplied by 2.2; otherwise ζ may be taken per clause (3) (κζ = 3/Rξ, etc.).  
   - Sign convention: A positive R implies flange tension (i.e. fastener pull-out), a negative R implies flange compression (fastener in shear only).

3. Table layout  

  Beam and loading case        | R₁ (bottom-flange)               | R₂ (top-flange)  
  -----------------------------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------  
  Z-beam, gravity loading      |   (1 − ζ)·kₕ·qₑd·L / 2            |   (1 + ζ)·kₕ·qₑd·L / 2  
  Z-beam, uplift loading       |  −(1 − ζ)·kₕ·qₑd·L / 2            |  −(1 + ζ)·kₕ·qₑd·L / 2  
  C-beam, gravity loading      |  −(1 − ζ)·kₕ·qₑd·L / 2            |   (1 − ζ)·kₕ·qₑd·L / 2  
  C-beam, uplift loading       |   (1 − ζ)·kₕ·qₑd·L / 2            |  −(1 − ζ)·kₕ·qₑd·L / 2  

4. Interpretation of each case  
   • Z-beam, gravity: bottom-flange reaction is reduced by the factor (1–ζ), top-flange reaction is increased by (1+ζ).  
   • Z-beam, uplift: both flange reactions reverse their sign (indicating tension reversals under uplift).  
   • C-beam, gravity: the bottom flange is in compression (negative R₁) and the top flange in tension, both scaled by (1–ζ).  
   • C-beam, uplift: the sign pattern flips relative to gravity, again with (1–ζ) scaling.

5. How to use in design checks  
   - Compute R₁ and R₂ for the relevant beam shape and load case.  
   - For each flange fastener:  
     – If Rᵢ > 0, the fastener is loaded in tension (pull-out); if Rᵢ < 0, in shear (bearing).  
     – Combine with other shear forces (diaphragm action, stabilizing shear per EN 1993-1-1) as vector sums.  
   - For sloped roofs, decompose vertical loads into components perpendicular and parallel to the roof plane before applying qₑd.

6. Relation to adjoining clauses  
   - Clause (1) describes how to combine flange reactions (R₁, R₂) with diaphragm‐ and stabilizing‐shear forces for the sheeting-to-purlin fasteners.  
   - Clause (2) directs that R₂ (top flange force) must be transferred through the purlin-rafter connection or special shear connectors.  
   - Clause (3) offers guidance on selecting ζ for continuous purlin supports (ζ ≃ 3/Rξ, etc.).  

By following this table and the associated notes, an engineer can systematically determine and check each fastener’s load demand—both shear and tension—at purlin supports under live, dead, uplift, and wind loads.

  • Two vertical “web” panels rising from the edges of the wide flange.  
  • Two narrow horizontal “flanges” folded outward at the tops of those vertical webs.  
  • The narrow flanges are intended to be laterally braced by attachment to profiled steel decking or cladding.

1. Top View (first isometric):  
   - The geometry is shown before any dimensioning except for the overall section height h measured from the underside of the wide flange to the top of the narrow flanges.  
   - An arrow labeled s₁ points along the length of the tray, indicating the principal direction for shear‐force resistance.  
   - The wide flange in this depiction appears corrugated in small, regular trapezoidal ridges, but no specific depths or widths are dimensioned in this view.

2. Middle View (second isometric):

   - A dimension b_f (flange width) marks the horizontal projection of each narrow flange outward from its web.  
   - The corrugation pattern in the wide flange remains visible but undimensioned.  
   - The narrow flanges continue to provide lateral restraint to the webs.

3. Bottom View (third isometric):  
   - The overall clear width b_u of the wide flange is dimensioned between the base of the two vertical webs.  
   - The flange width b_f and depth h are re-shown for clarity in context of the full tray width b_u.  
   - The corrugations are again lightly sketched but without individual ridge spacing shown.

Below these three perspectives, two simplified cross‐sectional line diagrams illustrate the corrugation geometry along a transverse cut through the wide flange:

  • In both profiles, the top and bottom boundaries of the wide flange are marked by horizontal dashed lines labeled “a — a.”  
  • The first line diagram shows a series of narrow triangular peaks and valleys; the vertical distance from valley to peak is labeled h_u.

Under the figure, the caption reads “Figure 10.9: Typical geometry for liner trays.” The surrounding text specifies that these trays are large channel sections with two narrow flanges laterally restrained by profiled sheeting; that shear resistance of webs is calculated per clauses 6.1.5–6.1.11 using the moment resistance M_c,Rd computed via formula (3) or (4); and that geometric properties must lie within table 10.6. An additional design constraint, 0.75 mm ≤ I_a/b_u ≤ 10 mm^4/mm, is noted in the accompanying commentary. This overall depiction provides the necessary dimensional references (h, b_f, b_u, h_u, s₁) and the typical corrugation forms used to govern both analytical and test‐based determination of moment resistance for steel liner trays.

content:
Title: Table 10.6 – Validity Limits for Applying Formula 10.2.2 to Liner-Tray Cross-Sections

Overview  
This table specifies the geometric bounds within which the simplified moment-capacity formula (clause 10.2.2) may be used to calculate the bending resistance, Mc,Rd, of a liner tray. If any of these limits is exceeded, the designer must resort to full testing (clause 10.2.2(4)) or a more general approach. All dimensions refer to the cross-section as shown in Figure 10.9: two narrow flanges, two webs, and one wide flange having corrugations. The narrow flanges are laterally braced by the attached sheeting.

Entries in Table 10.6

1. Nominal thickness (tnom)  
   – Upper limit: 1.5 mm  
   – Explanation: tnom is the thickness of the sheet metal forming the tray. Keeping tnom ≤ 1.5 mm ensures the section remains sufficiently thin for the plate-buckling assumptions implicit in the formula.

2. Narrow-flange width (bf)  
   – Upper limit: 60 mm  
   – Explanation: bf is the width of each of the two narrow flanges. Limiting bf prevents excessive local buckling of the flange and maintains the validity of the strip-model simplification.

3. Overall depth (h)  
   – Upper limit: 200 mm  
   – Explanation: h measures the total vertical depth of the liner tray from the tip of the narrow flange to the tip of the opposite flange on the wide side. A maximum depth of 200 mm ensures that the bending stresses and buckling behavior do not stray from the calibrated range of the formula.

4. Wide-flange width (bu)  
   – Upper limit: 600 mm  
   – Explanation: bu is the overall width of the wide (outer) flange, including corrugations. Restricting bu to 600 mm ensures that the corrugated flange behaves predictably under bending and shear.

5. Second-moment ratio (Ia/bu)  
   – Range: 0.75 mm4 / mm ≤ Ia/bu ≤ 10 mm4 / mm  
   – Table entry: Ia/bu ≤ 10 mm4 / mm (the lower bound is provided in the accompanying note)  
   – Explanation: Ia is the second moment of area (about the horizontal axis) of the corrugated flange per unit length of flange width. Dividing by bu normalizes this stiffness parameter. Staying within this band guarantees that local flange buckling and overall tray flexure fall inside the behavior envelope for which the formula was derived.

6. Corrugation pitch (s1)  
   – Upper limit: 1000 mm  
   – Explanation: s1 is the center-to-center spacing of the corrugations on the wide flange. A maximum of 1 000 mm keeps the flange’s local stiffening effect within the proven range.

Practical Implication  
When designing liner trays used in composite floor systems, verify each of the six parameters against Table 10.6. If all criteria are met, Mc,Rd can be taken from clause 10.2.2. Otherwise, you must carry out physical testing per Annex A or apply a more refined structural-stability analysis.

The illustration in Figure 10.10 is divided into three logical parts—an initial section sketch, the “Step 1” centroid‐and‐effective‐width determination, and the “Step 2” stress‐block layouts—each shown twice to cover both possible flange-in-compression orientations (flange at bottom or at top).

1. Primary Cross-Section Sketch (leftmost drawing)  
   • Depicts a cold-formed “C” or channel section (liner tray) with its open side facing right.  
   • The vertical web is on the left, of total depth h (dimension line from bottom of lower flange to top of upper flange).  
   • The bottom (“wide”) flange extends rightward by half the gross flange width, labeled bᵤ/2.  
   • The upper flange is shorter and slopes slightly downward at its free end; its full width is labeled b𝒻.  
   • A horizontal dashed reference line (the neutral axis of the gross section) is drawn through roughly mid-depth. A vertical arrow at mid-height denotes the eccentricity e₀ from that axis.  

2. Step 1: Effective Cross-Section and Centroid  
   • Two nearly identical C-section sketches appear side by side, labeled “Step 1,” showing the two possible loading orientations (compression flange at bottom or flipped to top).  
   • On each, the web remains at full gross width, while the compression flange is replaced by an “effective” width bᵤ,eff (half of which is shown on either side of the web’s centerline) to account for local buckling.  
   • The distances from the determined neutral axis of the effective section to the extreme fibre in compression (zₜ) and to the extreme fibre in tension (z_c) are dimensioned by vertical arrows.  
   • A small note indicates that the smaller of the two depth ratios, Iᵧ,eff∕zₜ or Iᵧ,eff∕z_c, was used to limit bᵤ,eff.  

3. Step 2: Stress Distribution in Compression and Tension  
   • Again two variants of the C-section are shown, corresponding to flange-in-compression at bottom or at top.  
   • Adjacent to each section is a pair of hatched stress blocks:  
     – A triangular or trapezoidal block on the compressed flange, with its peak stress at σ₂ = 0.8·fᵧb / γₘ₀, tapering toward the neutral axis.  
     – A rectangular (or lightly hatched) block on the web and/or opposite flange representing σ₁, which may be either the same yield level (0.8 fᵧb / γₘ₀) or less, depending on whether the web has yielded.  
   • The two alternative stress layouts cover:  
     a. σ₂ reaches 0.8 fᵧb / γₘ₀ over the entire flange width while σ₁ remains below that value in the web.  
     b. σ₁ in the web has also reached 0.8 fᵧb / γₘ₀, while σ₂ in the flange is correspondingly reduced.  

4. Caption and Formula Reference  
   • Below the graphics is the caption “Figure 10.10: Determination of moment resistance — wide flange in compression.”  
   • The context text refers to equations for Mₙ,Rd, including the relation  
       Mₙ,Rd = 0.8·W_eff,min·fᵧb / γₘ₀  
     and the definition  
       W_eff,min = Iᵧ,eff / zₜ  or  Iᵧ,eff / z_c.  

Altogether, the figure guides the user through: (1) replacing the physical flange by an effective width, (2) locating the neutral axis of that modified section, (3) checking which flange-or-web element controls the section modulus, and (4) applying appropriate stress profiles to compute the plastic moment resistance in compression.

The illustration, titled “Figure 10.12: Stressed skin action in a flat-roof building,” is laid out in two principal parts.  On the left is a three-dimensional perspective of a simple portal-frame structure in which the roof sheeting is engaged as a stressed skin diaphragm; on the right is an exploded, schematic view showing how the sheeting and edge members behave together as a deep “plate girder” in shear.

Left-hand view (overall building frame and diaphragm action):  
• The building comprises a series of identical portal frames—five bays in a row—each frame having two sloping rafters meeting at a ridge, vertical legs, and a horizontal tie (shown faintly beneath the roof).  
• Each rafter pair supports a continuous sheeted roof. One of the roof panels (in the first bay) is hatched diagonally to indicate the active diaphragm.  
• Small solid-circle nodes mark where the sheet sheeting is attached to the underlying rafters or purlins by short drop rods or hangers. These connections ensure that in-plane shear loads in the sheet are transmitted into the frame.  
• Diagonal cross-braces appear in the wall planes of some bays, tying the rafters down to the base. These illustrate secondary bracing but are not the primary shear path in this stressed skin arrangement.  
• Thick, black arrows, drawn parallel to the plane of the roof panels, show the direction of applied transverse loads (for example wind or seismic forces acting in-plane) on the diaphragm. These loads are carried as shear through the sheet and then into the end gable frames (or into intermediate stiffened frames) via the hangers and rafters.  

Right-hand view (detail of plate-girder analogy):  
This exploded sketch breaks the system into three key components, labeled (a), (b) and (c):  
(a) Sheeting “web” – two hatched parallelogram plates, one above the other, represent the roof (or floor) cladding panels. Arrows along their long edges indicate the in-plane shear flow resisting transverse loads.  
(b) Flange members – the pairs of horizontal elements immediately adjacent to the webs depict the edge members of the diaphragm. On the lower plate these are in tension, shown by opposing arrows pulling outward; on the upper plate they are in compression, arrows pushing inward.  
(c) Connection between web and flange – diagonal lines or small arrows between the plates and their flanges illustrate the transfer of axial forces (tension/compression) from the sheeting into the edge members.  

In combination, the two sheets take the role of the “web” of a deep plate girder, resisting shear, while the edge members act as top and bottom “flanges” carrying axial forces. This captures the stressed-skin principle: the cladding contributes both strength and stiffness, turning the roof or floor into a continuous diaphragm that spans the building’s length and transmits lateral loads effectively to its supporting frames.

sections: 10 Special considerations for purlins, liner trays and sheetings

content:
(1) In stressed skin design, advantage may be taken of the contribution that diaphragms of sheeting used as roofing, flooring or wall cladding make to the overall stiffness and strength of the structural frame, by means of their stiffness and strength in shear.
 (2) Roofs and floors may be treated as deep plate girders extending throughout the length of a building, resisting transverse in-plane loads and transmitting them to end gables, or to intermediate stiffened frames. The panel of sheeting may be treated as a web that resists in-plane transverse loads in shear, with the edge members acting as flanges that resist axial tension and compression forces, see figures 10.12 and 10.13.
 (3) Similarly, rectangular wall panels may be treated as bracing systems that act as shear diaphragms to resist in-plane forces.

The figure is composed of two linked sketches that together explain how roof sheeting can act as a stressed‐skin diaphragm in a typical single-storey pitched-roof steel building.  The left‐hand drawing shows a three-dimensional perspective of the building, while the right-hand sketch isolates a pair of adjacent roof panels in plan to illustrate the flow of diaphragm forces and the roles of the various components.  Key elements are labeled (a) through (d).

Left-hand perspective view  
 1. Structural frames: A series of equally spaced portal or “A-frame” steel frames run along the building’s length to support the roof.  Vertical down-stand arrows at the ridge illustrate applied vertical loads (wind, snow, crane loads, etc.).  
 2. Roof sheeting (a): Corrugated or profiled metal sheeting is fixed continuously across each pair of rafters.  In addition to its weatherproofing function, this sheeting is used as an integral shear diaphragm—i.e. it resists in-plane horizontal displacement (‘drift’) induced by wind or other lateral loads.  
 3. Longitudinal edge members (b): At each eaves line and at the ridge, rigid members (tubes, angles or channels) run continuously along the building.  These are the flange elements of the “stressed‐skin” diaphragm and collect the shear stresses from the sheeting.  
 4. Shear fillet or panel field (c): The hatched region on one roof panel highlights where the sheeting actively resists shear.  The shaded area represents the portion of the panel that carries shear forces; its corrugations run parallel to the member direction so flange forces can be picked up by the sheeting itself.  
 5. Gable diaphragms or walls (d): At each end-wall (the gable) a framed diaphragm or braced wall assembly resists and anchors the in-plane forces collected by the roof diaphragm, transmitting them down to foundations.  

Right-hand plan view of two adjoining roof panels  
 • The two rectangular panels are hatched alternately to show individual diaphragm fields.  Each panel’s shear resistance is transmitted to the adjacent longitudinal edge members (b), indicated by double-headed arrows.  
 • Flange forces in the edge members due to diaphragm action are shown by large arrows running parallel to the sheet corrugations.  
 • The central hatched region on one panel (c) again depicts the active shear-resisting sheeting.  

How this layout satisfies stressed-skin design principles  
 - The sheeting (a) performs its primary weatherproofing role but also—as an inseparable structural component—forms a shear diaphragm in its own plane.  It cannot be removed without re-evaluating the building’s lateral stability.  
 - Longitudinal members (b) function as flanges to collect and distribute diaphragm shear forces.  
 - Diaphragm actions in the roof plane are taken to the gable walls (d), which are either braced frames or stressed-skin panels themselves, thus providing sway resistance.  
 - Connections between sheeting, flange members, trusses and gable diaphragms are designed to transfer diaphragm forces reliably into the main steel framework and thence to foundations.  
 - Project specifications and drawings must highlight that the building relies on stressed-skin action; all calculations and details reflect this intent.  
 - With corrugations oriented parallel to the ridge, flange stresses may be directly taken up by the sheeting section.  

Though stressed-skin diaphragms are most often used in low-rise structures, the same principles can apply to floors or facades of taller buildings, provided loads remain those applied through the sheeting (wind, snow, light transient loads) rather than permanent concentrated plant or heavy machinery.

content:
The drawing (Figure 10.14) shows a single stressed-skin diaphragm panel made from profiled steel sheets, supported on two longitudinal members, and subjected to in-plane shear forces.  Below is a structured description referencing the labels (a)–(g), the applied loads, key dimensions, and the relevant design provisions:

1. Overall Geometry and Loading  
  • The panel spans a length “a” between two supporting members (purlins or beams), shown as I-sections (e).  
  • The panel width is “b,” measured normal to the corrugations.  
  • In-plane shear forces F act at each end support, producing a uniform shear flow Fa per unit width (Fa/b) along both edges of the diaphragm. Arrows on the top surface (g) indicate the shear flow direction through the corrugated sheeting.

2. Profiled Steel Sheeting (g)  
  • Continuous corrugated steel sheet spanning between the supports.  
  • Corrugations run parallel to the shorter panel dimension b, so the sheet length corresponds to “b.”  
  • Sheets are designed primarily for bending (e.g. as roofing or cladding); their diaphragm action is secondary but must be verified for shear stresses not exceeding 0.25·fyb/γM1.

3. End Sheet-to-Member Connections (a) and (f)  
  • Label (a) marks fasteners (self-tapping screws, cartridge‐fired pins, bolts or welds) installed through the troughs of the sheet directly into the top flange of the supporting member (e).  
  • A bearing strip (f) may be provided under the trough to ensure a solid load path and avoid local indentation.  
  • These fasteners must be of a type that will not loosen, pull out, or fail in shear prematurely—i.e. they must tear the sheet before the fastener itself gives way.

4. Sheet-to-Sheet (Seam) Connections (b), (c) and (d)  
  • Adjacent sheets are joined at their longitudinal seams by fasteners along the crest or trough—these are shown as rivets or self-drilling screws (b), or as small intermittent welds (c).  Label (d) indicates the seam line.  
  • Fastener spacing along each seam shall not exceed 500 mm.  
  • Edge distances are maintained to prevent premature tearing of the sheet under diaphragm loads.

5. Supporting Members (e)  
  • Typically cold-formed or rolled I-beams/purlins that carry the diaphragm shear into the main structure.  
  • The spacing between these members is the panel length “a.”  

6. Design and Detailing Notes (from clauses 1–6)  
  • All fasteners in both seam and sheet-to-member connections must transmit the design shear forces without working loose or failing before the sheet tears.  
  • Small, randomly distributed perforations (up to 3% of the diaphragm area) are permitted without recalculation provided fastener count is unchanged.  Up to 15% perforation is allowed with detailed checks; larger openings must be isolated with full-action sub-diaphragms.  
  • The diaphragm shear stress in the sheet must not exceed 0.25·fyb/γM1 so that any sheet deterioration becomes apparent in bending before it compromises shear capacity.  
  • The ultimate shear resistance is governed by the weakest line of fasteners—either the seam fasteners or the sheet-to-member fasteners parallel to the corrugations (if edge-only support).  Any alternative failure mode must have a calculated capacity at least 25% higher, and for combined shear plus uplift (wind) at least 40% higher, than this governing tearing strength.

By following these detailing and fastening rules—direct penetration into supports, controlled seam spacing, adequate edge distances, and verified material strengths—the profiled steel diaphragm panel ensures reliable transmission of in-plane shear forces into the supporting framing without premature loss of load‐carrying capacity.

content:
(1) In a profiled steel sheet diaphragm, see figure 10.14, both ends of the sheets should be attached to the supporting members by means of self-tapping screws, cartridge fired pins, welding, bolts or other fasteners of a type that will not work loose in service, pull out, or fail in shear before causing tearing of the sheeting. All such fasteners should be fixed directly through the sheeting into the supporting member, for example through the troughs of profiled sheets, unless special measures are taken to ensure that the connections effectively transmit the forces assumed in the design.
 (2) The seams between adjacent sheets should be fastened by rivets, self-drilling screws, welds, or other fasteners of a type that will not work loose in service, pull out, or fail in shear before causing tearing of the sheeting. The spacing of such fasteners should not exceed 500 mm.
 (3) The distances from all fasteners to the edges and ends of the sheets should be adequate to prevent premature tearing of the sheets.
 (4) Small randomly arranged openings, up to 3% of the relevant area, may be introduced without special calculation, provided that the total number of fasteners is not reduced. Openings up to 15% of the relevant area (the area of the surface of the diaphragm taken into account for the calculations) may be introduced if justified by detailed calculations. Areas that contain larger openings should be split into smaller areas, each with full diaphragm action.
 (5) All sheeting that also forms part of a stressed-skin diaphragm should first be designed for its primary purpose in bending. To ensure that any deterioration of the sheeting would be apparent in bending before the resistance to stressed skin action is affected, it should then be verified that the shear stress due to diaphragm action does not exceed 0,25 fyb/γM1 .
 (6) The shear resistance of a stressed-skin diaphragm should be based on the least tearing strength of the seam fasteners or the sheet-to-member fasteners parallel to the corrugations or, for diaphragms fastened only to longitudinal edge members, the end sheet-to-member fasteners. The illustration is labelled “Figure A.1: Examples of appropriate test accessories” and is drawn in two stacked views—a three-dimensional perspective above and a simplified sectional elevation below—showing how profiled steel sheeting may be laterally restrained during laboratory loading tests.  

1. Three-dimensional view (upper drawing)  
- Depicts three identical trapezoidal “ribs” of profiled sheet running longitudinally, each with sloping sides and a flat crown. They sit on a continuous flat base plate (the test support).  
- On the left-hand rib, a small arrow marked (a) points to a rivet or self-tapping screw that fastens the crown of the sheet down into the test fixture. This represents a point-fixing to prevent any upward or lateral movement at the crest.  
- Beneath the center rib, an arrow labelled (b) indicates a pair of transverse ties—thin metal straps or bands—that wrap around the profile and clamp it down onto the base. These ties run approximately perpendicular to the ribs and serve to hold the sheeting firmly to the support so that its corrugations cannot spread out under load.  
- No accessory is shown at the right-hand rib in this view, but a small black square at the end of the base under that rib hints at another type of attachment.  

2. Sectional elevation (lower drawing)  
- Shows a cut-away side view through the same three ribs, each represented as an upright rectangle (the rib walls) topped by a flat horizontal bar (the rib crown). Below them lies the beam or test support, indicated by a long horizontal line flanked by end bearings. A centerline (dash-dot) marks the beam axis.  
- Under each rib, a heavily hatched block—labelled (c) with an arrow—represents a solid timber packing block inserted between the rib and the beam flange. These blocks serve to prevent the profile from clawing or deforming when uplift or downward loads are applied, and they distribute clamping pressure evenly across the bottom of each corrugation.  
- The combination of rivets (a), transverse metal ties (b) and timber blocks (c) illustrates three widely used methods for realistically reproducing the boundary conditions that profiled sheeting would experience in service: direct fasteners into the crests, band-type restraints across the troughs, and rigid packing under each profile to mimic purlin bearing.  

Overall, Figure A.1 conveys that when testing profiled or corrugated sheeting in bending, uplift or combined loading, it is essential to prevent the individual corrugations from “spreading” or twisting out of plane. The drawing offers clear, labeled examples of mechanical attachments and block elements that ensure the specimen behaves as it would in an installed roof-or-wall application.

The illustration (labelled “Figure A.2: Test set-up for single span tests”) is a composite of five schematic sub-figures, all drawn in simple line art, showing how to apply loads and supports when testing profiled steel sheeting or similar panels under a single span. From left to right and top to bottom the details are as follows:

1. Uniformly Distributed Loading (upper-left)  
- A straight horizontal beam of length L is shown in elevation, simply supported at its ends.  
- The left support is a pinned or hinged symbol (triangular bearing), the right support is a roller symbol.  
- A series of evenly spaced downward arrows along the top flange indicate a uniformly distributed load q (or total load F over the span).  

2. Equivalent Line Loads (immediately below the first)  
- The same beam and supports appear, but instead of a continuous load, four concentrated downward arrows are shown.  
- Each arrow carries a load of F/2, and they are located at distances L/8 from each support and then at intervals of L/4 (so at L/8, 3L/8, 5L/8, and 7L/8 measured from the left support).  
- The beam length is marked beneath as “L,” with subdivisions L/8, L/4, L/4, L/4, and L/8. This arrangement is described as “an example of alternative equivalent line loads,” reproducing the effect of uniform loading with discrete loads.  

3. Distributed Loading over Corrugations (upper-right)  
- A profiled (corrugated or trapezoidal) sheeting section is sketched in cross-section and shown supporting a continuous mattress or membrane (represented by a stippled oval shape above).  
- Downward arrows across the top of the membrane denote a uniformly distributed pressure (e.g. airbag or vacuum).  
- Below the panel a slender horizontal tie (labelled “(c) Transverse tie”) is drawn in contact with the peaks of the corrugations, to prevent the profile from spreading under loading.  

4. Support Arrangement to Prevent Distortion (center-right)  
- A length of profiled panel (length L) is shown supported at one end on a roller (small cylinder) and on the other by a flat bearing.  
- The free (roller) support is set back from the panel edge by a distance greater than the panel depth h. The panel depth itself is annotated as “h.”  
- A small vertical line just inside the roller indicates the need for a bearing length of approximately h to avoid local buckling or distortion of the corrugations.  

5. Example of Applying a Line Load (bottom)  
- A profiled panel is shown with its undulating web resting on regularly spaced timber blocks (transverse to the span).  
- On top of the membrane or panel sits a rigid beam (shown in elevation) receiving a concentrated force F at its midspan.  
- Arrows on the beam indicate the load application point and the reaction from the underlying blocks, demonstrating how to simulate a line load by distributing the force through blocks onto the corrugated profile.  

Together, these sub-figures define a standardised test arrangement for single-span bending and uplift tests on profiled steel sheeting, illustrating both uniform and equivalent discrete loading patterns, the use of transverse ties to stabilise the corrugations, and specific support configurations to ensure realistic restraint and prevent local distortion under test conditions.

The image is a black-and-white schematic line drawing labeled “Figure A.3: Test setup for double span tests.” It shows a continuous beam (or profiled sheet specimen) viewed in elevation, subjected to a uniformly distributed transverse load, and supported at two regularly spaced locations so as to create two equal spans.

At the top of the drawing there is a straight horizontal line representing the top flange (or the crest line) of the test specimen. Directly above this line, a succession of downward-pointing arrows is drawn at regular intervals along its full length. These arrows indicate a uniformly distributed load applied over both spans of the specimen (for example, by air bags, a vacuum chamber or steel cross-beams).

Beneath the beam there are two support symbols spaced along its underside. The left support symbol consists of a small rigid bearing icon (a block with a hinge-like line atop a semi-circular roller), representing a pinned-roller or fixed-pin support. Approximately one half of the overall length to the right of this first support sits a second support symbol — a simplified triangular block with a small roller at its base — indicating a roller support that allows longitudinal movement but resists vertical displacement. The two supports divide the beam into two spans.

Below the beam, two dimension arrows run horizontally: one arrow pair connects the left support symbol to the central support symbol and is labeled “L,” while a second arrow pair connects the central support back to the right end of the drawn beam and is also labeled “L.” This double-arrow/L notation makes clear that the beam is continuous over two identical spans of length L. No third support is explicitly drawn at the right end, but the dimension line shows that the right free end of the loaded region extends for a further span L beyond the mid support.

Directly underneath the schematic, the caption reads:  
Figure A.3: Test setup for double span tests

Overall, the drawing conveys a test configuration in which a profiled sheet or beam is continuously supported at two intermediate points to create two equal spans, loaded uniformly to generate combinations of moment and shear at the internal support. This arrangement is used to evaluate flexural stiffness, midspan moment resistance and support reaction capacity in cold-formed sheeting or purlin tests.

Both parts show the specimen supported at its ends (a pinned support on the left, a roller support on the right) and loaded by a series of vertical point‐loads F of equal magnitude.

1. Top sketch (single‐span, uniformly spaced loads)  
- Geometry: one simply supported span of total length L, pinned at the left end and roller‐supported at the right.  
- Supports: left symbol is a fixed‐pin, right symbol a free‐roller.  
- Loading: seven identical downward arrows, each labeled “F,” are applied along the span.  
- Spacing: the first and last loads lie a distance L/8 inboard of each support. Between successive loads the clear spacing is L/4. In other words, starting from the left support:  
 • at x = L/8: load F  
 • at x = L/8 + L/4: load F  
 • at x = L/8 + 2·(L/4): load F  
 • … continuing every L/4 …  
 • last at x = L – L/8 from left support (i.e. L/8 from right).  
- Purpose: to approximate a uniformly distributed line load by a series of equi-spaced point loads.

2. Bottom sketch (two-span continuous beam)  
- Geometry: a continuous member over three supports, forming two equal spans each of length L. The leftmost and rightmost supports use the same pinned and roller symbols; the mid‐span support is shown as a single triangular roller.  
- Span breakdown (each span length = L):  
 • From end support to first load: 0.125·L  
 • From first load to second load: 0.525·L  
 • From second load to the central support: 0.35·L  
 • Symmetrically on the right span: 0.35·L from mid support to third load, 0.525·L to fourth load, and 0.125·L to the right support.  
- Loading: four identical downward arrows labeled “F” are placed—two on each span—at the positions defined above.  
- Purpose: to generate internal moments and shear forces representative of a uniformly distributed load on a continuous two‐span member, including negative bending over the interior support.

Across both arrangements:  
- All point loads are of equal magnitude F.  
- The total projected length between the outer supports in the top sketch is L; in the bottom sketch the overall distance is 2·L (two spans of length L each).  
- Dimensions under the beam line are annotated with fractional multiples of L to define exact load positions.  
- Caption identifies these as “alternative line loads,” meaning they are substitute arrangements to emulate uniform or continuous loading in physical test setups.

content:
The drawing is composed of three schematic test‐setups (a, b and c), all collectively captioned “Figure A.5: Test set-up for internal support test.” Each setup shows a thin-walled cold-formed beam (for example a purlin section) of overall depth h, simply supported at its ends, and loaded in the middle on an internal support of width bB. To the right of each main elevation view is a matching cross-sectional inset showing how the beam interacts with a profiled steel sheeting (or similar cladding) that provides the internal restraint. Key features common to all three variants:  
• End supports: one end on a pinned (hinge) support, the other on a roller support, so that shear reactions develop but rotation about the beam axis at the supports is prevented (for example by cleats or by clamped sheeting).  
• Test span: the distance between end supports is chosen so that, under the expected combination of bending moment and shear, the internal midspan support reactions replicate design conditions. The dimension bB marks the width of the internal support head.  
• Section depth: the overall beam depth is labelled h.  

(a) Internal support under gravity loading  
– In the elevation view, a downward‐directed concentrated load F is applied at the beam’s upper flange, directly over the internal support.  
– The beam rests on the internal support via its top flange, with the sheeting beneath depicted in dashed outline.  
– The inset cross section shows a U-shaped profile of sheeting (hat or trapezoidal sheet) bolted or clipped to the top flange of the beam. The sheet provides lateral restraint and prevents flange rotation.  

(b) Internal support under uplift loading  
– Here the concentrated load F is again downward but is applied to the underside of the beam’s bottom flange, simulating an uplift or suction condition on the cladding.  
– The bottom flange engages the internal support through a short downward projection (e.g. a stiffener or connection plate).  
– The inset shows the profiled sheeting above the beam, acting as the anchor for uplift, with bolts or clips passing through the bottom flange into the sheeting.  

(c) Internal support with loading applied to the tension flange  
– In this configuration, the load F is applied downward on what, under gravity bending, becomes the tension flange (i.e. the underside of the beam when the moment reverses).  
– The elevation view shows the load bearing on a plate that is rigidly connected to the bottom flange, transferring the force into the internal support.  
– The inset cross section illustrates how an inverted U-shaped cladding profile or ancillary member is bolted into the tension flange, providing a pull‐down connection through the sheeting into the support.  

Across all three tests, the objective is to measure the internal support reaction and moment–rotation behavior at an intermediate support under different loading conditions (gravity, uplift, and reverse‐moment). Displacements are recorded both at the load application point and, in practice, at positions a distance e from the supports (not shown here) so that net deflections excluding end‐settlement can be determined. The sheeting or cladding in each inset is shown in dashed lines to indicate that it approximates the restraint conditions found in real roof or wall assemblies.

content:
The image is a schematic side-view of a thin, cold-formed steel sheet or beam set up for end-support shear tests (labelled “Figure A.6: Test set-up for end support tests”). A long, slender member is drawn as a solid horizontal line; its continuation beyond the supports is indicated by dashed outlines at both ends. Key dimensions and load/support features are annotated as follows:

1. Supports and Load Application  
   - At the left end, a rigid end support is shown as a small filled block under the member. An upward arrow labelled R_A indicates the reaction force to be measured at that support.  
   - At the right end, a roller support (depicted as a small wheel atop a textured base) resists vertical movement only.  
   - Between the two supports, a rectangular hatched “load plate” sits on top of the member. A vertical arrow labelled F points down onto this plate, representing a concentrated load applied through a rigid plate or block.

2. Span and Positioning  
   - The total centre-to-centre span between the two supports is marked “L” along the bottom. Directly below the load plate, the bottom annotation reads “300 mm,” indicating the plate’s offset of 300 mm from the left support.  
   - Above the member, the distance from the left support to the load is annotated “≈ L/3” and from the load to the right support “≈ 2L/3,” prescribing that the plate be located approximately one-third of the span from the left.  
   - To the right of the span, additional clearances on each side of the right support are annotated “≥ 3 h,” where h is the depth (height) of the member; this ensures adequate overhang beyond the support.

3. Support-and-Overhang Requirements  
   - Directly beneath the left support, a dimension “b_A ≥ h” specifies that the support bearing length b_A along the sheet must be at least as large as the member’s depth h.  
   - On the top left, a double-headed arrow labelled u indicates the length from the “internal edge of the end support to the end of the sheet,” ensuring a minimum overhang beyond the support. The key at lower left restates these two definitions:  
     • b_A = support length  
     • u = length from internal edge of end support to end of sheet

4. Scale and Slope Notation  
   - Immediately to the left of the left support, the member is depicted with a slight taper to its end and a small “1 : 20” notation, indicating that the specimen end may be trimmed to a 1:20 slope or chamfer.

Overall, the figure lays out a standardized laboratory test for determining the shear resistance of a profiled sheet or cold-formed member at an end support. It ensures that the load application, support conditions, clearances, and overhangs conform to the requirements for valid, repeatable test results in accordance with the referenced annex procedures.

content:
The table at hand, labelled “Table A.1,” appears in Annex A of EN 1993-1-3 (the Eurocode supplement for cold-formed members and sheeting) under the section on “Member buckling tests” (A.3.3). It specifies the minimum number of individual tests required to establish a reliable buckling curve for compression members of various relative slendernesses. Below is a breakdown of its structure and practical intent:

1. Table Structure  
 • Two horizontal rows and eight vertical columns.  
 • Top row: header entries representing discrete values of the non-dimensional relative slenderness parameter, λ (sometimes denoted λ̅ or λrel). These values are: 0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, 1.6, 2.0, and 3.0.  
 • Bottom row: the corresponding minimum number of separate buckling tests (n) to be carried out for specimens whose slenderness equals the column heading.  

2. Data Content  
 • For λ = 0.2, the table prescribes n = 3 tests.  
 • For all other listed slenderness values (0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, 1.6, 2.0, 3.0), n = 5 tests.  

3. Context and Application  
 • Relative slenderness λ is defined as the square-root of the ratio between the elastic critical buckling load Fcr and the squash load of the gross section. It is a key parameter in deriving buckling curves and reduction factors for design.  
 • Annex A.3.3 advocates that, to calibrate a buckling curve for a given grade of cold-formed steel and a given cross-sectional profile (and manufacturing process), a series of axial compression tests at different slendernesses must be conducted.  
 • Table A.1 provides guidance on how many individual tests are minimally necessary at each λ to achieve statistical reliability in the derived buckling curve.  
 • For relatively stocky members (λ = 0.2), three tests suffice because variability is low. As slenderness increases (λ ≥ 0.5), buckling behavior becomes more sensitive to imperfections and material variability, so five tests are recommended.  

4. Interpretation Notes  
 • Although the table only lists eight discrete λ values, engineers interpolating between these values should recognize that the requirement jumps from 3 to 5 tests at λ = 0.5 and remains constant thereafter.  
 • If a design or calibration program targets slenderness values outside this range, similar test‐series density (i.e. five tests) is advisable for λ above 0.5, and at least three tests for λ below 0.5, unless a national annex or further guidance dictates otherwise.  

5. Integration into RAG Vector Store  
 • As a concise reference, this table can be indexed under keywords such as “member buckling tests,” “relative slenderness,” and “number of tests.”  
 • The slug “Table A.1” and its clause reference (A.3.3.1 in EN 1993-1-3) should be stored to facilitate retrieval in an automated question-answering environment.  
 • Quantitative fields to extract for vectorization:  
  – λ_values = [0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, 1.6, 2.0, 3.0]  
  – required_tests = [3, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5]  

In summary, Table A.1 codifies the minimum test series size required to characterize buckling behavior across a spectrum of relative slendernesses, ensuring that empirical buckling curves for cold-formed steel members are underpinned by an adequate dataset.

content:
The image is a schematic line drawing of a beam test‐rig, labelled “Figure A.7: Test set-up for internal support tests.” It shows a straight horizontal beam, supported and instrumented to measure its mid-span response under a concentrated load. Key elements and dimensions are as follows:

1. Beam  
  – Depicted as a single straight heavy line, running horizontally from left to right.  
  – Three special points along the beam are identified by the letters A, B, C and D (the right-hand support E is implied in the normative text but not rendered in the clipped figure).

2. End Supports  
  – At point A (far left) a pinned support is shown by the standard triangular symbol with its apex touching the underside of the beam. This prevents vertical and horizontal translation but allows rotation.  
  – A roller support is prescribed by the standard at the opposite end (labelled E in the text, not visible in this cropped sketch). The roller would permit horizontal movement and rotation, resisting only vertical load.

3. Instrumentation—Deflection Gauges at B and D  
  – Two circular dial‐gauge symbols are drawn beneath the beam, one at B, the other at D. Each gauge has an arrow indicating the direction of measurement (upwards, at an angle), signifying that these are displacement transducers recording vertical deflection.  
  – The two gauges are mounted at equal distances “e” from the adjacent supports, B for the left support and D for the right support. The dimension “e” is annotated by a double‐headed arrow beneath the beam extending from the support to the gauge.

4. Test Span and Load  
  – The distance between the two measurement points B and D is labelled “s.” This span s corresponds to the portion of the beam over which the internal support (or mid-span) moment and shear conditions are to be evaluated.  
  – At the midpoint C of this span “s,” a single concentrated vertical load F is applied downwards. The magnitude of F represents the test load used to induce bending moment and shear in the beam.

5. Dimensional Annotations  
  – The distance from each end support to its nearest gauge is shown as “e.”  
  – The central region between gauges B and D is dimensioned “s,” indicating that the beam segment under direct instrumentation spans length s.  
  – These two parameters (e and s) allow the test to:  
    a. Measure gross deflection at C under load F,  
    b. Eliminate the contributions of support rotations or settlements by subtracting the average of the two measured deflections at B and D, yielding the net mid-span deflection.

6. Purpose and Context (from Additional Text)  
  – This arrangement is prescribed in Annex A.5 of the Eurocode National Annex for cold-formed members and sheeting, as a means of determining the moment resistance and flexural stiffness of a sheet-bearing or beam-sheathing system at an interior support.  
  – By plotting applied load versus corrected mid-span deflection, one derives the M–θ characteristic (moment versus rotation) for the beam over its internal support.  
  – The test is conducted with hinged (pinned) and roller supports to avoid rotational restraint influences, and deflections at B and D ensure support deformations are accounted for.

In summary, the drawing is a clear, annotated representation of an internal‐support bending test: a beam on pinned and roller supports, two deflection gauges at offset distance e, a central point load F over the span s, and the means to derive the true midspan deflection by eliminating support settlement effects.

content:
The illustration is a schematic, two‐dimensional plot (Figure A.8) from Annex A of EN 1993-1-3, showing how measured support moments (M) and support reactions (R) from full‐scale tests at different test spans are used to build a design interaction curve by linear interpolation.

Overall layout  
- A rectangular coordinate frame with a vertical axis at left and a horizontal axis at bottom.  
- The vertical axis is labelled “M” (support moment) and the horizontal axis is labelled “R” (support reaction). No numeric scales are shown – it is a conceptual diagram.  

Data points and envelope curve  
- Three hollow circles mark the key measured (M, R) pairs obtained from tests at three distinct test‐span values s. These circles lie roughly along a descending, piecewise‐linear path from upper left toward lower right of the plotting area.  
- A bold polyline connects these three circles, forming the “envelope” of measured results. This thick black line represents the envelope of the mean adjusted peak loads (support moment vs. reaction) for each test span, as described in clause A.6.2.2.2.  

Annotations and arrows  
- A small, filled circle on the left side, at approximately mid‐height, serves as a reference “origin” of arrows; it is not part of the bold envelope.  
- Two thin arrows radiate from that reference point toward two of the hollow circles on the envelope. Both of these arrows are labelled “(a)”, indicating “test results for different test spans s.”  
- A third arrow, labelled “(b)”, points at the segment of the bold polyline joining the mid and lower circles. This label denotes “linear interpolation” between measured points to find design values for intermediate (M,R) combinations.  

Caption  
Directly below the plot appears the small caption:  
  “(a) test results for different test spans s, (b) linear interpolation”  
Beneath that, in bold, is the figure title:  
  “Figure A.8: Relation between support moment M and support reaction R.”  

Interpretation in context  
According to the surrounding text, for each test span s one measures a peak support reaction R and computes the corresponding support moment M. Those (M,R) pairs are plotted and connected. To obtain design values for spans not explicitly tested, straight‐line (linear) interpolation is carried out along the curve (arrow (b)). The design characteristic M–R relationship is taken as 0.9 × the mean of the envelope curve values for each span. This graph thus encapsulates the test‐assisted procedure for evaluating combined support moment and reaction capacity of cold‐formed members under specified loading and support conditions.

content:
The sketch reproduced in “Figure A.9: Relation between load F and net deflection δ” is a highly schematic load–deflection curve, annotated to show how elastic and plastic components of deflection are extracted in a beam-test or sheet-restraint test. Visually it consists of:

• Axes and Curve  
  – A vertical axis, labeled F, with a series of horizontal tick-marks and labels F₅ (lowest), F₄, F₃, F₂, F₁, and F_max (highest).  
  – A horizontal axis, labeled δ (net deflection).  
  – A bold, continuous curve that rises from the origin, initially in a nearly straight line, then gradually “softens” and reaches a maximum load F_max before descending slightly (post-peak behaviour).

• Load Levels and Reference Lines  
  – Five light grey horizontal lines correspond to the discrete load steps F₁–F₅.  
  – The second load level, F₂, is highlighted by a darker horizontal line. This reference load is used to illustrate how elastic and plastic deflections are separated.

• Initial Tangent and Elastic Deflection (δ_lin,₂ and δ_el,₂)  
  – From the origin, a straight line is drawn tangent to the initial, linear portion of the curve. This line represents the “elastic stiffness” of the specimen.  
  – Where that tangent line meets the horizontal F₂ line, a vertical projection down to the δ-axis defines δ_lin,₂: the purely elastic deflection that would occur at F₂ if the specimen remained entirely in its initial stiffness range.  
  – Meanwhile, the bold curve itself intersects F₂ at a point whose projection to the δ-axis defines δ_el,₂: the actual (total) net deflection measured at that same load level.  
  – The difference δ_el,₂ – δ_lin,₂ corresponds to the “plastic” or inelastic component of deflection accumulated by load F₂.

• Plastic Deflection at Peak Load (δ_pl,₂)  
  – At the very top of the curve (load F_max), a short horizontal bracket indicates the breadth of the plastic plateau, and a vertical line dropped from the peak defines δ_pl,₂ on the δ-axis. In some testing procedures this is used as a second reference deflection corresponding to full plastic rotation or ultimate behaviour under that particular test span.

How It Is Used in RAG/Vector-Store Context  
– In full-scale beam or purlin tests (see Annex A.6 of the standard), the net deflection δ at a loading point C is obtained by subtracting support deflections (measured at nearby points B and D) from the gross deflection.  
– By plotting F vs. δ as in Figure A.9, one can read off δ_lin and δ_el at a chosen load level F₂, thus isolating elastic versus plastic deformation.  
– These deflections feed into subsequent calculations—e.g. computing the rotation θ of the cross-section at F₂ via θ = (δ_el,₂ – δ_lin,₂)/(s) or similar expressions—so that an M–θ characteristic curve (Figure A.10) can be generated for design verification and limit-state modelling.

content:
The image is a schematic line graph titled “Figure A.10: Derivation of moment-rotation (M – θ) characteristic.” It plots bending moment M (vertical axis) against rotation θ (horizontal axis) to illustrate how design values are derived from a series of test curves.

Axes and Scales  
• The vertical axis on the left is marked “M” (moment), with an upward arrowhead.  
• The horizontal axis along the bottom is marked “θ” (rotation), with an arrow at its right end. No numeric scales are shown—it is qualitative.

Individual Test Curves  
• A family of four smoothly declining, slightly curved lines runs from upper-left toward lower-right, each representing the measured moment-rotation response of a different test specimen.  
• Near the right side of the plot, two of those curves are annotated with circled numerals “①” (the uppermost) and “②” (the lowermost), indicating specific tests or sample groups.

Mean and Design Curves  
• Superimposed on the individual curves is a bold dashed line labeled “M_mean,” denoting the arithmetic mean of all measured test curves at each rotation. An arrow points to this dashed line with the label “M_mean.”  
• Also overlaid is a dash-dot line below the mean, labeled “M_d,” which is the design moment-rotation curve. An arrow points to this lower, dash-dot curve with the label “M_d.”

Reduction Factor Annotation  
• At the left side of the plot, a double-headed vertical bracket spans from the top of the mean curve downward to a point on that same curve marked “0,9 M_mean,” visually showing the 10 percent reduction applied to the mean to obtain the design value line.

Legend Text Below  
• Directly beneath the axes, small text reads: “M_mean = mean value, M_d = design value,” summarizing the notation.

Overall Impression  
This black-and-white schematic conveys the process described in Annex A.6 of the standard: obtain multiple moment-rotation test curves, compute their mean M_mean(θ), then derive a conservative design curve M_d(θ) by taking 0.9 × M_mean at each rotation. The circles ① and ② highlight individual specimen responses, while the annotations make clear how the characteristic (design) M–θ relationship is taken as 90 percent of the averaged test data.
