content:
The illustration is a two‐part, side-elevation line drawing titled “Figure A.11: Experimental determination of spring stiffness KA and KB.” It shows two alternative test setups—marked “Alternative 1” (upper half) and “Alternative 2” (lower right)—for measuring the combined lateral support stiffness provided by profiled sheeting fastened to a cold-formed beam.

Common to both schemes, a horizontal load (d) is applied at a prescribed height h above the plane of the sheeting by means of a hydraulic actuator or equivalent. The load pushes laterally on the web or flange of a cold-formed C-section profile (c). Displacement sensors (small dial gauges) are indicated pointing to the profile’s loaded face.

Alternative 1 (left and center)  
• Base support: trapezoidal steel sheeting (a) rests on a pair of rigid supports—at left by a roller or hinged bearing, at right by a fully clamped support (e). In the middle, an I-section purlin or channel section carries the sheeting.  
• Insulation or filler (e), if present, is shown between sheeting and purlin; short timber blocks (f) between the profile web and the sheeting prevent local corrugation spreading.  
• The cold-formed profile (c) is fastened to the sheeting by mechanical fasteners (b) such as self-drilling screws or rivets. Two fasteners are shown symmetrically about the specimen centerline, at a lateral spacing d on each side of the web. The fastener group must lie at least 2 b from the near support and at least 450 mm from the far support, where b is the overall width of the profile’s flange. The fastener spacing satisfies 1.5 d1 < d < 3 d1.  
• The actuator (d) engages the free flange of the profile, pushing horizontally. Displacement gauges are mounted near the load point.

Alternative 2 (right)  
• A simplified sub-assembly test of the sheeting alone: a short length of trapezoidal sheet (c) is clamped at its ends and loaded at midspan.  
• The corrugation pitch d1 is marked on the sheet. This layout isolates the panel distortion contribution (KB) by eliminating beam bending.  

Together, the two methods yield (a) KA, the rotational restraint stiffness per unit length from the fastener’s slip and (b) KB, the stiffness due to shear-panel distortion. In each case, the applied load F per unit length versus the net lateral displacement δ of the top flange defines the combined spring constant via KA+KB = F/(δ·L), where L is panel length under load.

content:
The table is a cross‐classification of six atmospheric‐corrosion environments (C1 to C5‐M, per EN ISO 12944-2) against combinations of sheet (“cladding”) materials and fastener materials.  Its purpose is to identify which fastener materials are suitable (marked “X”), conditionally suitable (“(X)ᶜ”), or not recommended (“–”) for each environment and sheet type.  Footnotes a–d explain exceptions (for rivets, screws, special stainless grades, Monel, etc.).

1.  Column headings  
   • “Classification of environment”: C1 (very low) to C5-M (very high, marine).  
   • “Sheet material”: codes A, B, C, D, E, S identifying the cladding or tray material (see notes at bottom of the standard):  
     – A = un-coated steel sheet  
     – B = (informative only) steel sheet categories not used here  
     – C = hot-dip zinc-coated (Z275) or Aluzink (AZ150)  
     – D = hot-dip zinc-coated + paint/plastic coating  
     – E = Aluzink (AZ185)  
     – S = stainless steel (EN 10088)  
   • “Material of fastener”: six columns  
     1. Aluminium  
     2. Electro-galvanized steel, coating > 7 µm  
     3. Hot-dip zinc-coated steel, coating > 45 µmᵇ  
     4. Stainless steel, case-hardened 1.4006ᵈ  
     5. Stainless steel 1.4301 or 1.4436ᵈ  
     6. Monelᵃ  

2.  Structure of the rows  
   • For each environment (C1, C2, C3, C4, C5-I and C5-M), the sheet materials are split into two (or three) sub‐rows when the recommendations differ.  An “X” means the fastener material is recommended; “–” means not suitable; “(X)ᶜ” means it is conditionally acceptable subject to design or assembly precautions (see note on fastener corrosion class C in the annex).

3.  Summary by environment  
   • C1 (very low corrosivity): for all sheet groups (A,B,C and D,E,S), every fastener material is marked “X.”  
   • C2 (low): all sheet groups (A; C,D,E; S) permit aluminium, hot-dip, case-hardened or 1.4301/1.4436 stainless, and Monel. Electro-galvanized steel is not recommended (“–”).  
   • C3 (medium):  
     – A and C,E,D permit aluminium and hot-dip; electro-galvanized remains “–.”  Case-hardened steel is “–” for A and D but conditionally acceptable (“(X)ᶜ”) for C,E; 1.4301/1.4436 stainless and Monel are OK except Monel is “–” for C,E.  
     – S (stainless roofing) forbids aluminium and galvanizing, but permits hot-dip, both stainless types and Monel without condition.  
   • C4 (high):  
     – A and E sheets: aluminium OK; hot-dip and 1.4301/1.4436 stainless are only conditionally usable (“(X)ᶜ”); galvanizing and case-hardened steel are “–”; Monel is “–.”  
     – D: only hot-dip and stainless are conditionally acceptable; aluminium is “–”; Monel “–.”  
     – S: only hot-dip, 1.4301/1.4436 stainless or Monel are OK; aluminium and galvanizing are “–.”  
   • C5-I (very high, industrial):  
     – A: aluminium is OK; case-hardened steel “–”; 1.4301/1.4436 stainless is “(X)ᶜ”; all others “–.”  
     – D: only hot-dip and 1.4301/1.4436 stainless are conditionally OK; others “–.”  
     – S: only stainless 1.4301/1.4436 is recommended; Monel “–.”  
   • C5-M (very high, marine):  
     – A: aluminium and conditionally 1.4301/1.4436 stainless are marked “X.”  
     – D: only hot-dip and 1.4301/1.4436 stainless are conditionally OK; others “–.”  
     – S: only 1.4301/1.4436 stainless and Monel are allowed; other fasteners are “–.”  

4.  Footnotes (selected)  
   a. Monel refers to nickel–copper alloy fasteners.  
   b. Applies to rivets.  
   c. Applies to screws and nuts; “(X)ᶜ” denotes use with insulating washers or special design to avoid bimetallic corrosion.  
   d. Stainless grades per EN 10088.  

In practice, you match your site’s environment class and the cladding material code to this table to pick a fastener material that will resist corrosion over the intended lifespan.

content:
The source table (Table B.2 from the National Annex to EN 1993-1-3) presents a six-class system for atmospheric corrosivity in temperate climates, aligned with EN ISO 12944-2. It is organized in four columns and six rows (one per corrosivity category), and is intended to guide material selection and protective treatments by matching environmental aggressiveness with steel-sheet and fastener performance classes.

Structure and Fields  
• Corrosivity category (first column): C1 through C5-M. These are the standardized codes denoting increasing levels of atmospheric aggressiveness.  
• Corrosivity level (second column): textual descriptors—Very low, Low, Medium, High, Very high (industrial) and Very high (marine)—that correspond to each code.  
• Examples of typical temperate-climate environments (third and fourth columns), split into:  
  – Exterior: representative outdoor settings at each corrosivity level.  
  – Interior: typical indoor settings that experience equivalent corrosive effects.

Row-by-Row Content  

1. Category C1 (Very low)  
   • Exterior: “–” (essentially no outdoor corrosion risk in temperate climates).  
   • Interior: heated buildings with clean atmospheres—offices, shops, schools, hotels—where humidity and pollutants are minimal.

2. Category C2 (Low)  
   • Exterior: rural or semi-rural outdoor air with low pollution levels.  
   • Interior: unheated buildings prone to occasional condensation, such as depots or sport halls.

3. Category C3 (Medium)  
   • Exterior: urban and industrial atmospheres with moderate sulfur dioxide pollution; coastal zones with low salinity.  
   • Interior: production rooms with high humidity and some airborne contaminants—for example food-processing plants, laundries, breweries, dairies.

4. Category C4 (High)  
   • Exterior: heavy industrial areas and coastal zones with moderate salt spray.  
   • Interior: chemical plants, swimming pools, or boatyards—indoor areas with aggressive chemical or humid conditions.

5. Category C5-I (Very high, industrial)  
   • Exterior: industrial zones with high humidity and aggressive airborne chemicals.  
   • Interior: buildings or enclosed areas subject to almost continuous condensation and heavy pollution—paper mills, textile plants, laundries, etc.

6. Category C5-M (Very high, marine)  
   • Exterior: coastal and offshore environments with sustained salt spray.  
   • Interior: enclosed or semi-enclosed spaces where high salinity air and near-permanent condensation coincide—ship holds, coastal garages, salt-laden processing rooms.

Key Usage Notes  
- This table is informative: it does not impose new technical requirements but illustrates how to map real-world service conditions to EN ISO 12944-2 corrosivity classes when specifying coatings, fastener materials or cold-formed steel sheeting.  
- Designers and specifiers should select materials and protective systems whose durability ratings match or exceed the corrosivity category of the intended application—e.g., coating class C5-M for marine-exposed purlins.  
- The division between interior and exterior service environments helps differentiate between outdoor exposure (higher UV, temperature swings, salt spray) and controlled or industrial indoor conditions (high humidity, chemical fumes).  
- National Annexes may refine or adjust these environment examples or correlate them with local climatic data.

sections: 10 Special considerations for purlins, liner trays and sheetings

content:
The image is a small schematic from Annex C of EN 1993-1-3, showing how a thin-walled cross-section is broken into straight segments (parts) and nodes in order to compute its gross area and, ultimately, its torsion constant and shear-centre location. At the top is the differential-area formula:  
 dAᵢ = [tᵢ · √((yᵢ – yᵢ₋₁)² + (zᵢ – zᵢ₋₁)²)]  
where tᵢ is the (effective) thickness of the iᵗʰ segment, and (yᵢ, zᵢ) and (yᵢ₋₁, zᵢ₋₁) are the Cartesian coordinates of its end-nodes. Below this, “Cross section area” is indicated as the sum of all such dAᵢ over n parts.  

To the right is Figure C.1, a simplified three-node cross-section. It consists of:  
• Node 0 at the top of a short, slightly inclined flat segment of thickness t₁. This “leg” leans outward from node 1 at an oblique angle.  
• Node 1 at the bottom-right corner, where the inclined t₁ segment meets the horizontal leg. A small coordinate triad is drawn here: the y-axis arrow pointing right, the z-axis arrow pointing upward.  
• Node 2 at the bottom-left corner, connected to node 1 by a horizontal flat segment of thickness t₂.  
• The final segment between node 2 and node 0 is a vertical flat element of thickness t₃, closing the open profile.  

Each straight‐line part carries its own thickness label (t₁ on the slanted leg, t₂ on the base, t₃ on the vertical leg). Numbers 0, 1 and 2 mark the node indices in sequence around the section. The figure illustrates how one would list node coordinates (y₀, z₀), (y₁, z₁), (y₂, z₂), and thicknesses; compute the length of each segment via the distance formula; multiply by its thickness; and sum all contributions to obtain the total gross cross-section area.  

In context, this procedure underpins the calculation of torsion constant (J) and shear centre location for closed or open thin-walled cold-formed sections. By discretizing the profile into linear elements, the standard provides a systematic way to derive geometric properties that feed into bending, buckling or torsion‐related design rules elsewhere in EN 1993-1-3.

sections: 10 Special considerations for purlins, liner trays and sheetings

content:
The figure before you (labelled “Figure C.2 Nodes and parts in a cross section with branches”) is presented in three side-by-side views, each showing the same cold-formed steel profile—an open cross-section with a branched top flange—first in true shape and then in two stages of idealization for calculation of torsional and warping properties.

1) Leftmost drawing (“Cross section”)  
- A solid, hatched outline of the actual profile, viewed in its transverse (y–z) plane.  
- The top flange consists of three plate elements:  
  • An inclined branch on the left (thickness labelled t₁),  
  • A central horizontal plate (thickness t₂),  
  • An inclined branch on the right (thickness t₃).  
- A vertical web (thickness t₆) runs down from the junction at the mid-span of the top flange to the bottom flange.  
- The bottom flange (thickness t₈) is a single horizontal plate.  
- All thicknesses are indicated by dimension arrows and text (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₆, t₈).

2) Centre drawing (“Nodes and elements”)  
- The same profile reduced to its centrelines with eleven line segments connecting a series of numbered “nodes” (0 through 8).  
- Node layout:  
  • Node 0 at the outer tip of the left inclined branch.  
  • Node 1 at the junction between that branch and the central top flange.  
  • Node 2 at the start of the right inclined branch.  
  • Node 3 at the outer tip of the right inclined branch.  
  • Node 4 at the return corner where the right branch meets the horizontal web junction plate.  
  • Node 5 at the branching point where top flange and web meet.  
  • Node 6 at the junction of web and bottom-flange branch.  
  • Node 7 at the first corner of the bottom flange.  
  • Node 8 at the outer tip of the bottom flange.  
- Each line segment between node pairs represents one “part” of the cross-section whose thickness is identified (t₁ through t₈, with t₇ implied for the small junction piece at the bottom).  
- This discretization shows clearly where more than two parts meet (the “branch” at node 5).

3) Rightmost drawing (“Line model”)  
- The same node-and-element connectivity rendered as a plain stick-figure (no hatching), suitable for numerical integration.  
- The global axes y (horizontal) and z (vertical) are shown in the lower right corner.  
- Thickness labels (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₅, t₆, t₇, t₈) remain attached to each segment.  
- This skeletal model is exactly what would be used when applying the formulae of C.1 and C.2 for open cross sections with branches: you sum over all parts, use node coordinates to compute sectorial coordinates ωⱼ, and then assemble warping constant Iw and torsion constant It.

Caption summary  
• Demonstrates how to break an open, branched profile into discrete line-elements for the purpose of computing shear-centre offsets, sectorial coordinates and warping functions.  
• “Branches” occur at nodes where three or more plate parts meet—in this example, the junction of top flange and web.  
• Once nodes and parts are defined in this manner, the general expressions of clause C.1 may be applied unchanged.

sections: 10 Special considerations for purlins, liner trays and sheetings

content:
The illustration shows a generic thin-walled steel cross-section that contains both an open boundary and an enclosed (closed) loop. It is intended to support the derivation of torsion constants and the shear-centre location for profiles with one or more closed parts, as described in Clause C.3 of the standard.  

Overall layout  
– The heavy continuous line traces the actual mid-line of the sheet-steel profile. All plate elements are assumed to have uniform thickness t.  
– The dashed line marks the boundary of the closed portion (the “closed cell”) whose enclosed area is required in the sectorial-coordinate solution for torsion.  

Node numbering and part sequence  
– Nodes are numbered sequentially from 0 up to n around the open part of the section. The closed loop uses a subset of those nodes.  
– Starting at node 0 on the top left, a horizontal element runs to node 1. That is the beginning of the closed loop.  
– From node 1 an inclined leg slopes down toward node n (left‐hand side). This is one side of the closed loop.  
– The closed loop continues with a horizontal top flange from node 1 to node 2, then down along a second inclined leg from node 2 to node 4, and finally back along an inclined segment from node 4 to node n. These three elements (1→2, 2→4, 4→n) are drawn in dashed outline. They form a single closed circuit.  

Open part of the contour  
– Beyond the closed loop, the heavy line continues from node 0 inward toward the bottom of the profile. In practice that means node 0→1 is open, but all segments outside the dashed loop are the “open” parts of the section.  
– After returning to node n from the closed loop, the contour proceeds to node n–1 at the lower left corner, then horizontally to the bottom right corner at node 5.  
– From node 5 it ascends along an inclined web to node 4 (which is also part of the closed path), then up the second of the closed-loop legs back to node 2 on the top flange. Finally it closes the open boundary by running from node 2 to an external support or flange at node 0 (not shown here).  

Key geometric features  
– Two horizontal flanges: top flange between nodes 1–2 and bottom flange between nodes n–1–5.  
– Three webs: one left‐hand web connecting 1–n, one right‐hand web connecting 2–4, and one lower web connecting 4–5–n–1.  
– The dashed polygon 1–2–4–n encloses a finite area Aclosed; this area appears in the torsion constant formula T = 4A² / ∑(si / ti), where si is the length of each element in the closed loop.  
– The rest of the contour (0→1, n→n–1, n–1→5, 5→4) is treated as an open boundary for the sectorial coordinate approach.  

Annotation and intended use  
– Each node label (0, 1, 2, 4, 5, …, n–1, n) corresponds to a joint between straight plate segments or a bending line in the cold-formed profile.  
– The dashed outline clarifies which subset of the profile forms the closed cell; the remainder is open.  
– By subdividing the cross section into closed and open parts in this way, one can compute warping functions, sectorial coordinates ω, the shear centre offset, and the torsion constant for complex cold-formed shapes.  

In summary, Figure C.3 provides a schematic reference for identifying and numbering the segments of a thin-walled cross section that includes a single closed cell. The heavy continuous line is the physical profile; the dashed line marks the closed‐loop path whose enclosed area enters directly into the calculation of closed‐section torsional stiffness.

sections: 10 Special considerations for purlins, liner trays and sheetings

content:
This description refers to “Table D.1,” which is part of Annex D (“Alternative effective-width method for outstand compression elements”) of EN 1993-1-3. Table D.1 defines the so-called stress-relation factor ψ, used in the buckling factor kσ to reflect how the assumed stress distribution over an outstand plate element deviates from uniformity. In practice, when determining the elastic buckling resistance of a plate strip under compression, kσ is taken as 1⁄ψ times the value that would apply for a uniform stress distribution; ψ therefore corrects the slenderness reduction for non-uniform stresses.

Key features of Table D.1:

• Scope and Purpose  
 – Provides ψ values for various idealized stress distributions across the width of an outstand element in compression.  
 – Enables designers to replace the uniform-stress assumption (ψ = 1) with a more accurate factor when the actual stress varies linearly, parabolically or in another prescribed form.  

• Typical Layout (columns and content)  
 1. “Stress distribution” – delineates the shape of the stress across the strip (for example: uniform, linear triangular, parabolic).  
 2. “ψ (stress-relation factor)” – gives the numerical expression or value of ψ for that distribution (e.g. ψ = 1.0 for uniform stress; ψ < 1.0 or ψ > 1.0 for more concentrated or more spread-out stress profiles).  
 3. “Notes/Remarks” – may explain the derivation or conditions of applicability (for instance, whether the distribution refers to edge-stabilized conditions or simply elastic bending profiles).  

• Application in Buckling Factor  
 – The standard buckling factor for a simply supported, uniformly compressed plate is kσ,uniform = 4 (for pinned‐pinned long edges) or kσ,uniform = 0.425… (for one free edge, one simply supported). By introducing ψ from Table D.1, the designer uses kσ = kσ,uniform / ψ.  
 – ψ thus scales the critical stress downward (if ψ < 1) when the real stress is more severe at one edge, or upward (if ψ > 1) when the stress is more evenly distributed.  

• Notes Accompanying the Table  
 (1) “The stress-relation factor ψ in the buckling factor kσ may be based on the stress distribution over the cross section.”  
  – This permits use of actual calculated stress profiles (e.g. from membrane action, bending or combined axial + bending) rather than strictly the idealized cases.  
 (2) “The resistance of the section should be based on elastic stress distribution over the section.”  
  – Even when using ψ to adjust for buckling slenderness, the section’s ultimate design resistance is still derived from the elastic (fully linear) stress distribution. Plastic redistribution or post-buckling strengths are not assumed.  

Integration with Annex D methodology:  
In Annex D’s alternative approach to effective width for outstand plates, the elastic critical stress fcr is first determined using σcr = (π² E) / (λ² ψ (…)), where λ is the slenderness and ψ the stress-relation factor. The effective width (or effective area) is then set so that the nominal compressive stress equals fcr. Table D.1 supplies the ψ needed to capture how the actual through-thickness bending or membrane stress alters the buckling resistance.  

By embedding Table D.1 into a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) vector store, one would index:  
• The list of supported stress distribution types.  
• The corresponding ψ formulas or numeric values.  
• The two governance notes on elastic distribution and permissible use of actual stress profiles.  
• Cross-references to where kσ and λ appear in EN 1993-1-3 (clause 5.5.2) and to the broader effective-width replacement procedure in Annex D.

sections: 10 Special considerations for purlins, liner trays and sheetings

content:
The excerpt you provided includes “Table D.1: Outstand compression elements,” which offers an alternative to the usual effective-width method for calculating the design resistance of thin, unsupported (outstand) plate elements under longitudinal compression.  In context, Annex D of EN 1993-1-3 describes a two-stage approach in which an outstand element of total width bₚ is divided into:  
  • an “effective” strip of width bₑ₀ at the free or supported longitudinal edge, with full nominal plate thickness t, and  
  • the remaining strip of width (bₚ − bₑ₀) with a reduced “effective” thickness tₑff.  

Table D.1 then defines bₑ₀, tₑff and the associated buckling coefficient kσ according to the sign and magnitude of the non-dimensional slenderness parameter ψ, defined elsewhere in EN 1993-1-3 (this ψ is related to plate slenderness λ and reduction factor ρ from clause 5.5.2).  The table is presented in two blocks:  
  A. “Maximum compression at free longitudinal edge”  
  B. “Maximum compression at supported longitudinal edge”

Within each block the table subdivides into two ψ-ranges, prescribing different formulae for the effective strip and buckling factor in each.  A detailed breakdown follows:

1.  Maximum compression at the free longitudinal edge  
  a.  Case 1: 1 ≥ ψ ≥ 0  
     – Effective width:  
         bₑ₀ = 0.42 · bₚ  
     – Effective thickness of remainder:  
         tₑff = (1.75 · ρ − 0.75) · t  
     – Buckling factor:  
         kσ = 1.7 / (3 + ψ)  
  b.  Case 2: ψ < 0  
     – Effective width (limited to < bₚ):  
         bₑ₀ = 0.42 · bₚ / (1 − ψ) + bₜ  
         where bₜ = ψ · bₚ / (ψ − 1)  
     – Effective thickness:  
         tₑff = (1.75 · ρ − 0.75 − 0.15 · ψ) · t  
     – Buckling factor for −2 > ψ ≥ −3:  
         kσ = 3.3 · (1 + ψ) + 1.25  
       and for ψ < −3:  
         kσ = 0.29 · (1 − ψ)²  

2.  Maximum compression at the supported longitudinal edge  
  a.  Case 1: 1 ≥ ψ ≥ 0  (essentially the same as for the free edge)  
     – bₑ₀ = 0.42 · bₚ  
     – tₑff = (1.75 · ρ − 0.75) · t  
     – kσ = 1.7 / (1 + 3ψ)  
  b.  Case 2: ψ < 0  
     – bₑ₀ = 0.42 · bₚ / (1 − ψ)  
     – bₜ = ψ · bₚ / (ψ − 1)  
     – tₑff and bₑ₀ formulas mirror the free-edge case, but the buckling factor changes:  
         • For 0 ≥ ψ ≥ −1:  
             kσ = 1.7 − 5 ψ + 17.1 ψ²  
         • For ψ < −1:  
             kσ = 5.98 · (1 − ψ)²  

Key points:  
  – The 0.42 coefficient arises from a standardized konservative assumption about effective width under buckling.  
  – ρ is the reduction factor from clause 5.5.2 (it depends on slenderness λ).  
  – ψ combines slenderness and reduction factor into one parameter that controls both width and stiffness reductions.  
  – Different buckling factors kσ reflect the change in curvature of the stress–mode shape for highly slender (negative ψ) versus moderately slender (positive or near-zero ψ) plate elements.  

This table thus allows a design engineer to split an outstand element into two parts—one at full thickness and one at reduced thickness—and to assign an appropriate plate buckling coefficient, all without resorting to more involved finite-width integration or iterative effective-width procedures.

sections: 10 Special considerations for purlins, liner trays and sheetings

content:
The table reproduced (Table E.1) characterizes the geometric limits under which the “simplified design method” may be used for cold-formed purlins (C-, Z- and Σ-profiles) in accordance with clauses 5.1 and 5.2 of the standard.  It applies only when the following preconditions are met: the cross-section dimensions fall within specified ranges; the purlins are horizontally and rotationally restrained by trapezoidal sheeting satisfying the given restraint equations; and the spans and loading are uniform.  The coordinate axes y and z are taken parallel to, and at right angles with, the plane of the top flange.  

Column descriptions  
– “purlins”: two schematic icons, one showing a generic C- or Z-section (upper row), and the other a Σ-section (lower row).  These diagrams indicate the dimensions b (flange width), c (lip or return width), and h (overall depth), all measured in the planes defined by y and z.  
– “t [mm]”: the nominal thickness of the steel sheet, in millimetres.  
– “b/t”: the ratio of flange width to material thickness.  Controls flange slenderness.  
– “h/t”: the ratio of overall profile depth to thickness.  Controls web slenderness.  
– “h/b”: the ratio of overall profile depth to flange width.  Indicates relative squatness or depth.  
– “c/t”: the ratio of lip (or return) width to thickness.  Controls lip slenderness.  
– “b/c”: the ratio of flange width to lip width.  Indicates lip aspect ratio.  
– “L/h”: the ratio of span to profile depth.  Controls overall flexural slenderness of the beam.  

Limiting values (identical for both profile types)  
– t ≥ 1,25 mm  
– b/t ≤ 55  
– h/t ≤ 160  
– h/b ≤ 3,43  
– c/t ≤ 20  
– b/c ≤ 4,0  
– L/h ≥ 15  

Interpretation and use  
1. If all seven geometric ratios lie within these bounds, the purlin may be designed using the simplified method of Annex E rather than the full elastic or inelastic buckling calculations of Sections 5.1 and 5.2.  
2. Values outside any of these limits require a more rigorous check, including verification of local, distortional and lateral‐torsional buckling per the general rules.  
3. Although these criteria are conservative, they ensure that local instability modes will not govern and that the simplified method remains safe and economical for standard trapezoidal-sheet‐restrained systems.

sections: 10 Special considerations for purlins, liner trays and sheetings

content:
The input is Table E.2 from Annex E of NS-EN 1993-1-3 (with Norwegian National Annex), which supplies numerical coefficients a₁ and a₂ to be used in equation (E.5) for calculating the lateral-torsional buckling reduction factor χ_LT of cold-formed purlins braced by trapezoidal sheeting.  Equation (E.5) has the general form  
  χ_LT = 1 / [ a₁ + a₂·(λ_LT)² ]  
where λ_LT is the appropriate non-dimensional slenderness for lateral-torsional buckling.  Table E.2 distinguishes three purlin cross-section families (Z-, C- and Σ-purlins) and lists four discrete sets of (a₁, a₂) pairs for each family.  A detailed breakdown follows.

1. Table structure  
 • Three groups of columns, one for each purlin family: “Z-purlins,” “C-purlins” and “Σ-purlins.”  
 • Within each group there are two sub-columns: a₁ and a₂.  
 • Four data rows (implicitly numbered 1 through 4) give the coefficient pairs.  

2. Coefficient values by row and purlin type  
Row 1  
 – Z-purlins: a₁ = 1.0, a₂ = 0  
 – C-purlins: a₁ = 1.1, a₂ = 0.002  
 – Σ-purlins: a₁ = 1.1, a₂ = 0.002  

Row 2  
 – Z-purlins: a₁ = 1.3, a₂ = 0  
 – C-purlins: a₁ = 3.5, a₂ = 0.050  
 – Σ-purlins: a₁ = 1.9, a₂ = 0.020  

Row 3  
 – Z-purlins: a₁ = 1.0, a₂ = 0  
 – C-purlins: a₁ = 1.6, a₂ = 0.020  
 – Σ-purlins: a₁ = 1.6, a₂ = 0.020  

Row 4  
 – Z-purlins: a₁ = 1.4, a₂ = 0.010  
 – C-purlins: a₁ = 2.7, a₂ = 0.040  
 – Σ-purlins: a₁ = 1.0, a₂ = 0  

3. Design context and usage  
 • Annex E presents an alternative to the standard effective-width method for horizontally continuous C-, Z- or Σ-section purlins of cold-formed steel, restrained laterally and torsionally by cladding.  
 • The values in Table E.2 are valid under the assumptions that spans and loading are uniform, trapezoidal sheeting provides the necessary horizontal and rotational restraint (see equations (10.1a) and E.6–E.9), and no axial force N_Ed is applied.  
 • For a given purlin family and its corresponding slenderness λ_LT, one selects the matching row of coefficients and computes χ_LT via (E.5).  The resulting χ_LT is then used in (E.6) or (E.7) to verify M_Ed ≤ χ_LT·M_pl,Rd.  

4. Typical ranges and trends  
 – Z-purlins: a₁ varies between 1.0 and 1.4; a₂ is zero in three cases and small (0.010) in one.  
 – C-purlins: a₁ ranges widely (1.1 to 3.5) with a₂ from 0.002 up to 0.050.  
 – Σ-purlins: a₁ from 1.0 to 1.9; a₂ from 0 up to 0.020.  
 – Higher a₂ values increase the sensitivity of χ_LT to slenderness (quadratic in λ_LT).  

By capturing this table’s structure and numerical content, one can index the four coefficient sets per purlin family and readily retrieve the appropriate a₁, a₂ pair when assembling a RAG-vector entry for lateral-torsional buckling design of cold-formed purlins.

content:
The table shown at the end of the National Annex serves as an index that links each “nationally determined parameter” (NDP) in EN 1993-1-3:2006 to  
a) the clause in the Eurocode where the choice arises,  
b) any related Eurocode clauses that depend on that choice, and  
c) the location in the National Annex (NA) where the Norwegian provision or guidance is given.  

Structure of the table  
– Four columns:  
  1. NDP reference in EN 1993-1-3 requiring national choice (e.g. “2(3)P”).  
  2. The primary Eurocode clause where the parameter appears.  
  3. Other Eurocode clause(s) that apply or cross-refer once the choice is made.  
  4. The clause in the Norwegian National Annex where the value, factor or additional rule is specified.  

– Five rows, each mapping one NDP:  

Row 1  
• NDP: 2(3)P – partial factor for ultimate limit-state verifications (γMi).  
• Eurocode clause where choice appears: 8.3(5) – design resistances of mechanical fasteners.  
• Dependent clause: 8.4(5) – design of spot welds.  
• National Annex: A.1(1) – no further testing rules (i.e. the recommended γMi is adopted unchanged).  

Row 2  
• NDP: 2(5) – partial factor for serviceability limit-state verifications (γS).  
• Eurocode clause: 8.3(13), Table 8.1 – shear resistance of blind rivets.  
• Dependent clause: 8.5.1(4) – design of lap welds.  
• National Annex: A.1(1) – again, no additional national choices beyond the core standard.  

Row 3  
• NDP: 3.1(3) – permitted steel grades and any reduction factor for strip thickness ≥ 600 mm.  
• Eurocode clause: 8.3(13), Table 8.2 – shear/tension resistance of self-tapping screws.  
• Dependent clause: 9(2) – design assisted by testing.  
• National Annex: A.6.4(4) – definition of the resistance adjustment coefficient μR for calibrating test results.  

Row 4  
• NDP: 3.2.4(1) – core thickness ranges for products (tcor limits).  
• Eurocode clause: 8.3(13), Table 8.3 – cartridge-fired pins.  
• Dependent clause: 10.1.1(1) – testing of sheeting used to restrain beams.  
• National Annex: E(1) – informative Annex E method for cold-formed purlins.  

Row 5  
• NDP: 5.3(4) – geometric imperfection e0/L for buckling verifications.  
• Eurocode clause: 8.3(13), Table 8.4 – pull-through resistance of bolts in tension.  
• Dependent clause: 10.1.4.2(1) – determination/use of reduction factors for lateral-torsional buckling.  
• National Annex: (none specified) – the standard recommendation is applied without change.  

Purpose and Use  
– By cross-referencing in this way, a designer can quickly see which partial factors, thickness limits or imperfection values must be adopted (or may be modified) for use in Norway, and exactly where in the NA to find the national value or rule.  
– Where the NA column is blank or points back to the core text (A.1(1)), the Eurocode’s recommended value is taken as is; where a specific NA clause is given, the national provision must be used.

 (1) This annex A gives appropriate standardized testing and evaluation procedures for a number of tests that are required in design.
 NOTE 1: In the field of cold-formed members and sheeting, many standard products are commonly used for which design by calculation might not lead to economical solutions, so it is frequently desirable to use design assisted by testing.
 NOTE 2: The National Annex may give further information on testing.

 (2) This annex covers:
 - tests on profiled sheets and liner trays, see A.2;
 - tests on cold-formed members, see A.3;

 (1) Although these test procedures are presented in terms of profiled sheets, similar test procedures based on the same principles may also be used for liner trays and other types of sheeting (e.g. sheeting mentioned in EN 508).
 (2) Loading may be applied through air bags or in a vacuum chamber or by steel or timber cross beams arranged to approximate uniformly distributed loading.
 (3) To prevent spreading of corrugations, transverse ties or other appropriate test accessories such as timber blocks may be applied to the test specimen. Some examples are given in figure A.1.
 (4) For uplift tests, the test set-up should realistically simulate the behaviour of the sheeting under practical conditions. The type of connections between the sheet and the supports should be the same as in the connections to be used in practice.
 (5) To give the results a wide range of applicability, hinged and roller supports should preferably be used, to avoid any influence of rotational restraint at the supports on the test results.
 (6) It should be ensured that the direction of the loading remains perpendicular to the initial plane of the sheet throughout the test procedure.
 (7) To eliminate the deformations of the supports, the deflections at both ends of the test specimen should also be measured.
 (8) The test result should be taken as the maximum value of the loading applied to the specimen either coincident with failure or immediately prior to failure as appropriate.

 (1) Each test specimen should be similar in all respects to the component or structure that it represents.
 (2) The supporting devices used for tests should preferably provide end conditions that closely reproduce those supplied by the connections to be used in service. Where this cannot be achieved, less favourable end conditions that decrease the load carrying capacity or increase the flexibility should be used, as relevant.
 (3) The devices used to apply the test loads should reproduce the way that the loads would be applied in service. It should be ensured that they do not offer more resistance to transverse deformations of the cross- section than would be available in the event of an overload in service. It should also be ensured that they do not localize the applied forces onto the lines of greatest resistance.
 (4) If the given load combination includes forces on more than one line of action, each increment of the test loading should be applied proportionately to each of these forces.
 (5) At each stage of the loading, the displacements or strains should be measured at one or more principal locations on the structure. Readings of displacements or strains should not be taken until the structure has completely stabilized after a load increment.
 (6) Failure of a test specimen should be considered to have occurred in any of the following cases:
 - at collapse or fracture;
 - if a crack begins to spread in a vital part of the specimen;
 - if the displacement is excessive.
 (7) The test result should be taken as the maximum value of the loading applied to the specimen either coincident with failure or immediately prior to failure as appropriate.
 (8) The accuracy of all measurements should be compatible with the magnitude of the measurement concerned and should in any case not exceed ± 1% of the value to be determined. The following magnitudes (in clause (9)) must also be fulfilled.
 (9) The measurements of the cross-sectional geometry of the test specimen should include:
 - the overall dimensions (width, depth and length) to an accuracy of ± 1,0 mm;
 - widths of plane elements of the cross-section to an accuracy of ± 1,0 mm;
 - radii of bends to an accuracy of ± 1,0 mm;
 - inclinations of plane elements to an accuracy of ± 2,0°;
 - angles between flat surfaces to an accuracy of ± 2,0°;
 - locations and dimensions of intermediate stiffeners to an accuracy of ± 1,0 mm;
 - the thickness of the material to an accuracy of ± 0,01 mm;
 - accuracy of all measurements of the cross-section has to be taken as equal to maximum 0,5 % of the nominal values.
 (10) All other relevant parameters should also be measured, such as:
 - locations of components relative to each other;
 - locations of fasteners;
 - the values of torques etc. used to tighten fasteners.
 (1) Stub column tests may be used to allow for the effects of local buckling in thin gauge cross-sections, by determining the value of the ratio βA = Aeff / Ag and the location of the effective centroidal axis.

 (3) The lengths of specimens with perforated cross-sections should include at least 5 pitches of the perforations, and should be such that the specimen is cut to length midway between two perforations.
 (4) In the case of a cross-section with edge or intermediate stiffeners, it should be ensured that the length of the specimen is not less than the expected buckling lengths of the stiffeners.

The ball bearings should be located in line with the centroid of the calculated effective cross-section. If the calculated location of this effective centroid proves not to be correct, it may be adjusted within the test series.

 (1) This acceptance test may be used as a non-destructive test to confirm the structural performance of a structure or portion of a structure.
 (2) The test load for an acceptance test should be taken as equal to the sum of:
 - 1,0 × (the actual self-weight present during the test);
 - 1,15 × (the remainder of the permanent load);
 - 1,25 × (the variable loads).
 but need not be taken as more than the mean of the total ultimate limit state design load and the total serviceability limit state design load for the characteristic (rare) load combination.
 (3) Before carrying out the acceptance test, preliminary bedding down loading (not exceeding the characteristic values of the loads) may optionally be applied, and then removed.
 (4) The structure should first be loaded up to a load equal to the total characteristic load. Under this load it should demonstrate substantially elastic behaviour. On removal of this load the residual deflection should not exceed 20% of the maximum recorded. If these criteria are not satisfied this part of the test procedure should be repeat. In this repeat load cycle, the structure should demonstrate substantially linear behaviour up to the characteristic load and the residual deflection should not exceed 10% of the maximum recorded.
 (5) During the acceptance test, the loads should be applied in a number of regular increments at regular time intervals and the principal deflections should be measured at each stage. When the deflections show significant non-linearity, the load increments should be reduced.
 (6) On the attainment of the acceptance test load, the load should be maintained for being no changes between a set of adjacent readings and deflection measurements should be taken to establish whether the structure is subject to any time-dependent deformations, such as deformations of fasteners or deformations arising from creep in the zinc layer.
 (7) Unloading should be completed in regular decrements, with deflection readings taken at each stage.
 (8) The structure should prove capable of sustaining the acceptance test load, and there should be no significant local distortion or defects likely to render the structure unserviceable after the test.
 (1) This strength test may be used to confirm the calculated load carrying capacity of a structure or portion of a structure. Where a number of similar items are to be constructed to a common design and one or more prototypes have been submitted to and met all the requirements of this strength test, the others may be accepted without further testing provided that they are similar in all relevant respects to the prototypes.
 (2) Before carrying out a strength test the specimen should first pass the acceptance test detailed in A.4.1.
 (3) The load should then be increased in increments up to the strength test load and the principal deflections should be measured at each stage. The strength test load should be maintained for at least one hour and deflection measurements should be taken to establish whether the structure is subject to creep.
 (4) Unloading should be completed in regular decrements with deflection readings taken at each stage.
 (5) The total test load (including self-weight) for a strength test Fstr should be determined from the total design load FEd specified for ultimate limit state verifications by calculation, using:

 structure, or portion of a structure, due to the effects of variation in the material yield strength, local buckling, overall buckling and any other relevant parameters or considerations.
 (7) Where a realistic assessment of the load carrying capacity of the structure, or portion of a structure, may be made using the provisions of this Part 1-3 of EN 1993 for design by calculation, or another proven method of analysis that takes account of all buckling effects, the load adjustment coefficient μF may be taken as equal to the ratio of (the value of the assessed load carrying capacity based on the averaged basic yield strength fym ) compared to (the corresponding value based on the nominal basic yield strength fyb ).

 NS-EN 1993-1-3:2006 allows the determination of national provisions in some of the clauses of the standard, often referred to as nationally determined parameters (NDP). This National Annex specifies the provisions that shall be applied when using NS-EN 1993-1-3:2006 for structural design in Norway.
 National choices are permitted in connection with the following numbered provisions in NS-EN 1993-1-3:2006:
 All provisions in this annex have the prefix "NA" to indicate that the provisions are a part of this National Annex.
